books.title: Ships of Discovery
books.art_why: Ancient and historical ships from eras before photography existed.

pages.text: Egypt AFRICA Nile River Early Years The oldest record of sea travel comes from Egypt. More than 6,000 years ago, Egyptians took to the water. They built boats by carving out the trunks of trees. But the Egyptians were not the only people to make boats from trees. Many other cultures that looked for ways to cross the water also carved boats from trees. These were sturdy boats, but they couldn’t carry very much.
pages.brief: On the bank of the Nile River in ancient Egypt, people hollow out a fallen tree trunk to make a simple boat. A finished dugout rests on the water nearby, showing the oldest recorded sea travel.

pages.text: Over time, people wanted to move larger things over waterways. They wanted to build boats to carry many people. They also wanted to be able to carry food, animals, and other items to trade. Canoes made from oak trees were good boats for crossing a lake or going down a river. However, they didn’t work as well for carrying large things. Imagine trying to row a canoe across a lake with six sheep crammed around you. The space just wasn’t big enough. Humans have always been driven to improve things. So it was natural that long ago people looked for ways to build bigger, faster, and safer boats. People also realized that they needed better boats to explore places far from their homeland.
pages.brief: A rower struggles in a small oak canoe on a lake, six sheep packed tightly around them. The canoe sits low in the water, making clear that there is little room for people, food, animals, or trade goods on a long river journey.

pages.text: The next step in boat building was using wooden beams to make a frame. The frame was then covered with wooden planks or bark from trees. Some cultures even used animal skins stretched over the frame. These boats were bigger and more streamlined and able to hold more cargo. The Egyptians were the first to cover a wooden frame with long, flat pieces of wood to create a hull, the outer shell of a boat. Some of their boats were as long as 21.3 meters (70 ft). The Egyptians were also the first to use sails. Sails reduced the need for people to row the boats. Some larger boats used both rowers and sails.
pages.brief: Egyptian boat builders cover a wooden beam frame with long flat planks to form a hull. A long Egyptian boat with a sail and rowers moves on the Nile. Other frame boats covered with bark or animal skins rest on the shore.

pages.text: Greek ship Soon, the Greeks and other peoples around the Mediterranean Sea were building large boats powered by sails. About 3,000 years ago, sailing ships were built with two masts, each one carrying a sail. The addition of a second mast made ships easier to steer and also made them much faster. Five hundred years later, the Greeks developed a ship with four sails. Some of the fastest ships at the time were built for battle. Some warships had as many as three levels of rowers on each side. These larger ships also allowed people to travel to and explore distant places. During this period, exploration and trade moved beyond the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: In a Mediterranean harbor, Greek sailors work a ship with two masts and two sails. Beside it, a long warship shows three levels of rowers on each side, while other sailing ships move out toward open water and distant coasts.

pages.text: The Polynesians In the South Pacific, groups of Pacific Island peoples were building boats that could sail in the open ocean. Over 3,500 years ago, these people were traveling east, well beyond the islands where they lived. They also explored areas off the Asian mainland. These Polynesian sailors built a boat that was an early version of the modern catamaran. They took two canoes and connected them using large wooden poles. A deck was then built to span the poles. These boats were usually about 15 to 18 meters (50–60 ft) long. The central deck held masts for sails and had enough space for several people and their supplies during a long voyage. Polynesian catamaran.
pages.brief: Polynesian sailors launch a catamaran made from two long canoes joined by wooden poles. A broad deck spans the poles, holding masts, sails, supplies, and several people. The craft sits on the open South Pacific, ready for a long voyage between islands.

pages.text: These early boats provided a means of safe travel from one island to another. The Polynesians settled each new island they discovered. By the beginning of the year 1000 ce, they lived on nearly every island they could find in the Pacific Ocean. Their new homes included Hawaii, New Zealand, and Rapa Nui (Easter Island). The Polynesians were skilled sailors. They became so familiar with the ocean that they could tell their location by the size and shape of the waves. They could easily travel great distances by going from island to island. The Polynesians grew to accept sea travel as a way of life. PACIFIC OCEAN ASIA Hawaiian Islands Easter AUSTRALIA Island New Zealand Routes of Polynesian expansion.
pages.brief: Polynesian sailors guide a canoe across the Pacific Ocean, reading the size and shape of waves. In the distance lie several islands, including Hawaii, New Zealand, and Rapa Nui. Families and supplies are aboard as the voyagers settle each new island they discover.

pages.text: The Vikings More than 1,300 years ago, a group of people in another part of the world began to build larger boats. These people were the Vikings. They lived in the northern part of Europe. The Vikings were well known as warriors and conquerors, and they were accustomed to traveling over water. By the year 700, they were sailing boats that were better than any others on the ocean. The boats they built, called knarrs (kuh- NARS), were used mostly for trading. These boats were up to 16.5 meters (54 ft) long and 4.5 meters (15 ft) wide. Because they were flat bottomed, the knarr boats could carry heavy loads. They were also stable and could travel safely across the open ocean. Vikings were willing to travel into the unknown to conquer new lands. They were the first Europeans to visit North America.
pages.brief: Viking traders load heavy cargo onto a broad, flat-bottomed knarr in northern Europe. The sturdy wooden ship rests low in the water, ready to cross the open ocean. In the background, Viking people prepare for a voyage into unknown lands.

pages.text: Vikings also built warships known as longships. It often was difficult to tell if a longship was coming or going because it looked the same in the front and in the back. Using this design, Viking attackers could easily change direction. Longships were able to travel as fast as 15 knots. A knot is a way to measure speed on water. Some of the larger longships carried as many as 200 warriors. The combination of large, speedy, easy- to-handle ships and a fierce fighting spirit made the Vikings tough to defeat. The Vikings ruled the ocean for nearly three centuries.
pages.brief: A Viking longship speeds across the sea, its front and back shaped alike so attackers can change direction quickly. Rows of warriors fill the deck, oars bite the water, and a sail catches the wind. The sleek warship shows the speed and power that made Vikings hard to defeat.

pages.text: Age of Discovery Until the 1400s, most sailors still kept close to their home waters. But with the coming of the Age of Discovery, things changed dramatically. Every European sailing country wanted to find new lands. The race was on, and the Americas were the prize. Shipbuilders had to find ways to build faster and safer ships. In the 1400s and 1500s, sea explorers used small, sturdy ships known as caravels. These ships had three masts to carry sails. This design made the ships fast and easy to steer. Caravels had square sails on the front and the middle masts and a triangular-shaped sail on the back mast. Consider the Conquered What impact did these discoveries have on the people already living in these places? Too often, the impact was a tragic one. Christopher Columbus, Hernan Cortes, and other Europeans who led these expeditions often exploited both the land and people they found. Their motive was usually greed. Before long, ships would also be used to carry people across oceans and enslave them far from their homes.
pages.brief: A caravel with three masts sails toward a distant coast during the Age of Discovery. On shore, local families watch the approaching European ship, hinting at the tragic impact explorers could bring. The ship’s square and triangular sails fill with wind.

pages.text: Christopher Columbus sailed three of these ships. The largest was 27.4 meters (90 ft) long and 9.1 meters (30 ft) wide. Compared to modern ocean liners and cargo ships, caravels were tiny. But even though they were quite small, the explorer Ferdinand Magellan set out to sail five caravels around the world with a crew of 260 sailors. Almost three years after they began the trip, one of Magellan’s ships and eighteen of the original crew members made it around the world. Magellan was not one of the survivors. He was killed somewhere in the Philippine Islands.
pages.brief: Three small caravels sail on the open ocean, led by Christopher Columbus’s largest ship. Far across the water, another fleet of caravels presses onward around the world. On a distant Philippine shore, rough waves and a lonely coastline suggest the voyage’s dangers.

pages.text: The Chinese While European explorers were sailing the world, the Chinese had also taken to the sea in another part of the world. They were skilled sailors. Their most famous explorer, Zheng He, traveled in a fleet of sixty-two ships that were much larger than European ships. His largest ship was so big that it could have held all three of Columbus’s ships on its deck. This huge ship was 121 meters (400 ft) long and 45.7 meters (150 ft) wide. In addition to the sixty-two main trading ships, more than a hundred smaller support boats were in the fleet. ASIA China PACIFIC AFRICA OCEAN INDIAN OCEAN AUSTRALIA Route of Chinese exploration and trading.
pages.brief: Zheng He’s enormous Chinese flagship towers over the water, surrounded by a fleet of sixty-two trading ships and many smaller support boats. The fleet sails from China toward Africa, with crowded decks and many sails, showing the scale of Chinese exploration and trade.

pages.text: Chinese junk These Chinese explorers sailed all the way to Africa to trade. However, war with their Asian neighbors caused the Chinese to turn their attention away from exploration. Do You Know? Christopher Columbus’s entire crew was about 90 sailors on three ships. The Chinese explorer Zheng He had more than 162 ships and 30,000 sailors on one of his voyages.
pages.brief: A large Chinese junk with wide sails carries traders along the coast of Africa. In the background, Chinese officials look back toward Asia, where war with neighboring lands is turning their attention away from exploration. The ship’s wide deck is stacked with trade goods.

pages.text: Later Years As sea exploration continued, the Spanish led the way. By the 1500s, European ship designs had improved. The newest ships, called galleons, were larger, faster, and more comfortable. These vessels were as long as 42.7 meters (140 ft), but were still small compared to the Chinese ships. Many of them had nice, comfortable living quarters. Galleons were capable of serving both as trading vessels and warships. Because of their size, galleons were able to carry many cannons on board, making them dangerous in battle.
pages.brief: A Spanish galleon sails on the open sea, larger and more comfortable than earlier ships. Its long hull carries comfortable living quarters and rows of cannons along the side. The heavily armed vessel could serve as both a trading ship and a warship.

pages.text: In the late 1700s, British captain James Cook undertook some of the greatest explorations of his time. On his first ship, Endeavour, Cook sailed around the world. His ship was only 32 meters (105 ft) in length. It was smaller than many other ships and had a shallow hold, sitting only 4.3 meters (14 ft) deep when fully loaded. Cook was an and a great sailor who also knew how to keep his crew healthy. He made them eat such as limes and cabbages, to remain free from disease. Endeavour Until Cook’s time, up to one-half of the crew on a long voyage would die of scurvy or other diseases. Cook knew his success as an explorer depended on keeping his crew healthy.
pages.brief: British captain James Cook’s ship Endeavour sails on a long voyage, its hull small and shallow in the water. On deck, sailors eat limes and cabbages to stay healthy. Cook stands among his crew, showing how careful food and leadership helped prevent disease on the journey.

pages.text: Conclusion By the middle of the 1800s, sailors had explored and mapped most of the world’s coasts. As people settled farther from their homelands, better ships were needed to move people and supplies great distances. Fast ships called clipper ships carried people across oceans in a matter of days. Some of these ships had as many as thirty- five sails. In only a few years, however, the steam engine would replace wind power, ending the age of sailing ships. When we look back at some of the ships used by early explorers, we have to admire the skill of the people who designed those ships of discovery. Setting sail into the unknown helped create the world we know today.
pages.brief: A fast clipper ship races across the ocean under many sails, its tall masts crowded with canvas. In the distance, an early steam-powered vessel hints at the coming end of the sailing age. Sailors and designers look back with admiration at the skill that created these ships of discovery.

books.title: Living in Deserts
books.art_why: Modern Bedouin, O'odham and Mongolian people and desert places exist today and the book itself shows photographs, old and new.

pages.text: Bedouin friends stop for a picture in the Sahara in Morocco.
pages.brief: A group of Bedouin friends in traditional robes stand close together on the sand in the Sahara in Morocco, pausing to have their picture taken. Behind them stretch rolling orange dunes under a bright desert sky, with no buildings or plants in sight.

pages.text: All deserts have something in common. Compared with the rest of the world, deserts are arid places. They usually get less than 25.4 centimeters (10 in.) of rain or snow each year. Deserts tend to have dry soil and not much plant life. Although some deserts can get very cold, most deserts are sunny and hot. Palm trees near an oasis in the Sahara in Egypt (top left); flowers in sand dunes in Australia (bottom left); running water in the Sonoran Desert (top right); the world’s largest salt flat, in Bolivia (bottom right)
pages.brief: Four desert scenes: palm trees standing near an oasis in the Sahara in Egypt, small flowers blooming among red sand dunes in Australia, water running through the Sonoran Desert, and the wide pale cracked expanse of the world's largest salt flat in Bolivia under the sun.

pages.text: Children run together in India’s Thar Desert. Five of the seven continents have hot deserts. Some deserts are small, but others are huge. Let’s take off and jet around the world. We will learn about some of the world’s deserts and the people who have called them home for thousands of years. People who live in the desert survive by adapting to their surroundings. They find food, water, and shelter, as in any other place on Earth. For people who live in desert areas, though, the desert isn’t just about getting by. The desert is so much more than that. It is home and a way of life.
pages.brief: Children run together across the sand of India's Thar Desert, laughing and spread out in a loose group as they race along. Low dunes and dry scrub surround them, the sun is high, and the pale sandy ground stretches away in every direction.

pages.text: The Tohono O’odham and the Sonoran Desert The Sonoran Desert stretches for 310,800 square kilometers (120,000 sq. mi.) across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Months may pass without any rain. Summer days can reach 49º Celsius (120ºF). Winter nights can dip below freezing, however. It rains more in the Sonoran Desert than in any other desert in the world! The Tohono O’odham (toe-HOE-noh OH-eh-dom) are Indigenous people who live in the Sonoran Desert. Tohono O’odham means “desert people.” The Sonoran Desert California New Arizona Mexico PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico NORTH NORTH AMERICA AMERICA More than 2,500 native plants grow in the Sonoran Desert, more than in any other desert in the world.
pages.brief: The Sonoran Desert stretches across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, a hot, dry land of sandy ground and rocky slopes. Tall saguaro cacti and hundreds of other green native plants stand across the landscape, and summer heat shimmers over the open desert.

pages.text: For hundreds of years, people from Europe and the United States have taken land that the O’odham lived on for thousands of years. Today, the land where many O’odham live is divided among four groups. One is the Tohono O’odham Nation. The others are the O’odham people at the Gila River Indian Community, the Ak-Chin Indian Community, and the Salt River (Pima Maricopa) Indian Community. All four groups speak the O’odham language, but there are differences from tribe to tribe. O’odham people live in towns and cities, and on reservations. Francine Jose shows baskets made by her family long ago.
pages.brief: Francine Jose, an O'odham woman, stands holding and showing coiled baskets woven by her family long ago. The baskets are patterned and tightly made, and she displays them carefully in front of her so they can be seen clearly.

pages.text: Over time, as more of their land was taken, the O’odham began to lead more modern lives. However, the O’odham people fought to keep their traditions over the years. Most O’odham include aspects of their traditions in their modern lives, such as farming, cooking traditional recipes, and basketmaking. Saguaro Fruit Harvesting The saguaro (suh-WAR-oh) cactus is an important part of O’odham culture. Each spring, beautiful flowers bloom on the cactus. Large red fruit then ripens in mid-June. The O’odham harvest the fruit from the tops of the giant cacti, which can reach upwards of 22 meters (75 ft.), using special tools. They turn the fruit into wine for their New Year ceremony in early July. An O’odham woman harvests saguaro fruit around 1907 (left). Today, O’odham still use traditional tools to harvest the fruit (right).
pages.brief: Two scenes of saguaro fruit harvesting: on one side an O'odham woman in 1907 reaches high with a long special tool to pull ripe red fruit from the top of a giant cactus; on the other, O'odham people today use the same traditional tools on tall blooming cacti.

pages.text: Bedouin children prepare to race their camels. Bedouin children prepare to race their camels. The Bedouin and the Sahara The Sahara stretches across northern Africa for 8.6 million square kilometers (3.3 million sq. mi). It is very hot and dry in the Sahara. Bedouin (BED-oo-in) people live in the Sahara and beyond. Because little rain falls in the Sahara, Bedouin have traditionally been nomadic. The Sahara Desert Morocco Tunisia Western Sahara Algeria Libya Egypt Mauritania Mali Niger Chad Sudan EUROPE EUROPE ATLANTIC AFRICA OCEAN In some parts of the Sahara, it rains less than AFRICA AFRICA 25 millimeters (1 in.) per year!
pages.brief: Bedouin children in the Sahara prepare to race their camels, standing beside the tall animals on open sandy ground in northern Africa. The children wear light clothing suited to the heat, and the saddled camels wait with flat desert and pale sky stretching behind them.

pages.text: Homes in this Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara have walls made out of dried plants (top). The inside of this Bedouin home in Oman is colorful (bottom). Bedouin are animal herders who roam the desert during the rainy winter. Traditionally, they moved from oasis to oasis and also dug wells for water. Bedouin returned with their herds to farmland during the dry summer.
pages.brief: Homes in a Bedouin village in Egypt's Sahara have walls made of dried plants, standing on sandy ground. Inside another Bedouin home in Oman, the walls and furnishings are brightly colored. Outside, Bedouin herders lead their animals across the desert, moving from oasis to oasis and digging wells.

pages.text: Umm Sayhoun is a Bedouin village in Jordan. Traditional Bedouin homes were low, black, portable tents, called bayts, made out of goat hair or sheep’s wool. Bayts protect people from the sun, wind, and blowing sand. For the past have been taking over the land where Bedouin have lived for thousands of years. Many Bedouin are no longer nomadic. Instead, they live in houses and apartments in A Bedouin mother smiles with her son villages and cities. inside their home in Oman.
pages.brief: In Umm Sayhoun, a Bedouin village in Jordan, low black tents called bayts, woven from goat hair and sheep's wool, stand on the desert ground beside simple village buildings. In Oman, a Bedouin mother smiles with her son inside their colorful home, the two sitting close together.

pages.text: The Gobi Desert ASIA ASIA INDIAN OCEAN Mongolia China The Gobi is called a rain shadow desert. Mountains block rainy weather that would have let plants grow there. Mongolian Nomads of the Gobi The Gobi stretches for 1.3 million square kilometers (500,000 sq. mi.) from southern Mongolia to in Asia. Mongolian nomads live in the Gobi. Traditionally, the Gobi’s sand dunes and rocky mountains in cold, sheep, goats, cattle, A Mongolian woman herds her animals and camels. in the Gobi.
pages.brief: The Gobi stretches from southern Mongolia into China, a cold, dry land of sand dunes and rocky mountains. Mountains block the rainy weather, so few plants grow. A Mongolian woman herds her animals across the open desert, with sheep, goats, cattle and camels spread out around her.

pages.text: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. Traditionally, home in the Gobi was a round tent or yurt covered in felt, called a ger. Inside, people were kept safe from cold nights and other weather. Fewer and fewer Mongolian nomads are left today. Harsh winters killed the herds of thousands of families. Changes in government also made life difficult for herders. Over the past thirty years, almost half a million nomads moved to the capital of Mongolia to look for work and food. Many brought their gers with them.
pages.brief: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family's ger in the Gobi, a round tent covered in felt that keeps people safe from cold nights and harsh weather. The white ger sits on open desert ground, and the boy runs across the dry land with mountains in the distance.

pages.text: A Way of Life Each desert has different challenges, but the Indigenous peoples who live there have always found their own solutions. In the past, people who lived in the desert relied only on what they could find around them. Today, much has changed, and many people lead modern lives in the desert. However, some continue to live as their ancestors once did, and many continue to celebrate the traditions of their desert communities. Life in the desert is as demanding as it is rewarding. The people who make the desert their home have deep respect for their surroundings. They use its offerings while also honoring its power and beauty. A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates.
pages.brief: A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates, the tall animal stepping past modern buildings. People and cars pass by on the paved road, showing how city life and old desert traditions now share the same space in the hot sunshine.

books.title: Australia
books.art_why: Mixed historical and modern content; keyword check indicates drawing.

pages.text: Australia.
pages.brief: A panoramic Australian scene introduces the country with sunlit coast, dry inland plains, native animals, distant city shapes, and a great rock formation. Different regions blend together to suggest the broad topics of land, people, history, wildlife, and travel.

pages.text: Tirhatuan Wetlands Conservation Reserve in Melbourne, Australia The Land Australia covers 7,692,024 square kilometers (2,969,907 sq. mi.) of land. The Indian Ocean borders Australia on the west and south. The Pacific Ocean surrounds the northern and eastern edges. Australia has three main areas: the Western Plateau, the Central Lowlands, and the Eastern Highlands. The Western Plateau covers over half of Australia. It is a flat, dry desert area with hot weather. Scientists have found the world’s oldest rocks in the Western Plateau. Dry grasslands are found in the Central Lowlands. There, it is hot all year during the day but can be very cold at night. The Great Dividing Range is part of the Eastern Highlands. It is home to rivers, valleys, and Australia’s highest mountains.
pages.brief: A wide view of Australia shows the flat, dry Western Plateau with ancient rocks, the dry grasslands of the Central Lowlands, and the Great Dividing Range with rivers, valleys, and high mountains. Ocean edges surround the land, with the Tirhatuan Wetlands in Melbourne in the foreground.

pages.text: Some of Australia’s habitats include desert, grasslands, rainforests, and heathlands. Heathland areas are usually coastal, with low plants covering the ground. Northern Australia has a tropical climate, while the southeastern and southwestern areas are mostly mild. The middle of the country is mainly desert. Most areas in Australia have very few people living in them. Today, around ninety percent of Australians live in cities, mainly along the coasts. In Australia, most cities are located long distances from one another. Canberra is Australia’s capital city. Sydney is its largest city, with a population of more than five million.
pages.brief: A coastal Australian city with more than five million people has dense neighborhoods beside the sea, while inland stretches of desert, grasslands, rainforest, and low coastal heathland spread across the country. A separate capital city sits far away, with long empty distances between settlements.

pages.text: Australia’s huge, dry inland area is known as the Outback, and few people live there. The Outback has enormous deserts and some mountainous regions. The landscape seems to stretch on forever. Rain may not fall there for years at a time. “Towns” in the Outback are typically made up of just a few buildings and are spread far apart. Some residents of the Outback live and work on enormous ranches called stations. Other people work in mining and oil production. Do You Know? Australia has over twenty thousand species of plants and animals. Eucalyptus, or gum trees, are Australia’s most common tree. Eucalyptus tree.
pages.brief: The dry Outback stretches to the horizon with desert, rocky mountains, and a tiny cluster of a few buildings far apart. A huge ranch station and distant mining or oil work show how some people live and work there. A eucalyptus tree stands in the foreground among open land.

pages.text: The People Thousands of years ago, Australia was home to many Indigenous peoples. Some think that around one million Indigenous peoples lived in Australia, while others think the number is lower. After the British colonized the continent, it was changed forever. Today, Australia is a nation with more than 25 million inhabitants. In 2020, around 91 percent of Australians were white and 7 percent were Asian. Less than 3 percent were Indigenous peoples. Different groups of Indigenous peoples speak more than 250 different languages.
pages.brief: A contemporary Australian crowd includes Indigenous people and people of different backgrounds, reflecting a nation of more than twenty-five million. A small group speaks together, suggesting the many Indigenous languages, while modern city life and older community scenes appear behind them.

pages.text: History Two distinct groups are considered Indigenous Australians—Aboriginal peoples from the mainland of Australia and Torres Strait Islanders. After fifty thousand years of living in Australia, the lives of Indigenous peoples came to a stark halt in the seventeenth century. Europeans began to explore and colonize their land. The British saw Australia as a way to solve the problem of overcrowding in British prisons. In 1788, a settlement arrived in Australia from England with around 759 prisoners (568 men and 191 women). The settlement also had 200 soldiers and 40 wives and children of the soldiers. They lived in tents and ate native animals as well as food sent from England. A commander places the British flag in Sydney.
pages.brief: A 1788 British settlement camp in Sydney shows tents, soldiers, wives, children, and prisoners newly arrived from England. A commander plants the British flag near the shore, while people gather around native animals and supplies brought from England.

pages.text: Before the British colonized the land, Indigenous people belonging to more than 500 different groups lived in Australia. They had their own distinct languages and cultures. Between 1788 and 1798, about 90 percent of Australia’s Indigenous population was killed. Some died during violent encounters with the British and others from diseases brought by the colonizers. Indigenous peoples continually fought for their lands. They kept their cultures, languages, and traditions. By 1901, the population of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had dropped to about 117,000. However, it has since risen to around pre-colonization numbers. The Stolen Generation Between 1910 and the 1970s, the Australian government took tens of thousands of children from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families. The children were adopted by white Australians and were forced to stay away from their indigenous cultures and traditions. The impact on these children, known as the “Stolen Generation,” is far-reaching. Indigenous people still struggle to recover from the terrible experience. Members of the Stolen Generation gathered when the Australian Prime Minister apologized to Indigenous Australians in 2008.
pages.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people stand together as families and communities, holding onto culture and language. A somber background suggests loss and struggle, while Stolen Generation members gather to hear an Australian Prime Minister apologize in 2008.

pages.text: Wildlife Australia’s history also affected its wildlife population. As cities have expanded, natural areas have grown smaller. This is making habitats and food scarce for some animals. The continent’s isolation and harsh conditions make it an ideal home for some animals. Animals found nowhere else on Earth live in Australia. Many of Australia’s marsupials, such as kangaroos and wallabies. These animals give birth to tiny babies that must live in a pouch or pocket on its mother’s body to continue to develop. Most marsupials disappeared long ago on other continents This baby kangaroo, or joey, is around four weeks old. (South America still has some). But Australia’s isolation allowed many types of marsupials to thrive. Scientists aren’t exactly sure why.
pages.brief: A mother kangaroo stands in a dry Australian landscape with a tiny four-week-old joey in her pouch. Around her are open natural areas near the edge of a growing city, where habitat and food are becoming scarce. Wallabies appear in the distance.

pages.text: The platypus is an animal unique to Australia. It has four legs, fur, and beady eyes. It also has a tail like a beaver’s, a duck’s bill, and webbed feet. Adult males have venomous spurs on their back ankles. A platypus uses its beak to Although a platypus is a hunt along the sea floor. mammal, females lay eggs. One of Australia’s most extraordinary places is the Great Barrier Reef, which is located off the coast of northeastern Australia. It is the largest coral reef system in the world. Over 1,500 types of fish, 2,000 kinds of coral, and other sea creatures, sea plants, and birds live there. Climate change, fishing, coastal construction, and pollutants are all major threats to the reef. Many people are working to save the Great Barrier Reef. Coral Bleaching When reef water gets too warm due to climate change, coral react by casting out the algae that live on them. Then the coral change color to all white and Bleached coral are likely to die, but they can still survive. begin to starve.
pages.brief: A platypus swims along a sea floor with its duck-like bill, webbed feet, and beaver-like tail. Beyond it, the Great Barrier Reef teems with fish and coral, including pale bleached coral among colorful reef life, as warming water and pollution threaten the habitat.

pages.text: Punamii-unpuu (Mitchell Falls) Things to Do The Sun is usually shining in Australia. Many Australians like to go to the beach and spend time out on the water. Some typical activities include swimming, surfing, snorkeling, scuba diving, and boating. Australia’s largest bay is Shark Bay. It is on the western part of the island and home to an incredible array of wildlife. The western area’s Kimberley region has breathtaking gorges, rocky shores, waterfalls, rivers, and beaches. Bondi Beach, in the southeast near Sydney, is one of the world’s most famous beaches.
pages.brief: People swim, surf, snorkel, scuba dive, and boat in bright sunshine along Australian beaches and clear water. Shark Bay and the Kimberley region show wildlife, gorges, rocky shores, waterfalls, and rivers, while Bondi Beach near Sydney has sand and waves. Mitchell Falls cascades in the wild.

pages.text: Uluru A three- or four-day train journey across the entire continent takes visitors through Australia’s different habitats. They can witness breathtaking sights, such as the rocky peaks and gorges of the Flinders Ranges in the Outback. Trips to explore the Outback never disappoint. Visitors hike, discover wildlife, and swim in wild water holes. Uluru, the world’s largest monolith, or single rock, is a sacred site of the Anangu peoples. It is located about two hundred miles west of Alice Springs, in a region called Red Centre. Sydney is an important destination in Australia. Visitors enjoy the city’s harbor and the Sydney Harbor Bridge, the largest steel arch bridge in the world. They also take in the beauty of one of the most famous modern buildings, the Sydney The Sydney Opera House has millions of Opera House. roof tiles.
pages.brief: A long train crosses Australia's varied habitats toward the Outback, where travelers hike and swim in wild water holes near rocky peaks and gorges. Uluru rises as a huge single rock in Red Centre, while in Sydney visitors view the harbor, the steel arch Harbour Bridge, and the Opera House with many roof tiles.

pages.text: Down Under Australia’s isolated location has allowed it to develop in many unique ways. The island is celebrated for its natural beauty. It is also known for being the world’s biggest island and the only country to also be a continent. Much about the land Down Under, from its unique creatures to its incredible landscapes, is unlike any place else on Earth. Many Australians enjoy surfing the waves along the country’s beautiful beaches.
pages.brief: A wide island-continent view of Australia shows unique creatures and striking landscapes, from beaches and waves to inland natural beauty. Surfers ride waves along the coast, while the surrounding ocean emphasizes the country's isolated place as the world's biggest island and only country that is also a continent.

books.title: Giant Insects
books.art_why: The book includes prehistoric giant insects and fossil-based reconstructions, so drawings suit it.

pages.text: Insects Are Everywhere! Every time you step outside your door, you probably look right past hundreds— even thousands—of insects. Scientists estimate that there are around ten quintillion (10,000,000,000,000,000,000) insects alive on Earth at any given time. So far, they have identified over 900,000 different insect species —about 80 percent of all the world’s animal species. They think that two to thirty million more species remain undiscovered or unidentified. It’s no surprise that many people are glad most insects are small. This wasn’t always the case, though. Hundreds of millions of years ago, before dinosaurs walked on Earth, insects were already buzzing around. Using fossil evidence, we know these insects were similar to modern insects—they each had three body sections, six legs, and often two sets of wings. They were a bit different in other ways, though. These critters were titans!
pages.brief: A person steps outside a door into a world full of insects. Hundreds or thousands of insects are all around, and a vast swarm suggests the ten quintillion insects alive on Earth. Ancient fossil-like insects with three body sections, six legs, and two sets of wings appear as titans.

pages.text: This drawing shows what a Meganeura might have looked like. The prehistoric Meganeura looked like a dragonfly. However, it had a wingspan of well over 30 inches (72.2 cm). Scientists think insects grew so huge partly because back then, Earth had more oxygen in the air. Over hundreds of millions of years, the amount of oxygen dropped from about 35 percent to today’s 21 percent. As a result, the insects adapted, evolved, and became smaller. A few insects, however, have remained the giants of their world. These beasts spark many people’s curiosity, and hopefully they’ll spark yours as well. You’re about to set out on a bug- hunting adventure around the world. You might call it a giant insect safari. You’ll pass by billions of smaller insects as you search the globe for these huge monsters. You’ll have the chance to see them with your own eyes and learn some fascinating details about them. Prepare your pack—you’re about to head out. Get ready to be surprised!
pages.brief: A prehistoric Meganeura dragonfly-like insect is shown with a wingspan well over 30 inches. The scene suggests Earth long ago had more oxygen, about 35 percent, before it dropped to today’s 21 percent, and insects evolved smaller. A bug-hunting safari is about to begin.

pages.text: Giant Darner Dragonfly: The Speed Demon Your journey starts by a slow-running stream in the southwestern United States. You hear the buzzing of a giant darner dragonfly. It uses its 5-inch (12.7 cm) wingspan to zip through the warm air at speeds of over 35 miles per hour (56.3 kph). These insects are so good at turning that they can completely shift direction in a split second. That’s when you catch a glimpse of one. This insect’s speed and ability to move come in handy as it hunts mosquitoes and other small insects. The dragonfly lands on your arm, but you have nothing to worry about. The giant darner dragonfly is harmless. You look at it just long enough to see the shimmering wings and black, blue, and green 5-inch (12.7 cm) body before it takes off again. As you walk through the tall grass on your way to your next destination, you see flashes of other dragonflies—giant darners and their smaller cousins. You wish them good hunting. Giant darner dragonflies live near streams like this one in the southwestern United States.
pages.brief: Beside a slow-running stream in the southwestern United States, a giant darner dragonfly zips through warm air at over 35 miles per hour. It lands on a person’s arm, showing shimmering wings and a black, blue, and green five-inch body, then takes off over tall grass.

pages.text: (12.7 cm) female giant darner dragonfly male giant darner dragonfly.
pages.brief: A female giant darner dragonfly and a male giant darner dragonfly are shown for comparison. Each insect is about 12.7 cm, and both are displayed so their bodies and wings can be seen. The two dragonflies are the focus of the page.

pages.text: Titan Beetle: The Pencil Breaker You’ve arrived in the steamy Amazon rainforest. It’s dark, and you can hear the tapping of rain on the leaves overhead. Something flies through the beam of your flashlight. At first, you think it’s a bird. You look closer and see it’s a 7-inch (17.8 cm) titan beetle—the biggest beetle in the world. This nocturnal creature was attracted to your light. As you watch it crawl its way through the dead leaves and dirt, you see the thick mandibles on its head. They’re strong enough to snap through a pencil. You’re tempted to find a stick to see if the titan beetle can break it. When you get near, though, it hisses and you back off. Like many beetles, this one has only a few weeks to live as an adult. It doesn’t have time to mess with you—it needs to find a mate. Though it can fly, it’s too heavy to take off from the ground. It uses its powerful, spiny legs to climb a tree and launch itself from a branch. You duck as it flies toward your face. Laughing, you continue your journey. titan beetle.
pages.brief: In the dark, steamy Amazon rainforest, a seven-inch titan beetle flies through a flashlight beam and crawls over dead leaves and dirt. Its thick mandibles look strong enough to snap a pencil. When approached, it hisses, then uses spiny legs to climb a tree.

pages.text: (17.8 cm) titan beetle taking off from a branch.
pages.brief: A titan beetle, about 17.8 cm long, is shown taking off from a branch. Its heavy body, spiny legs, and thick mandibles are visible as it launches into the air. The insect is caught in mid-flight after climbing to a high branch.

pages.text: Giant Water Bug: The Toe Biter The afternoon in Thailand is hot and humid. You stop to look into a clear, cool-looking freshwater pond. The idea of dangling your aching feet in the water is tempting, but then you see the giant water bug. You recognize it because this insect is found in bodies of fresh water all around the world. It’s about 5 inches (12.7 cm) long. It clings to an underwater plant while holding a minnow in its powerful front legs. It eats by using its strong jaws to force digestive juices into the struggling fish. Then it sucks out the remains. You see a few other giant water bugs. One must be a male, as it has round eggs stuck on its back. After mating, the female giant water bug glues the eggs there for safety until they hatch. Another giant water bug tries to catch a tadpole and misses. These bugs will eat pretty much anything they can overpower, including frogs, snakes, and even baby turtles. Their bite isn’t dangerous to people. Even so, you remember one of the local people saying they have one of the most painful bites of all insects. She said this just before taking a big, crunchy bite out of a grilled giant water bug. The water may look perfect, but you decide not to stop.
pages.brief: In a clear freshwater pond in hot, humid Thailand, a giant water bug clings to an underwater plant while holding a minnow in its powerful front legs. Another has round eggs glued to its back, and another misses a tadpole. The water looks tempting, but the person decides not to stop.

pages.text: N Where they live Putting the Bite on Insects: People have been eating insects since prehistoric times. Over 1,000 types are eaten in many parts of the world. They include water bugs, cockroaches, ants, dragonflies, and grasshoppers.
pages.brief: A world map shows where giant insects live. Nearby, a scene about eating insects explains that people have eaten over 1,000 types since prehistoric times, including water bugs, cockroaches, ants, dragonflies, and grasshoppers. The map and the eating-insect scene connect habitats with a long human practice.

pages.text: Goliath Beetle: The Heavyweight You’re back to walking through a rainforest. You’re not surprised since most of Earth’s insects live in rainforests. This time you’re in Central Africa. The rainy season has made the air feel heavy and thick. You hear a shuffling sound and look around. You find a female Goliath beetle using her head to dig in the soil. She’s making a safe place to lay her eggs. You take a moment to examine the patterns on her shell. Another beetle buzzes by and lands on a tree. It’s a male Goliath beetle. You can tell by the Y-shaped horns on the front of his head. He’s almost 5 inches (12.7 cm) long; the female is smaller. These beetles didn’t get their name for their length. They earned it for being the heaviest insects in the world. This male looks as if he will weigh in near the top of the range at over 3.5 ounces (100 g). The Goliath beetle is big but harmless. It eats the waste that falls to the forest floor. You think about getting the male to climb on your arm, but you change your mind when another male shows up. If you wait, the two males may fight each other using their impressive strength and horns. The smaller male flies away quickly, though. That means it’s time for you to move on, too.
pages.brief: In a Central African rainforest made heavy by the rainy season, a female Goliath beetle digs in the soil with her head to lay eggs. A male with Y-shaped horns lands on a tree; he is almost five inches long and very heavy. Another male arrives, then flies away.

pages.text: (12.7 cm) female Goliath beetle male Goliath beetle.
pages.brief: A female Goliath beetle and a male Goliath beetle are shown for comparison. The male has Y-shaped horns on the front of his head and is almost five inches long; the female is smaller. Both are among the heaviest insects in the world.

pages.text: African Driver Ant: The Ultimate Army You’re about to leave the African rainforest when you come upon what looks like a dark stream running across the ground. You move closer, but not too close. Millions of African driver ants march along the ground. In the center, you see the small worker ants. They aren’t much bigger than the ants you see at home. Along the edges, the soldier ants, each almost 1 inch (2.5 cm) long, form a wall. Their large mandibles point outward to protect the ants within. These insects are on the hunt, so they’re very dangerous. Though blind, they find their way easily using touch, smell, and chemical signals. Colonies can have over twenty-two million ants (the largest colonies of any insect on Earth), and they’re all hungry. Millions upon millions of ants swarm in search of food. They eat pretty much any animal they can overpower—including people. a column of African driver ants.
pages.brief: A dark stream of African driver ants marches across the ground. Small worker ants fill the center, while almost one-inch soldier ants form a wall along the edges with large mandibles pointing outward. Blind, they find their way by touch, smell, and chemical signals, hunting food in huge numbers.

pages.text: You decide to follow the ant column to see if you can find the nest. Against a large rock, you see a dark wall of movement. The ants have formed a temporary nest made out of living ants. As you watch, this nest begins to break up. They must have exhausted the food supply of the area. The ant column carries away food, millions of eggs, and the queen. At over 2 inches (5.1 cm) long, she is the largest ant on Earth. She can lay up to two million eggs each month. Despite the amazing sight, you start to notice a few ants crawling in your direction and decide it’s probably best to get out of there. 1 inch (2.5 cm) larger soldier ants protecting the smaller worker ants.
pages.brief: Against a large rock, a temporary nest made of living ants forms a dark wall of movement, then begins to break up. The column carries away food, millions of eggs, and the queen, who is over two inches long. A few ants crawl toward the visitor, who decides to leave.

pages.text: Madagascar Hissing Cockroach: The Noisy Pet It’s a lovely day in tropical Madagascar as you walk through the forest. You decide to sit down on a log beside a slow-moving stream. When you do, the log moves—and something hisses. You look down to see you’ve upset a colony of Madagascar hissing cockroaches. Each about 2 to 3 inches (5.1–7.6 cm) long with a shell of black and dark orange, they crawl back into the shade of the log. It’s too early for them to be out. At night, this colony would be crawling along the forest floor, looking for fallen fruit and dead plants. Unlike most species of cockroaches, the Madagascar hissing cockroach can’t fly, and the females give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. You reach out and touch a cockroach. It’s a male by the look of the long horns on its head. It hisses, pushing air out through small holes along its body, and then spits. You laugh because these insects are gentle and harmless. In fact, you have a friend who keeps a number of them as pets. You’d like to stay and watch, but it’s time to move on. Besides, you can watch your friend’s cockroaches. a pet Madagascar hissing cockroach.
pages.brief: On a log beside a slow-moving stream in tropical Madagascar, a colony of Madagascar hissing cockroaches crawls into the shade. One male, two to three inches long with black and dark orange shell and long head horns, hisses and spits when touched. The person laughs because these insects are gentle and harmless.

pages.text: Madagascar hissing cockroaches 2–3 inches (5.1–7.6 cm)
pages.brief: A colony of Madagascar hissing cockroaches is shown together, each about two to three inches long. Their black and dark orange shells and the long horns on the males’ heads are visible as they gather in the shade. The group is the focus of this close-up view.

pages.text: Wetapunga: The God of Ugly Things On Little Barrier Island off the coast of New Zealand, you hunt through the trees in search of the endangered wetapunga, or giant weta. These strange cricketlike insects’ name means “the god of ugly things” in the native Maori language. They have lived on these islands for millions of years. Over the last few hundred years, however, they have almost been wiped out due to the introduction of rats and mice, which eat the slow wetapunga. As the Sun begins to set, you find a wetapunga hiding among the leaves of a tree. It looks like a cross between a cricket and a grasshopper, only much bigger. The largest one ever found was about 4 inches (10.5 cm) long and 2.5 ounces (70.9 g). This one looks to be almost that big. It crawls slowly along the branch, nibbling on leaves. It will spend almost its entire life in trees. You could catch it if you wanted, as these insects can’t fly or jump, nor do they kick or bite. You decide to leave it alone since you have to run back to town. A group that is trying to bring back wetapungas plans to release a number of them into the wild, and you want to be there. giant weta.
pages.brief: On Little Barrier Island off New Zealand, a giant weta called the wetapunga hides among tree leaves as the sun sets. It looks like a much bigger cricket or grasshopper, about four inches long, and crawls slowly along a branch nibbling leaves. It cannot fly or jump.

pages.text: 4 inches (10.5 cm)
pages.brief: A female giant wetapunga is shown among leaves on Little Barrier Island, about four inches long. Its cricketlike body and long legs are visible as it clings to a branch. This endangered insect is slow and cannot fly or jump, so it relies on hiding in the trees.

pages.text: Queen Alexandra’s Birdwing Butterfly and Atlas Moth In a rope chair high above the ground, you look around at the forest canopy of Papua New Guinea. Lush green surrounds you for miles. Then you see a flash of blue rise up. It’s a male Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly flapping its shimmering blue-green and brown wings, which span almost 8 inches (20.3 cm). You look around for a female but don’t find one. Females would be larger, with a 12-inch (30.5 cm) wingspan of a lighter shade of brown. Other than in zoos, this rare species can only be found in the wild in Papua New Guinea, and only in the forest canopy. You watch in awe as the male feeds on a flower and flutters away. On your way down, something else catches your eye. You stop and pull yourself closer to a branch where an atlas moth sits, its wingspan 11 inches (27.9 cm) wide. The hooks on the ends of its wings remind you of this moth’s other name: the snake head moth. The Queen Alexandra’s butterfly lives up to three months or more and feeds regularly. However, the atlas moth lives only a few weeks and never feeds. You’ve seen this species before, as it’s fairly common throughout Southeast Asia, but it’s still an impressive sight.
pages.brief: High in the forest canopy of Papua New Guinea, a male Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly flashes blue-green and brown wings almost eight inches wide. A female would be larger and lighter brown. Lower down, an eleven-inch atlas moth rests on a branch, its wing hooks reminding the viewer of a snake’s head.

pages.text: (20.3 cm) male Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly 11 inches (27.9 cm) atlas moth.
pages.brief: A male Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly and an atlas moth are shown for comparison. The male butterfly has shimmering blue-green and brown wings spanning almost 20.3 cm. The atlas moth has an 11-inch wingspan, and hooks at the ends of its wings resemble a snake’s head.

pages.text: Chan’s Megastick: The Hidden Wonder Your final stop brings you to the London Natural History Museum. You’ve come to view the world’s longest insect: Chan’s megastick. One of only six found in the world so far (all of them in Borneo), this one is the longest. The whole insect, with its legs extended, stretches 22 inches (55.9 cm) under the glass. The body alone is 14 inches (35.6 cm) long. 22 inches (55.9 cm) It really does look like a plain old stick, which might explain why scientists didn’t discover it until 2008. Like other stick insects, this species is believed to hide within the forest canopy while it feeds on leaves. 14 inches (35.6 cm) Chan’s megastick.
pages.brief: At the London Natural History Museum, Chan’s megastick lies under glass as the world’s longest insect. With legs extended it stretches 22 inches, while its body alone is 14 inches long. It looks like a plain stick, which helps explain why scientists did not discover it until 2008.

pages.text: As you leave the museum, you begin to wonder how many new species of insects you passed during your travels. They might be heavier than a Goliath beetle, stronger than a titan beetle, or more dangerous than a colony of driver ants. The only way to know is to keep learning, keep exploring—and keep your eyes open. three-horned beetle peacock katydid with wings flared.
pages.brief: A hickory horn devil caterpillar, a giant stag beetle, a three-horned beetle, and a peacock katydid with wings flared are shown together. The visitor leaves the museum wondering how many new insect species were passed during the journey and decides to keep learning and exploring with eyes open.

books.title: Woods of Wonder
books.art_why: Real forests, trees, and animals shown exist today.

pages.text: Four Old-Growth Forests Around the World Sequoia and Kings Sequoia and Kings Great Smoky Great Smoky Shirakami-Sanchi, Shirakami-Sanchi, Canyon National Parks, Canyon National Parks, Mountains National Mountains National Japan Japan United States United States Park, United States Park, United States Western Caucasus, Western Caucasus, Russia Russia.
pages.brief: A wide view of four old-growth forests around the world: giant sequoias in California, autumn woods in the Great Smoky Mountains, a beech forest in Japan, and mountain conifers in the Western Caucasus of Russia.

pages.text: Some old-growth forests look like this scene. Others look very different. Some have only one type of tree, while others have many. Some have trees that seem to touch the sky. Others have trees shorter than a house. Because of all these differences, scientists do not have one definition for an old-growth forest. However, they have found some things that many old-growth forests share. Many scientists agree that an old- growth forest must be at least 150 years old. The trees within the forest might be many different ages, though, including large trees, both living and dead (or dying). Standing dead trees, called snags, and fallen trees provide food and shelter for different animals, plants, and fungi. Looking up in an old-growth forest can make you dizzy!
pages.brief: A dense old-growth forest with very tall trees, a standing dead snag, and a fallen log. Small animals, plants, and fungi find food and shelter around the log while young and old trees grow together beneath the high canopy.

pages.text: Forest Levels Canopy Tall trees like Understory Small trees Forest floor Grasses, mosses, ferns, and logs The forest’s canopy should have more than one layer. Fallen trees make holes in the canopy where young trees can find sunlight to grow. Old-growth forests are some of the most beautiful and interesting places on Earth. By studying and taking care of them, we can learn a lot.
pages.brief: A forest shown in layers: tall canopy trees overhead, smaller understory trees below, and a forest floor with grasses, mosses, ferns, and logs. A gap where a fallen tree opened the canopy lets sunlight reach young trees growing up toward the sky.

pages.text: United States Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California together cover more than 1,353 square miles (3,504 sq km). They hold more than 300 square miles (777 sq km) of old-growth forest, made up mostly of coniferous trees. Among these are giant only in California. These huge trees are among the oldest on Earth. They can live for more than 3,000 years. A giant as the General Sherman Tree is the largest tree in the world. The General Sherman Tree.
pages.brief: Giant sequoias stand in Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California, among a coniferous old-growth forest. One enormous sequoia, the General Sherman Tree, has a massive trunk and rises among the other huge, ancient trees.

pages.text: The Pacific fisher lives in the forest, under the thick canopy. It hunts birds and Fisher small mammals. Its favorite meal is porcupine. Because its habitat is limited to old-growth forests, some states are taking steps to protect it. Sequoia Redwood Sequoia vs. Redwood Giant redwoods and giant sequoias both grow in California. They have the same color bark. Both are huge, but they’re different. Giant redwoods are the tallest trees in the world. They can reach up to 378 feet (115 m)! Giant sequoias are the largest. At up to 40 feet (12 m) in diameter, a sequoia can grow almost twice as wide as a redwood. Redwoods grow best in fog. Sequoias need dry heat for their cones to open. Redwoods grow near sea level. Sequoias grow at 5,000 to 7,000 feet (1,524 to 2,134 m).
pages.brief: A Pacific fisher hunts under a thick forest canopy, near a bird, a small mammal, and a porcupine. In another California scene, a tall redwood rises in fog while a wide sequoia stands in dry mountain heat.

pages.text: Autumn is colorful in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Across the United States in North Carolina and Tennessee, Great Smoky Mountains National Park covers more than 800 square miles (2,072 sq km). Almost all of the park is forest. Old-growth forests only make up about a quarter of the park. Deciduous trees make up most of the old-growth forests in this area.
pages.brief: Autumn colors fill Great Smoky Mountains National Park, where North Carolina and Tennessee meet. Colorful deciduous trees cover the mountain slopes, with old-growth forest making up about a quarter of the nearly all-forest park.

pages.text: The endangered Northern flying squirrel Carolina northern flying squirrel makes its home here. These small mammals don’t really fly. They use skin attached to their front and back paws to glide. They mostly eat fungi but may also eat fruits and nuts. Without the old-growth forest, these animals would vanish. Tough, Not Tall Not all old-growth forests have towering trees. In some harsh places with wild and icy winds, pines, spruces, and other coniferous trees grow short and twisted. These trees are called Krummholz, a German word meaning “crooked wood.” They are only about 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, but don’t let their size fool you: Some are one thousand years old.
pages.brief: A Carolina northern flying squirrel glides between trees, skin flaps stretched between its front and back paws, near fungi, fruits, and nuts. On a harsh, icy slope, short twisted pines and spruces grow low, though some are a thousand years old.

pages.text: A Japanese beech tree reaches for the sun in Shirakami-Sanchi, Japan. Japan In the northern part of Japan is Shirakami- Sanchi. It’s one of the last old-growth forests in East Asia. Made up mostly of beech trees, the area covers just 65 square miles (170 sq km) of the mountains. Forests like this one once covered most of northern Japan, but people have cut many down.
pages.brief: A tall Japanese beech tree reaches for the sun in Shirakami-Sanchi, in northern Japan. Beech trees cover the mountain slopes of this last old-growth forest in East Asia, a small protected area where forests once spread across most of northern Japan.

pages.text: Shirakami-Sanchi has no trails or buildings, and animals in the area are protected. The forest is home to the Japanese serow. This goatlike animal is only found here and in two other small areas in Japan. More than 2,100 types of insects and 87 types of birds live in the forest. These include the black woodpecker, which is endangered in Japan. Japanese serow Black woodpeckers.
pages.brief: A goatlike Japanese serow stands among beech trees in a wild forest with no trails or buildings. A black woodpecker clings to a trunk, while many insects and birds live around this protected Shirakami-Sanchi forest.

pages.text: Fallen trees like this fir can nurse along other plants in this old-growth forest in the Caucasus of Russia. Russia Russia’s Western Caucasus area stretches about 1,062 square miles (2,750 sq km) from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains. The area has many different plants and animals. Coniferous trees make up most of the forests.
pages.brief: A fallen fir tree lies in an old-growth forest in Russia’s Western Caucasus, with young plants growing along its trunk. Coniferous trees cover the mountain slopes stretching from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains, where many plants and animals live.

pages.text: Snow leopards Different kinds of endangered animals make these forests their home. Some scientists think that a few endangered snow leopards live here. Scientists sometimes find signs of the large cats, such as paw prints and droppings. The endangered wisent has also been brought back into the forest. Wisents are European bison.
pages.brief: A snow leopard moves through the forest, leaving paw prints and droppings, while a wisent, a European bison, stands among the trees. Both are endangered animals that live in these Western Caucasus forests.

pages.text: Conclusion Old-growth forests often have very complex ecosystems. They may have been supporting life for hundreds or thousands of years. Governments, national parks, and other groups protect many of these places. However, other old-growth forests, both small and large, are in danger. Human actions can damage or destroy environments. Once gone, the beauty and that these old-growth forests hold may be lost forever. Laws prevent logging in some old-growth forests but not others. People continue to debate how much protection is enough.
pages.brief: A complex old-growth forest full of tall trees, fallen logs, plants, and animals stands beside an area where trees have been cut. People debate how much protection is enough, while laws stop logging in some old-growth forests but not others.

books.title: Owls Overhead
books.art_why: Owls exist today and real photographs can show them clearly.

pages.text: Boreal owlets.
pages.brief: Two boreal owlets perch quietly close together, one beside the other. Their round faces and dark eyes are visible, and their soft fluffy feathers blend into the surrounding shadows. No other creatures appear with them.

pages.text: Eyes for the Night Many of the adaptations that help owls survive also make them seem mysterious. For instance, most owls hunt at night. As a result, they don’t have to compete with daytime hunters such as eagles, hawks, and falcons. Like most birds, owls can’t move their eyes in their sockets. Instead, owls must turn their heads to track a moving object. Owls are able to rotate their heads almost all the way around—280 degrees. They can even turn their heads upside down. Northern hawk owl Burrowing owl.
pages.brief: An owl perches at night, hunting while eagles, hawks, and falcons are active by day elsewhere. The owl twists its head almost all the way around, even upside down, to track movement. A northern hawk owl and a burrowing owl are also shown.

pages.text: An owl’s pupils are small in bright light (top) and large in low light (bottom). Owls’ big eyes are an adaptation, too. These birds can’t see in total darkness. However, their pupils—the black circles in the center of their eyes—can grow large to let in more light. Their large pupils let them see better in low light than most animals. In fact, when light is low, tawny owls see as much as one hundred times better than humans.
pages.brief: Close views show an owl’s eye in bright light with small pupils and in low light with large pupils. The owl’s big eyes fill much of its face. A tawny owl is shown seeing in dim conditions, with its large pupils letting in more light than a human’s.

pages.text: The hairlike feathers on owls’ faces help them react to things they touch. Some owls even have these feathers on their feet! As good as their night vision is, owls can’t see things close to their faces. Instead, hairlike feathers work like feelers to help owls react to things they touch, sort of like a cat’s whiskers. Pellets! Owls can’t chew or grind their food. Instead, they often swallow small prey whole. They can’t digest the unwanted parts of the animals. Teeth, claws, and Owl pellet small bones, stuck together with bits of fur or feathers, end up in the gizzard. That’s a part of their stomach with strong muscles that roll those parts into small balls, called pellets. A few hours after they eat, owls cough up a pellet. Scientists look through the pellets to learn what owls eat.
pages.brief: An owl’s face shows hairlike feathers, and some of these feathers appear on its feet. The owl swallows a small prey animal whole. Later, a pellet made of teeth, claws, bones, fur, or feathers is coughed up, and a scientist examines it to learn what the owl ate.

pages.text: Owl skull Owls have very large ears, which are hidden under feathers. Some owls have thin skin Upper ear Lower ear that covers the ears’ openings. Even Better Ears To hunt, however, most owls rely on their hearing. Most owls have huge ears, with one higher than the other. The higher one hears sounds from above, while the lower one hears sounds from below. Their flat, round faces help funnel sounds to their ears. By moving the feathers around their faces, owls can send more sound to one ear or the other. Doing this helps them locate prey.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of an owl skull shows large ears hidden under feathers, with one ear higher than the other. The owl’s flat, round face funnels sound toward the ears. By moving facial feathers, the owl sends more sound to one ear and locates prey.

pages.text: Owls, such as this barn owl, often crush their prey with their strong feet and sharp talons. The grip of some owls can be ten times stronger than a human’s grip. Their hearing is so good that they can hear bugs in grass or mice in snow. In fact, owls have better hearing than any other group of birds. Great gray owls can hear a mouse hidden under 18 inches (46 cm) of snow. Once they’ve located their prey, they can dive under the snow to grab a meal. Barn owls can hear a mouse moving 90 feet (27 m) away and catch one in complete darkness. They have the best hearing of any animal ever tested.
pages.brief: A barn owl grips prey with strong feet and sharp talons. In snow, a great gray owl listens for a mouse hidden beneath 18 inches and dives down to grab it. Another owl hears a mouse moving 90 feet away in complete darkness.

pages.text: Silent Hunters Many animals that owls hunt also have excellent hearing. So if an owl wants to eat, it must attack by surprise. The soft feathers that cover owls’ bodies allow them to fly silently. A great horned owl will sit high on a tree branch, the time is right to attack. A skillful hunter, it feeds on many kinds of animals, even snakes. In Florida, one great horned owl tackled a 6-foot (2 m) indigo snake and won. It also eats birds, other owl species. In fact, many large owls eat small Great horned owls are excellent hunters. They can even catch another bird in flight. owls.
pages.brief: A great horned owl sits high on a tree branch, ready to attack by surprise. Its soft feathers let it fly silently. It catches another bird in flight and feeds on many animals, including snakes; in Florida, one tackles a 6-foot indigo snake and wins.

pages.text: Elf owl Snowy owl While most owls hunt only at night, snowy owls hunt mostly during the day. That’s because summer nights in the Arctic are so short. The tiny elf owl hunts during the day as well, feeding mostly on insects. The main diet for most owls, though, is small mammals—lots of them. A hungry great gray owl may eat 1,400 voles in a year. In its lifetime, a barn owl may eat 11,000 mice!
pages.brief: A snowy owl hunts in daylight under the Arctic summer sun, while a tiny elf owl also hunts by day for insects. A great gray owl is shown with many voles, and a barn owl with mice, showing the huge numbers owls eat over time.

pages.text: A barn owl lives up to its name by raising its young in a barn. Where Owls Live Some owls can live in many different habitats. The great horned owl lives in swamps, forests, prairies, mountains, and deserts. Barn owls live under bridges as well as in caves, empty houses, church towers—and barns, of course!
pages.brief: A barn owl raises its young in a barn. A great horned owl appears in several habitats: swamp, forest, prairie, mountain, and desert. Barn owls are shown living under a bridge, in a cave, in an empty house, in a church tower, and in a barn.

pages.text: An Owl’s Housekeeper Screech owls in Texas hunt snakes. However, they bring one kind of snake back to their nest alive: the blindsnake. They let it go inside the nest, where it eats the maggots that feed on the dead animals stored there. The a housekeeper! Burrowing owls can scare away other animals by making a sound like a rattlesnake’s. Some owls require a special habitat, though. Burrowing owls live mostly on the prairie and nest underground, using old burrows dug by mammals. When open spaces are hard to find, they move to cemeteries and golf courses, and even near airport runways.
pages.brief: In Texas, a screech owl brings a blindsnake back to its nest alive. The snake eats maggots on stored dead animals, acting as a housekeeper. A burrowing owl stands at an old mammal burrow on the prairie, and others appear in a cemetery, on a golf course, and near an airport runway.

pages.text: Spotted owls do not fly south for the winter. Spotted owls can only survive in old-growth forests. By 1994, 80 percent of their former habitat had been destroyed by logging. To protect the spotted owl, loggers cut down fewer trees, but barred owls have since taken over spotted owl habitat. Today, they outnumber spotted owls in the northwestern United States.
pages.brief: A spotted owl perches in an old-growth forest, staying through winter instead of flying south. Logging has destroyed much of its habitat. A barred owl appears nearby in the same northwestern forest, where barred owls now outnumber spotted owls.

pages.text: Owl Sounds Owls aren’t always silent, nor do they all hoot. They use different sounds to call a mate, warn of danger, or claim an area. Each species has its own calls that set it apart from other owls. A great horned owl can bark like a dog and meow like a cat. Barn owls don’t hoot—they scream. Their strange cry and ghostly appearance once made some people think of barn owls as bad luck. Photographers take pictures of a great gray owl, the largest species of owl in the world. Owls Are Out There It’s rare to see an owl, but they’re out there. If you’re in the country and want to spot one, try going out at dawn or dusk. Listen for their calls. If you stay out late enough, people might think you’re an owl—a night owl, that is.
pages.brief: A great horned owl calls with a doglike bark and a catlike meow. A barn owl opens its beak in a scream, looking ghostly. Photographers photograph a great gray owl, the largest owl species. At dawn or dusk in the country, a person listens for owl calls.

On August 20, fierce winds caused 165,000 acres to burn in just one day—a day that came to be known as Black Saturday. Firefighters fought the flames for nearly two months. pages.text: Costs of Fire Forest fires are often destructive and sometimes deadly. In the case of severe forest fires, superheated gases can reach 1,600°F (871°C). Blasts of heat have cracked boulders in half and melted chainsaws. Types of Fire There are three types of forest fires: ground fires, surface fires, and crown fires. A ground fire travels low to the ground and sometimes underneath it. It feeds on ground fuel and rarely shows a flame. You might walk right over it and not even know it’s there. A surface fire stays low but burns hotter, burning trees and brush. When it grows fierce enough, it turns into a crown fire. Crown fires are the big fires. They can travel 10 miles (16 km) per hour. Flames can reach up to 300 feet (91 m). A single forest fire can include all three types of fires.
pages.brief: A towering crown fire races through the tops of a pine forest, flames leaping high above the trees, while below it a low surface fire creeps through brush and a smoldering ground fire burns unseen in the duff, cracked boulders and a melted chainsaw nearby.

People and Fire Forest fires are nothing new, but attitudes toward them have changed over time. The Europeans who settled the West in the 1800s fought them at every turn. Until then, fires and forests had managed to find a balance. Nobody fought the wildfires, in part because nobody owned the forests. When Yellowstone became a national park in 1872 and for a long time after, both visitors and the people who ran the park continued to see fire as destructive. The early caretakers of national parks and forests thought that putting out fires was just good stewardship. In 1935, the U.S. Forest Service established a rule about putting out all fires the day after they started. This all sounded sensible at the time. After all, putting out fires protects the forest. Right?
