pages.text: For thousands of years, fire has been one of the forces that have shaped certain forests—not just lodgepole forests, but other kinds as well. Fire burns the forest here and there until it has cycled through the entire landscape. Burned areas become grassy meadows that eventually grow new trees. Together, these different areas create a system of food and shelter for many species. Different forests complete this cycle in different spans of time. One type of forest might take a thousand years, while another type may only take a hundred years. In these forests, many plant species are adapted to fire. The very trees that burned in Yellowstone offer a great example because some lodgepole pines need fire to reproduce. Fire allows the pinecones to open and release their seeds. Without fire, the cones just sit and wait. Within a month of Yellowstone’s 1988 monster fire, snow covered the park. When the snow melted the following spring, it watered the roots and seeds that had survived underground. Nutritious grasses sprouted from the charred earth, attracting elk and deer. Wildflowers bloomed the next spring and summer. As it turned out, the burned park wasn’t ruined after all.
pages.brief: Lodgepole pinecones open on a scorched branch and release seeds onto charred ground, while snow melts into the blackened soil, green grass sprouts, wildflowers bloom and elk and deer graze in the sunny new meadow.

pages.text: Fire removes undergrowth to allow light to reach the forest floor and foster the growth of new plants. Too Much Fuel Many people can find it hard to adapt to fire. Everyone knows fire is dangerous and can cause great damage. People’s view of the forest can vary greatly. Some may see the forest only as a source of wood, grass for cattle grazing, or a beautiful spot to pitch a tent—not as an ecosystem that sometimes needs to burn. Viewed that way, it seems only logical to put out forest fires. Yet not letting fires run their course can cause a problem for forests and people alike. Without fire, needles, brush, and logs build up over time. Once a fire does start, the built-up debris on the forest floor causes the fire to become more severe. Too much fuel can make a fire almost impossible to control.
pages.brief: Sunlight reaches the forest floor where fire has cleared away needles, brush and fallen logs, and fresh green shoots and small plants push up through the ash between the trunks of surviving trees.

pages.text: Many severe forest fires have burned across the West in recent years. While other factors, such as climate change, have also played a role, most forest experts agree that these severe fires are caused by too much fuel on the ground—and stamping out so many wildfires is to blame. Fighting fires is also expensive. Since 1960, the annual cost to federal, state, and local governments to fight wildfires has grown from less than $100 million to more than $3.3 billion. This huge expense takes money away from programs that clear trees and brush in high-risk areas— programs that would prevent, or at least reduce, the scope and severity of fires. Firefighters may spray a fire with water, do controlled burns, or clear plants to create a break in the fire.
pages.brief: Firefighters spray water onto a wall of flame in a western forest, others set a controlled burn along the ground, and a crew clears brush and small trees to leave an open break ahead of the fire.

pages.text: Too Many People So why not let some of these fires burn? In some remote places, that’s possible. The trouble is, there aren’t as many remote places as there once were because people keep moving in. Since 1990, areas near U.S. wildlands are being developed at a rate of 2 million acres per year. That’s about three acres per minute. Between 1990 and 2008, 10 million homes were built in U.S. wildlands near urban areas. Many are at high—or very high—risk of wildfire. It’s no surprise, then, that more homes are burning. In the 1960s, about 200 homes a year were lost to wildfires. By the 2000s, an average of 2,700 homes burned in wildfires each year. In California alone, wildfires destroy an average of 700 homes every year. That state spends $165 million each year on homes lost to or damaged by wildfire. California spends millions more trying to keep those homes from burning in the first place. Letting fires burn near these homes is risky. Yet we now know that it’s also risky if none of these fires are allowed to burn. A home in Santa Barbara, California, is threatened by an approaching wildfire in 2009.
pages.brief: A house in Santa Barbara, California, stands on a hillside with a wildfire approaching, flames and thick smoke on the ridge behind it, and a neighbourhood of homes spread out into the dry wildland below.

pages.text: Visitors to Yellowstone can witness the natural cycle of trees growing out of the ashes of the massive fire in 1988. Rethinking Fire When a wildfire burns, it’s hard to remember that something so destructive is also so productive. Yellowstone is living proof that it is. After the 1988 Yellowstone fire, dead gray stands of lodgepole pines covered the mountains for miles. Today, those trees’ seedlings form lush stands of young trees that grow taller every year. Someday, their offspring will do the same— thanks to fire. Wildfire serves a role in nature. People need to consider that role. In some cases, we might do well to stand back and let the fire do its work.
pages.brief: Visitors stand on a Yellowstone trail looking out over mountains where grey stands of dead lodgepole pines still rise, and among them lush young trees grow thick and tall from the soil of the old burn.

pages.text: Scientists still discover hundreds of new animal species every year. Animal Discoveries reveals some fascinating recently discovered species from locations around the world. The book also teaches students about valuing and protecting species new and old. Written by Karen Mockler.
pages.brief: A scientist stands in a remote habitat observing several different animals, with forest and ocean environments in the background. The scene suggests that hundreds of new animal species are discovered every year and that these species, old and new, are worth valuing and protecting.

pages.text: Monkey Mania In 2007, a new species of monkey was found in the forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The lesula has large eyes and is shy and quiet. The first one found by scientists was being kept as a pet. The Caquetá titi monkey lives in the Amazon jungle with about twenty other species of titi monkey. The Caquetá is known for its bushy red beard. It doesn’t have a white bar on its forehead as other titi monkeys do. Its babies purr like cats. Only around 250 Caquetá titi monkeys are alive today, meaning the species is endangered.
pages.brief: In a Congo forest, a shy lesula monkey with large eyes sits quietly, while nearby an Amazon jungle scene shows a Caquetá titi monkey with a bushy red beard and no white forehead bar. A tiny baby titi clings close, and the monkeys look endangered and few.

pages.text: Freaky, Fabulous Frogs The Matang narrow-mouthed frog is the size of a pea. It was discovered on Borneo, an island in Southeast Asia, in 2010. It turns out that scientists had seen these frogs before but thought they were the young of a different species. Then they heard the frogs calling. Since only adult frogs make calls, they realized that these tiny frogs must be full-grown.
pages.brief: On Borneo, a tiny Matang narrow-mouthed frog sits on a leaf, no bigger than a pea. Nearby, scientists listen as the little frog calls, realizing these frogs are full-grown adults rather than the young of another species.

pages.text: A herpetologist discovered the long-nosed tree frog in 2010 while exploring the Foja Mountains of New Guinea. The area is so remote that it has been called the “Lost World.” This tree frog is known for its long, unique nose. When the male frog calls, its nose points up like a spike. When the frog is done calling, its nose falls. No one knows why. The frog has another name: the Pinocchio frog. The herpetologist spotted it sitting on a bag of rice in his campsite.
pages.brief: In the remote Foja Mountains of New Guinea, a long-nosed tree frog sits on a bag of rice at a campsite. The male frog calls with its nose pointing up like a spike, then its nose falls when the call ends, while a herpetologist watches.

pages.text: Interesting Invertebrates Scientists estimate that vertebrates—animals with backbones—make up only 3 percent of all species. The remaining 97 percent of animal species known to scientists are invertebrates— animals without backbones. Sazima’s tarantula has a special beauty. Its dark blue body almost glows. This fantastic arachnid has an extremely limited habitat, only living high in the mountains of Brazil.
pages.brief: High in the mountains of Brazil, a Sazima’s tarantula rests on the ground, its dark blue body almost glowing. It represents invertebrates, animals without backbones, which make up nearly all animal species known to scientists, while vertebrates with backbones are only a small fraction.

pages.text: The “troll-haired” planthopper was discovered in 2013 in the rainforests of South America. It may not be good-looking, but at least it has good hair. The wild hair isn’t hair at all, but instead waxy secretions from the insect’s belly. When a predator attacks, the “hair” breaks off, and the planthopper can jump to safety. That’s what scientists think, anyway, but they aren’t sure.
pages.brief: In a South American rainforest, a troll-haired planthopper clings to a plant, its wild, waxy belly secretions looking like messy hair. A predator approaches, the strange “hair” breaks away, and the insect springs to safety, though scientists are not certain this is why.

pages.text: Underwater Wonders Scientists discovered the Gorgon’s head starfish in 2010 in the Atlantic Ocean, about half a mile (800 m) beneath the surface. The Gorgon’s head, a species of basket star, has five curly, branching arms that split off from its body. The five arms include as many as five thousand tips. The tips help it find food floating by in the water. It also uses its arms to walk along the ocean floor and to protect itself.
pages.brief: Deep in the Atlantic Ocean, a Gorgon’s head starfish rests on the seafloor. Its five curly, branching arms spread out with thousands of tiny tips to catch food floating by, and it uses those same arms to walk slowly along the bottom and protect itself.

pages.text: Since Earth’s oceans are so huge, large parts have yet to be explored. However, that’s not the reason it took until 2013 to discover the walking bamboo shark. Like most sharks, the walking bamboo shark is no threat to humans. It lives off the coast of Indonesia. Scientists discovered it because its coloration differs from that of other bamboo sharks. This new species is thought to reach about 30 inches (80 cm) in length. It uses its fins to push itself along the ocean floor in search of food. The wiggling movement makes it look as though the shark is walking.
pages.brief: Off the coast of Indonesia, a walking bamboo shark moves along the ocean floor, using its fins to push itself forward in a wiggling motion that looks like walking. The shark, about 30 inches long, searches for food and is no threat to humans.

pages.text: Hiding in Plain View In 2013, researchers discovered that for more than a hundred years, olinguitos (oh-lin-GEE- tohs) had been identified as the wrong species. These mammals, which look like teddy bears, leap through trees at night. The smallest member of the raccoon family, the olinguito can be found in Ecuador and Colombia. It is the first species of this type to be discovered in the Americas in thirty- five years. Mistaken Identity Humans may encounter an unidentified species for years while mistaking it for a familiar species. This often happens because the two species look the same, at least on the outside. These are called cryptic species. They are only found to be distinct when scientists study their genetic code. As DNA technology is used more and more, reports of distinct new species are on the rise.
pages.brief: In the forests of Ecuador and Colombia, a small olinguito that looks like a teddy bear leaps through trees at night. Researchers compare it with similar-looking animals, showing how a cryptic species can hide for years until scientists study its genetic code and find it is distinct.

pages.text: Finding new species of birds is almost as rare as finding new mammals. In 2009, researchers discovered the Cambodian tailorbird near the city of Phnom Penh. Tests showed that this tailorbird was a separate, new species. Besides studying its DNA and feathers, scientists studied its pretty song. While all tailorbirds warble, no two species sound quite the same. Sure enough, the song of the Cambodian tailorbird sets it apart from all the rest.
pages.brief: Near Phnom Penh, Cambodia, a small Cambodian tailorbird perches on a branch and sings its pretty, warbling song. Researchers study its feathers and DNA, showing that this bird is a separate new species because its song sounds different from every other tailorbird.

books.title: Mexico
books.art_why: The book is a country profile of real places, people, animals, and landforms, not a biography of a named famous person.

pages.text: A monument to war heroes greets visitors as they enter Chapultepec Park (bottom). The park includes history museums (top left) as well as lakes (top right). Mexico City, one of the oldest cities in North America, is the capital of Mexico. It sits in a basin surrounded by mountains and is home to more than nineteen million people. Mexico City contains many beautiful parks. Chapultepec (chah-pool-te-PEK) Park is the largest. It contains a zoo, gardens, fountains, museums, lakes, and forests.
pages.brief: A tall monument to war heroes greets visitors at the entrance to Chapultepec Park. Inside the park are history museums and lakes, along with gardens, fountains, forests, and a zoo. Beyond the park, Mexico City sits in a basin surrounded by mountains and is home to more than nineteen million people.

pages.text: People Thousands of years ago, Indigenous peoples lived on the land that is now Mexico and built amazing civilizations. Then, Spanish explorers came to Mexico in 1517. By 1521, the Spanish had colonized Mexico. As a result, about two thirds mestizos of modern Mexico’s people are (mes- TEE-zohz). This means they are the descendants of both Indigenous and European ancestors. The other third of the population consists of Indigenous peoples, Spanish descendants, and other people who have come to the country. Today, Mexico has a population of more than 120 million people. Most Mexicans speak Spanish. More people speak Spanish in Mexico than any other country in the world. Some people speak Indigenous languages. Most of the population lives in cities. More than three fourths of Mexico’s people live in cities.
pages.brief: A busy city street in Mexico is filled with many people of Indigenous and Spanish descent, including mestizos, descendants of both. Most Mexicans live in cities and speak Spanish. The scene recalls thousands of years ago, when Indigenous peoples built civilizations, and 1517, when Spanish explorers arrived; by 1521 Spain had colonized Mexico.

pages.text: Mexico is rich in natural resources such as oil and silver. It exports tons of coffee, sugar cane, and cotton throughout the world each year. The country is also famous for its art and artists. Painting, sculpture, and dance have a long and rich history in Mexico. Do You Know? Mexico is famous for its large paintings called murals. One of its most famous muralists was Diego Rivera. In this famous mural, he shows the Zapotec and the Mixtec, two Indigenous groups of ancient Mexico, at work making jewelry from gold and precious stones such as jade and turquoise. The mural, along with many others, is in the National Palace in Mexico City.
pages.brief: Inside the National Palace in Mexico City, Diego Rivera’s large mural shows Zapotec and Mixtec people at work making jewelry from gold, jade, and turquoise. Near the artwork are signs of Mexico’s natural resources and exports: oil, silver, coffee, sugar cane, and cotton.

pages.text: Mexico’s Landforms Sonoran Desert Copper Canyon Baja Chihuahuan Peninsula Desert Sierra Madre Oriental Mexican Mountains Gulf of California Plateau Gulf of Yucatán Mexico PACIFIC Peninsula Mexico OCEAN Mexico City Pico de Sierra Madre del Orizaba Sur Mountains Land Mexico has many mountain ranges, and some mountains are also volcanoes. The highest mountain is a volcano 5,700 meters (18,701 ft.) high named Pico de Orizaba (PEE-koh day OR- ee-SAH-bah). Mountains run along the west, east, and south. Mexico also has canyons that reach amazing depths. Copper Canyon in northern Mexico is known for being larger than the Grand Canyon. The center of the country is a plateau. The raised, flat land makes it ideal for building roads and towns. Most people live in this area.
pages.brief: Mexico’s landforms stretch across the country: mountain ranges run along the west, east, and south, and the volcano Pico de Orizaba rises highest. Copper Canyon cuts deep in the north, while a central plateau provides raised, flat land where many people live and where roads and towns are built.

pages.text: Two peninsulas, the Baja and the Yucatán, jut into the ocean. The Yucatán Peninsula is made of limestone that has dissolved away over thousands of years in some places. The result is spectacular caves, including underground caves filled with water called cenotes (sih-NOH-teez). The Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts stretch across northern Mexico. The Sonoran Desert has more types of plants than any desert in North America. Warm, wet rainforests cover parts of southeastern Mexico. These forests are home to many different types of plants and animals. Mexico’s coastal lowlands contain lagoons, marshes, and swamps. Past the eastern coast lies the Caribbean Sea. Mexico does not have many lakes and rivers, but one is very well known because it forms the border between Mexico and the United States. Mexicans call this river the Rio Bravo del Norte, which means “wild river of the north.” People of the United States call it the Rio Grande.
pages.brief: The Baja and Yucatán peninsulas jut into the ocean. In the Yucatán’s limestone, underground caves filled with water form cenotes. The Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts stretch across northern Mexico, while warm, wet rainforests cover parts of the southeast. Coastal lowlands hold lagoons, marshes, and swamps; the Rio Bravo del Norte forms the border with the United States.

pages.text: History The earliest people in Mexico peoples. One of the most well is the Mayan Visitors to Mexico can see El Castillo Maya built great (kahs-TEE-yoh), a pyramid built by the Mayan people long ago. and pyramids without the help of the wheel or animals. They also created beautiful works of art, studied the stars and planets, and developed a calendar. In the early 1300s, the Aztec people arrived in central Mexico. They built their capital city on an island in a lake. The Aztec were also known as the Mexica, and from that name comes the name Mexico. The site of the Aztec capital city, Tenochtitlán (tay-nohch-teet-LAHN), would become Mexico City. The Aztec built a huge empire. In 1519, the Spanish explorer Hernán Cortés arrived in the Aztec capital. Within two years, he and his followers had taken over the land and conquered the Aztec people.
pages.brief: Visitors stand before El Castillo, a pyramid built long ago by the Maya. In central Mexico, the Aztec built their capital city on an island in a lake; that site would become Mexico City. In 1519, Spanish explorer Hernán Cortés arrives in the Aztec capital.

pages.text: Pancho Villa (left) and Emiliano Zapata (right), were the leaders of the Mexican Revolution. In 1521, Mexico became a Spanish colony. It remained a colony until 1821, when the people fought and won a war to be free from Spanish rule. In the century that followed, many people were poor farmers who struggled to survive. Wealthy Europeans owned 95 percent of the land. Farmers and workers had few rights and little money. During the Mexican Revolution (1910–1920), the people rose up and changed the government. Mexico became a democracy, which helped to improve daily life for people who were poor. Today, Mexico is still a land of extremes. There are two main social classes, the rich and the poor, with a very small middle class.
pages.brief: Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata, leaders of the Mexican Revolution, stand with their followers. The revolution changed the government and helped poor farmers and workers. Mexico became a democracy, yet today the country still has rich and poor people and a very small middle class.

pages.text: Although the jaguar is active during the day, it hunts mainly at night. Animals Many different types of animals live in Mexico. The jaguar plays an important role in the stories, songs, and prayers of Mexico’s ancient Indigenous peoples. It lives mainly in the rainforests of Mexico. The largest of all the cat species in North America, it can measure about 2 meters (6 ft.) in length. It has black spots and a roar that sounds like a loud cough. Unlike many other cats, the jaguar likes to swim, play, and hunt in water. Its main source of food is the peccary, a small, wild member of the pig family. Sadly, the jaguar is in danger of extinction; however, many people are trying to save them.
pages.brief: A jaguar with black spots moves through a Mexican rainforest at night, hunting. It can swim and play in water, and its roar sounds like a loud cough. Its main food is the peccary, a small wild pig. The jaguar is in danger of extinction, though many people try to save it.

pages.text: The sacred bird of the ancient Maya and the Aztec, the quetzal (keht-SAHL) lives in the rainforests of Mexico. Like many types of birds, the male is brightly colored, and the female is plainer in appearance. The male’s head and chest are bright golden green. pages.brief: In the rainforest, a male quetzal displays bright golden-green, blue, red, and very long tail feathers to attract a mate, while a plainer female watches. In the mountains, a large, hairy red-knee tarantula with reddish-orange leg joints rests; its legs can detect vibrations, smells, and tastes.

pages.text: Mexico’s Copper Canyon is a popular tourist site, although it is difficult to reach. A train takes visitors through the area. Conclusion Mexico is a country of diversity. It has modern cities and ancient ruins. Deep canyons lie within high mountains. Dry deserts and wet rainforests cover the land. Its long history and natural beauty fascinate people around the globe. If you were to visit Mexico, what would you want to see first?
pages.brief: A train carries visitors through Copper Canyon, a popular tourist site that is difficult to reach. Around it, Mexico shows diversity: modern cities and ancient ruins, deep canyons within high mountains, dry deserts, and wet rainforests. The country’s long history and natural beauty fascinate people around the globe.

books.title: Brazil
books.art_why: Brazil is a real modern country with real places, people and wildlife.

pages.text: People wear colorful costumes and dance in parades during Carnaval, a holiday in Brazil.
pages.brief: People wearing colorful costumes dance together in a Carnaval parade in Brazil, moving through a festive street scene. Crowds watch the holiday celebration as dancers in bright outfits fill the parade route with color and movement.

pages.text: To the east of Brazil is the Atlantic Ocean. The country’s coastline is more than 7,400 kilometers (4,600 mi.) long. The capital of Brazil is Brasília (bruh-ZIL-yuh), which is located near the middle of the country. However, Brasília wasn’t always the capital. The larger city of Rio de Janeiro (REE-oh DAY zhuh- NAIR-oh), located on the east coast of the country, was the capital until 1960. The government decided to build a new capital city farther inland. Although it is still new, Brasília is growing quickly. More than two live and work there. Many people work for the government, since the city is Brazil’s political center. Brasília is filled with many modern buildings.
pages.brief: An aerial view of Brazil's long Atlantic coastline, with Rio de Janeiro on the east coast and Brasilia near the middle of the country. Modern government buildings fill Brasilia, where people work, showing the inland capital that replaced Rio de Janeiro in 1960.

pages.text: People More than two hundred million people live in Brazil, and eight out of every ten people live in cities. The country has several large cities, including São Paulo (SOW POW-low), the largest city in South America. Many people in Brazil work in service industries, such as construction, banking, education, and healthcare. Large hotels and restaurants line many of the country’s beaches, providing work for people living along the coast. Other Brazilians work in factories, making cars, airplanes, and steel. Many of these factories are located around São Paulo. In the countryside, people work in mining and farming. Brazil is a leading producer of minerals such as iron ore, tin, and even gold. Brazil’s farmers grow much of the world’s coffee on huge plantations. They also grow oranges, cassava, and soybeans. Some farmers raise hogs and chickens, and Brazil grows the most popular type of coffee, called Arabica. ranchers raise cattle.
pages.brief: A busy city scene in Sao Paulo with people working in construction, banking, education and healthcare, and factories making cars, airplanes and steel nearby. Along the coast, hotels and restaurants line beaches. In the countryside, farmers tend coffee, orange, cassava and soybean crops while ranchers raise cattle and hogs.

pages.text: Futebol Many Brazilians enjoy watching and playing soccer, which they call futebol (FOOT-bohl). Brazil has won the World Cup, the world’s largest soccer tournament, more than any other country. The country’s most famous known around the world. Pelé led his team to victory in the World Cup in 1958, Pelé 1962, and in 1970. Brazilians come from many different backgrounds. Some are descended from the Native peoples who first lived there. Others are descendants of people from Angola, the Congo, and other African countries, who were enslaved and brought to Brazil to work on plantations and in mines. Many others are descended from people who came to Brazil from far-away countries such as Portugal, Spain, Germany, and other places in Europe. In fact, Brazil was a colony of Portugal for three hundred years, and the main language in Brazil is Portuguese (POR-chuh-geez).
pages.brief: A crowded soccer stadium in Brazil, with players in bright uniforms competing in a futebol match and fans cheering. Nearby, a group of Brazilians from Native, African, European and other backgrounds stand together, reflecting the country's mixed heritage and Portuguese-speaking culture.

pages.text: Land Many rivers flow through Brazil, making the soil rich and good for growing crops. However, one river clearly stands out. The Amazon River is one of the widest and longest rivers in the world, flowing for at least 6,400 kilometers (4,000 mi.) through northern Brazil. Its waters feed the vast Amazon basin, The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth. which covers nearly half of Brazil and about 7 million square kilometers (3 million sq. mi.). The largest tropical rainforest in the world, the Amazon rainforest, is also located here. Brazil is so large that it includes five main regions. The landforms in each region are so different that they are like separate countries. The north and southeast regions include highlands. In the north, the Guiana highlands consist of steep mountains and deep valleys. In the southeast, hills and low mountain plateaus make up the Brazilian highlands.
pages.brief: The wide Amazon River flows through northern Brazil, surrounded by the vast Amazon rainforest and basin. In the north, the Guiana Highlands rise with steep mountains and deep valleys. In the southeast, the Brazilian Highlands show hills and low mountain plateaus, making Brazil's regions look very different.

pages.text: Brazil’s Landforms ATLANTIC Guiana Highlands OCEAN Amazon River Amazon Basin Brasília Brazilian Highlands Pantanal Wetlands PACIFIC Coastal OCEAN Lowlands ATLANTIC OCEAN Brazil’s long east coast makes up another region. It includes beautiful sandy beaches, which are some of the main attractions for tourists visiting the country. The Pantanal is located in central Brazil. It is one of the world’s largest freshwater wetlands and extends for thousands of miles around the tributaries of several different rivers.
pages.brief: Sandy beaches stretch along Brazil's long east coast, with tourists relaxing by the Atlantic Ocean. In central Brazil, the Pantanal wetlands spread for thousands of miles around tributaries of several rivers, while highlands, the Amazon basin and coastal lowlands appear across the country's varied landforms.

pages.text: History The first known people who lived in Brazil were Native peoples such as the Guarani and Yanomami. Different groups of Native peoples still live in the rainforests and along the banks of the Amazon River today. In the early sixteenth century, Portugal conquered Brazil. The Portuguese enslaved many Native people and forced them to work on huge sugarcane plantations. Later, they enslaved people in Africa and brought them to work on coffee plantations and in diamond and gold mines. In 1822, Brazil became an independent country ruled by an emperor. Slavery ended in 1888. In 1889, the emperor at the time was forced by the military to step down, and Brazil became a republic. In a republic, the people usually choose their leaders, but this didn’t always happen in Brazil. Instead, the people were often led by dictators. After much turmoil, the country became a democracy in 1985.
pages.brief: A historical scene shows Portuguese colonizers overseeing enslaved Native people on a sugarcane plantation and enslaved African people working in coffee, diamond and gold mines. In the foreground, Guarani and Yanomami people stand in the rainforest and along the Amazon River, representing Brazil's first known inhabitants and their ongoing presence.

pages.text: Rio de Janeiro has the largest Carnaval celebration in Brazil. It is held in a special building called the Sambadrome. Celebrations Many holidays in Brazil are religious in nature. Most Brazilians belong to the Catholic faith, a religion that was brought to Brazil by the Portuguese. However, because Brazilians come from many different backgrounds, religious customs of other groups—such as Native and African peoples—are also followed. Carnaval is the largest and most popular holiday in Brazil. It is a four-day celebration leading up to Lent, which is the forty-day period in which Catholics prepare for Easter. During Carnaval, people crowd into Brazil’s streets for parades and dancing. Many people wear elaborate costumes with masks and headdresses.
pages.brief: Inside the Sambadrome in Rio de Janeiro, crowds fill the special building for Brazil's largest Carnaval celebration. Dancers in elaborate costumes, masks and headdresses parade through the streets during the four-day holiday before Lent, while Catholic and other religious customs are reflected in the celebration.

pages.text: Animals Brazil is home to the widest variety of life on Earth. The Amazon rainforest provides a home to more animals —and plants—than any other environment in the world. Colorful birds such as the toucan (TOO-kan) live there, as well as jaguars and ocelots (OS-uh-lotz). Slow-moving sloths hang from trees, and giant anacondas slither along the forest floor. Many different types of monkeys swing from the trees. In the Amazon River, meat-eating fish called piranhas (pi-RAH-nuhz) hunt in groups of one hundred or more. Large manatees swim through the water.
pages.brief: In the Amazon rainforest, a toucan perches among colorful plants while a jaguar and an ocelot move through the trees. A sloth hangs from a branch, an anaconda slithers along the forest floor, and monkeys swing overhead. In the river, a group of piranhas hunts together and a large manatee swims through the water.

pages.text: Other parts of Brazil, such as the Pantanal wetlands, also include unique animals. Storks and herons build nests in the Pantanal’s trees. Colorful parrots, such as the blue and yellow macaw, fly overhead. Deer and jaguar roam the land. Giant anteaters also live in the Pantanal. Sadly, some animals in the Amazon rainforest and the Pantanal could disappear from Earth forever. Every year, trees are cut down for timber and to clear land for farming. As a result, animals like the jaguar and the golden lion tamarin, a type of monkey, are losing their habitat. Many organizations are working together with the Brazilian government to keep this from happening. golden lion tamarin.
pages.brief: In the Pantanal wetlands, storks and herons build nests in trees while blue and yellow macaws fly overhead. Deer, jaguars and giant anteaters roam the land. Nearby, trees are cut down for timber and farming, leaving a jaguar and a golden lion tamarin without habitat as organizations work with Brazil's government to protect them.

pages.text: The large city of Rio de Janeiro is known for its many beautiful beaches. Conclusion Brazil is a country filled with life. The Amazon rainforest teems with more living things than anywhere else on Earth. The people in the cities and countryside have vibrant celebrations unlike any other. From its land to its animals and people, the vast country of Brazil has many things to learn about and explore.
pages.brief: Rio de Janeiro's beautiful beaches stretch beside the large city, with people enjoying the shore. Beyond the city, the Amazon rainforest teems with living things, while people in cities and the countryside take part in vibrant celebrations. The vast country of Brazil opens up to its land, animals and people for learning and exploration.

pages.text: Paris and the Arc de Triomphe Eiffel Tower The Louvre The capital of France is Paris, a city known around the world for its beauty. Millions of people visit Paris each year to see its famous landmarks. These sites include the Eiffel (EYE-ful) Tower, Notre Dame (no-truh DAHM) Cathedral, and the Louvre (LOO-vruh) art museum. A monument called the Arc de Triomphe (ARK du tree-OHMF) stands over one of the city’s main streets, the Champs-Élysées (SHAHM-zay-lee-ZAY). More than ten million people live in Paris. The city is France’s center for both business and culture. Paris is also considered one of the fashion capitals of the world.
pages.brief: In Paris, the Eiffel Tower rises above the city. Notre Dame Cathedral and the Louvre art museum stand among busy streets. The Arc de Triomphe overlooks the Champs-Élysées, where visitors walk. Crowds of tourists move through the city, looking at famous landmarks and experiencing France's capital.

pages.text: Paris and other cities are filled with restaurants and hotels for the more than eighty-two million tourists who visit France. People More than sixty-six million people live in France. Most people live and work in its cities and towns. Tourism is the largest service industry in France. In fact, France is the most visited country in the world! Many people work in hotels, restaurants, and museums that welcome these millions of visitors. Many French people also work in factories that produce goods such as cars, aircraft, and clothing. Other factories make chemicals and process food. Some people work in mines, digging resources such as coal out of the ground.
pages.brief: In a French city, hotel and restaurant workers welcome tourists, while museum staff guide visitors. Nearby, factory workers build cars, aircraft, and clothing, and other factories process food and chemicals. In a mine, a worker digs coal from the ground. Many people live and work in these cities and towns across France.

pages.text: Workers harvest grapes from a vineyard in France. The grapes are used mainly to make wine. More than half of the country’s land is used for farming. French farmers grow wheat, grain, sugar beets, and potatoes. Others raise animals, including cattle, hogs, and sheep. Some also grow grapes in vineyards. The majority of people in France are Roman Catholic. Others are Protestant, Muslim, or Jewish. The country’s main language is French, although people speak different dialects depending on the area.
pages.brief: Workers harvest grapes in a vineyard. Beyond the vines, farmland stretches across rolling land, with fields of wheat, grain, sugar beets, and potatoes. Cattle, hogs, and sheep graze nearby. The scene shows the farming life that uses more than half of France's land.

France is mostly covered in flat plains and low, rolling hills. It also has high plateaus. The Seine (SEN) River runs through Paris, and, along with smaller rivers, drains the Paris Basin. The country is also known for its beautiful beaches, especially along the Mediterranean Sea.

The Seine River runs through Paris, while the Loire Valley and Paris Basin spread nearby. Mountains rise in the French Alps, Pyrenees, Jura, and Massif Central. Beaches line the Mediterranean Sea and the coast of Corsica.

pages.text: Mont Blanc, located in the French Alps, is the tallest mountain in western Europe. France has five different mountain ranges. The most well-known ranges are the French Alps and the Pyrenees (PEER-uh-neez). The French Alps are part of the larger Alps mountain range that runs through many countries. The French Alps lie along the border between France, Switzerland, and Italy. The Pyrenees lie along the border between France and Spain. A large plateau spreads across southern France. It has ancient mountains and volcanoes, which are no longer active, as well as deep river gorges. France also includes some islands. The largest is Corsica, which is located off the southern coast in the Mediterranean Sea.
pages.brief: Mont Blanc rises in the French Alps, the tallest mountain in western Europe. The Alps run along the borders with Switzerland and Italy, while the Pyrenees lie between France and Spain. In southern France, a large plateau holds ancient mountains, inactive volcanoes, and deep river gorges. Corsica, France's largest island, sits in the Mediterranean Sea.

pages.text: History France has a long history. Experts believe that early humans lived in what is now France nearly two million years ago. More than two thousand years ago, France was known as Gaul. The people who lived there were called Celts. Around 50 bc, the Roman Empire took over Gaul and ruled Early humans painted animals the land for about five on the walls of a cave in hundred years. Lascaux (la-SKOH), France. Around ad 400, German tribes took Gaul from the Romans. These German people were called Franks. They named the land Francia, which is how France got its name. For the next thousand years, powerful kings ruled France. In 800, a French king named Charlemagne (SHAR-luh-mayn) became leader of the Holy Roman Empire. This empire included France and parts of what are now Belgium, Germany, and Italy. However, the empire fell apart after Charlemagne died in 814.
pages.brief: Early humans painted animals on cave walls at Lascaux. Long ago, Celts lived in Gaul before the Roman Empire ruled the land for about five hundred years. Later, German tribes called Franks took over and named the land Francia. A king named Charlemagne became leader of the Holy Roman Empire in 800.

pages.text: From about 1066 to 1453, many wars were fought over the land of France. Most of these wars were between France and England. This began in 1066 when a group from Normandy, a region in France, invaded England. Another famous war between the two countries began in 1337 and lasted until 1453. Today it is known as the Hundred Years War. For hundreds of years, France was ruled by kings, many of whom treated the people poorly. In 1789, the people rebelled against the king and the French Revolution began. France became a republic in 1792, though the revolution would not end until 1799. The French overthrew two more leaders, setting up new governments each time. Today, France is a republic with a strong democracy. Louis XIV One of France’s greatest kings was Louis (LEW-ee) XIV. He ruled from 1643 to 1715, the longest a king has ever ruled in Europe. He fought many wars, expanded France’s borders, and built a lavish palace called Versailles (vehr-SEYE).
pages.brief: Soldiers fight in wars between France and England, including the Hundred Years War. Ordinary people rebel against a king as the French Revolution begins in 1789. In another scene, King Louis XIV stands before his lavish palace at Versailles, having ruled from 1643 to 1715 and expanded France's borders through many wars.

pages.text: On Bastille Day, veterans of France’s armed forces often lead the parades. Celebrations The French celebrate many different holidays. The French Revolution began on July 14, which is now known as Bastille Day. On that day in 1789, the French people stormed the Bastille, a prison in Paris. They took control of the building so they could set the prisoners free. Today, the French people celebrate their freedom with parades and fireworks. Mardi Gras (MAR-dee GRAH) is another popular holiday. Mardi Gras is a Roman Catholic holiday held about six weeks before the Easter holiday. Many cities and towns have huge carnivals with parades and floats. People dress in costumes and dance in the streets.
pages.brief: On Bastille Day, veterans of France's armed forces lead parades through the streets. Fireworks light the sky as people celebrate freedom. At Mardi Gras, a carnival fills the streets with parades, floats, and people in costumes dancing. The holiday comes about six weeks before Easter and is celebrated in many French cities and towns.

pages.text: More than five hundred different kinds of cheese are made in France. Crêpes (KRAYPS), which are thin pancakes, and baguettes are also very common. Food France is famous for its food and cooking styles. Many French people consider good food to be one of the most important parts of life. One type of popular French cooking usually includes rich dishes made with butter, cream, eggs, and other flavors. The French enjoy many different types of fresh bread, and it is served at most meals. Breads are often sold as baguettes (ba-GETS), or long, thin loaves. France is also famous for its many different kinds of cheese. Many areas in France offer their very own type of cheese.
pages.brief: A table is filled with French foods: more than five hundred kinds of cheese, thin crêpes, and long, thin baguettes. A cook prepares a rich dish with butter, cream, and eggs. Fresh bread is served at most meals. Different areas offer their own special cheeses.

pages.text: The sidewalk cafes are popular in many parts of France. Conclusion France is a modern country with a long and interesting history. Its past is filled with powerful kings and empires. Today, France is the most visited country in the world. People travel from all over the world to see its beautiful cities, villages, and castles and to eat its rich foods. Vineyards and farms dot its rolling hills and plains. Delicious foods such as cheeses and fresh breads fill its shops. If you were to visit France, what would you like to see first?
pages.brief: People sit at sidewalk cafés in a French town. Beyond the town, vineyards and farms dot rolling hills and plains. Visitors travel from around the world to see beautiful cities, villages, and castles and to eat rich foods. Shops are filled with cheeses and fresh breads. France is a modern country with a long, interesting history.

books.art_why: The book covers ancient peoples and events from before photographs, so reconstruction drawings fit.
