pages.brief: A wide view of red-rock mesa country where Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico meet at the Four Corners. Flat-topped land and dry desert stretch under a broad sky, introducing the region and the story of the ancient cliff dwellers.

pages.text: Petroglyphs at Mesa Verde Evidence The early people who lived in the Four Corners area are called prehistoric because they left no written records. We know about them because we’ve found many remains of their culture buried in the ground. Mesa Verde is located in a high, flat desert surrounded by mountains. The arid, or dry, conditions at Mesa Verde are ideal for preserving skeletons, mummies, dwellings, tools, and trash piles. These remains have helped archaeologists to study the lives of the early people who lived in the area. Other Word Wise pictographs, or Mesa Verde is pronounced “MAY-suh VAIR-day.” Mesa, paintings on stone, which is Spanish for “table,” also and petroglyphs, refers to raised, flat-topped land. or pictures carved Verde is Spanish for “green.” in stone.
pages.brief: At Mesa Verde, flat-topped desert land rises among mountains. Carved pictures and painted images mark stone surfaces. Archaeologists examine old skeletons, mummies, dwellings, tools, and trash piles buried in dry ground, studying the lives of prehistoric people who left no written records.

pages.text: Paleo-Americans To understand the story of the cliff dwellers, we need to go back in time. Scientists know that at least 14,000 years ago, during the Ice Age, ancient people crossed a land bridge from northern Russia to Alaska in North America. Hundreds of years later, some of their descendants traveled far enough south to reach the Four Corners area. The first Four Corners people were called Paleo- Americans. They survived by hunting and gathering. Paleo-Americans used large spears to hunt huge herd animals, including elephant-like animals called mammoths and mastodons, and giant bison. They also gathered nuts, berries, and other wild plants. The Paleo-Americans did not have permanent homes. Instead, they moved from place to place following the animals they hunted. They camped in caves or built simple shelters.
pages.brief: During the Ice Age, ancient people cross a land bridge from northern Russia toward Alaska. Later descendants reach the Four Corners area. Paleo-Americans hunt mammoths, mastodons, and giant bison with large spears, gather nuts and berries, and camp in caves or simple shelters while following animals.

pages.text: Archaic People When the Ice Age ended about 10,000 years ago, temperatures became warmer. This caused the extinction of many large animals and turned large grasslands into deserts. The Four Corners people had to adapt to these changes and find new ways to survive. Archaeologists call these people the Archaic people. Like their Paleo-American ancestors, the Archaic people were hunters and gatherers. But the animals they hunted were smaller and provided less meat than the ones their ancestors hunted. The Archaic people began to rely more on plants for food. The Archaic people made different tools from those of the Paleo-Americans. They made smaller spear points for hunting deer and bighorn sheep. They also made nets and traps for catching rabbits and birds. They used special tools for chopping and grinding roots, seeds, nuts, and wild plants. Early Tools The first grinding stones and bowls were made during the Archaic people’s time. Similar tools are still used now.
pages.brief: After the Ice Age, warmer land turns grasslands into desert. Archaic people hunt smaller deer and bighorn sheep, set nets and traps for rabbits and birds, and use tools to chop and grind roots, seeds, nuts, and wild plants. Early grinding stones and bowls lie nearby.

pages.text: Corn was an important part of the Ancestral Puebloans’ diet. Ancestral Puebloans By about 2,000 years ago, life in the Four Corners had changed in important ways. People had learned to grow their own food instead of relying on wild animals and plants. Agriculture changed their way of life. These people were called the Ancestral Puebloans. The earliest Ancestral Puebloans still relied mostly on hunting and gathering. However, growing their own food, such as corn and squash, on the open, flat land allowed them to feed a larger group of people. It also gave them a source of food they could depend on.
pages.brief: On open, flat land, Ancestral Puebloans tend corn and squash. Some still hunt and gather wild foods. Rows of corn stand near the fields, and a larger group shares the dependable harvest, showing how farming changed their way of life.

pages.text: Making Baskets As the Ancestral Puebloans grew more food, they found ways to store it. They began to use plant fibers and tree bark to make baskets. Some baskets held food, while others were woven so tightly that they could hold water. Because baskets could not be placed over a fire, the Ancestral Puebloans cooked by placing hot rocks into baskets filled with water. They also began making sandals from plant fibers. Yucca plant (right) and sandals made of yucca fibers (top) As the Ancestral Puebloans grew more crops and made more tools and baskets, they moved around less. Even as agriculture became more important to the Ancestral Puebloan way of life, they continued to hunt using spears and nets. During this time, they lived in caves along cliffs and canyon walls.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans weave baskets from plant fibers and tree bark. Some baskets hold water; hot rocks are placed inside baskets to cook. They make sandals from yucca fibers, gather plants near cliffs, and still hunt with spears and nets. They live in caves along cliffs and canyon walls.

pages.text: Pit houses could be from 9 to 25 feet (2.74–7.62 m) in diameter. The walls were made of branches and brush or grass covered in clay or mud. Over time, the Ancestral Puebloans relied more on agriculture to feed their growing population. By about 1,500 years ago, they grew beans in addition to corn and squash. Having a reliable food source from farming allowed them to stay in one place. They built temporary houses, called pit houses, near their fields. These houses were built on top of shallow pits dug in the ground. The sides and ceilings were constructed of tree branches, bark, and soil. Archaeologists think the Ancestral Puebloans were a peaceful people because no weapons of war have been found. Also, the location of their houses suggests that they did not feel threatened by enemies since houses built in the open are hard to defend.
pages.brief: Near open fields, Ancestral Puebloans build round pit houses on shallow dug pits. Tree branches, bark, and soil form the sides and ceilings. They grow corn, squash, and beans. No weapons of war are found, and the houses stand in the open.

pages.text: Another important The first pottery of the Ancestral Puebloans changed their way change during this time of life. was the production of pottery. Although Ancestral Puebloans continued to make baskets, using clay pots allowed them to cook over an open fire. Clay pots also stored food better. The Ancestral Puebloans started using bows and arrows during this time, which was easier and more successful than spear hunting. These changes allowed the population to continue growing as food became more plentiful. They also used animal hair twisted with cotton string to make warm socks Cord made of yucca fibers and feathers and leg coverings. Sometimes they also wove feathers and string made plants to make clothing. Boot made of turkey feather yarn.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans shape clay pots for cooking over open fire and storing food. They hunt with bows and arrows. People twist animal hair with cotton string to make warm socks and leg coverings, and weave feathers and plants into clothing. A boot made of turkey feather yarn rests nearby.

pages.text: Pueblo Bonito Do You Know? Chaco Canyon, in northwestern New Mexico, was an important cultural center made up of 12 large pueblos. The largest was Pueblo Bonito. About 1,000 people lived there. Archaeologists think that Chaco Canyon was a trade center. Building Larger Houses Around 1,300 years ago, the Ancestral Puebloans were living in larger groups. They built rectangular houses completely aboveground. They used tree limbs and bark for a frame. Then they covered the wood with adobe (soil containing clay). Over time, they started building houses with sandstone blocks stacked and held together with adobe. The houses were built side by side, creating large buildings called pueblos. Pueblo is a Spanish word that means “town” or “village.” The Ancestral Puebloans also built underground circular structures called kivas. They were used for holding ceremonies.
pages.brief: In Chaco Canyon, Pueblo Bonito stands as the largest of twelve large pueblos, home to about one thousand people. Nearby, Ancestral Puebloans build rectangular aboveground houses of wood, adobe, and stacked sandstone. Houses stand side by side, and an underground circular kiva is used for ceremonies.

pages.text: The Ancestral Puebloan culture thrived for several hundred years. The people developed new ways to help their crops grow. They built structures, such as dams and terraces, to manage water for their fields. Successful crops allowed them to feed their growing population. The types of pottery the Ancestral Puebloans made changed. They made everyday pottery that was used for cooking and storing food. Everyday pottery was gray with a rough outer texture that helped heat the food inside. They also made pottery that was rubbed and polished to create a smooth surface for decoration or trade. They decorated this pottery with complex, colorful designs using paint made from wild plants. An example of Ancestral Puebloans’ pottery.
pages.brief: Ancestral Puebloans build dams and terraces to manage water for fields of crops. Potters make gray everyday pottery with rough outer texture for cooking and storing food, and smooth polished pots decorated with complex, colorful designs painted from wild plants for decoration or trade.

pages.text: Moving to the Cliffs Around 900 years ago, the Ancestral Puebloans moved to ledges on cliffs and canyon walls. The cliff dwellings found at Mesa Verde and other places in the Four Corners area are typical of this time period. These houses were up to five stories tall. They provided housing for hundreds of people. The cliff dwellers used ladders and ropes to get to their homes. They also cut finger and toe holds into the rocks for climbing up the walls. About 600 cliff dwellings are located in Mesa Verde National Park. Cliff Palace is the largest. It had 217 rooms and 23 kivas. The smallest rooms may have been used for storage.
pages.brief: On cliff ledges and canyon walls, Ancestral Puebloans build tall dwellings up to five stories for hundreds of people. They climb ladders and ropes or use finger and toe holds cut into rock. Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde is the largest, with 217 rooms and 23 kivas.

pages.text: A Safety Issue? Some archaeologists think the Ancestral Puebloans were being attacked by other nations. They needed homes they could easily defend. Many cliff dwellings could only be reached with ladders. The people in them could pull their ladders inside, leaving their enemies no way to enter. Although this idea makes sense, there is little evidence that this was the reason for the move. Montezuma Castle Archaeologists were puzzled by the Ancestral Puebloans’ move from open areas to cliff dwellings. They think that as the Ancestral Puebloan population grew, more farmland was needed. Moving to cliff dwellings freed more flat land for growing crops. The Ancestral Puebloans also may have needed to create new fields to replace old fields that were overused and had lost the ability to grow food well. Another possible reason for the move might have been for warmth during winter. The weather was getting colder during this time. Most cliff dwellings face south or southwest, where the Sun’s rays could warm the rock walls of their homes.
pages.brief: Archaeologists wonder why people moved to cliff dwellings. Some think ladders pulled inside helped defend against attackers, though evidence is slight. Others think the move freed flat land for crops or gave warmth: most cliff dwellings face south or southwest, where sunlight warms the rock walls.

pages.text: Building Dwellings Building the cliff dwellings was a huge challenge for the Ancestral Puebloans. They didn’t have machines and used only stone tools. They were skilled at designing structures that made the best use of the space. The builders made walls from large stones chipped into shape and held together with adobe. They covered the walls with adobe, sometimes painting designs on the insides of the walls. Builders made upper floors by laying large wooden poles across the tops of walls and placing smaller poles across the beams. Next, a layer of sticks or bark was piled on. Then they added a thick layer of adobe to hold it together. A dwelling with two floors.
pages.brief: Using only stone tools, Ancestral Puebloan builders chip large stones into shape and hold them with adobe. They cover walls with adobe and sometimes paint designs inside. For upper floors, they lay wooden poles across walls, add smaller poles, sticks or bark, then thick adobe. A two-floor dwelling stands.

pages.text: Daily Life The Ancestral Puebloans probably spent most of their time outside working together in groups. Some cooked, ground corn, carried water, and made pottery and baskets. Others wove cloth, farmed crops, and hunted. Others made tools out of stone, wood, and plant fibers. Children worked alongside their parents, learning by watching and practicing. They also took care of turkeys and played. During the winter, some work was done inside the dwellings. Archaeologists think that rooms were used year-round for sleeping. Trade with other nations was an important part of Ancestral Puebloan life. The map below shows some of the items they traded and where the items came from. Mesa Verde Trading Mesa Possible trade routes Verde P A C O I F I C C E A N.
pages.brief: Outside, Ancestral Puebloans work in groups: cooking, grinding corn, carrying water, making pottery and baskets, weaving cloth, farming, hunting, and shaping tools. Children help parents, tend turkeys, and play. In winter some work moves inside. Trade routes stretch toward the Pacific Ocean, bringing traded items to Mesa Verde.

pages.text: The outside of a kiva (inset); The inside of a kiva (main) Spiritual Life Modern kivas are still used by the descendants of the Ancestral Puebloans. That is how we know they were used for religious ceremonies. They were probably also used for family gatherings, as guest rooms, and as workspaces in winter. People entered kivas with ladders. Each kiva had a fire pit in the center and a shaft providing fresh air. Half of the Mesa Verde kivas also had a small hole in the floor called a sipapu. The hole represented a doorway between the spirit world and the physical world. Archaeologists think that the Ancestral Puebloans believed that all living things have both a spirit self and a physical self. They also believed in life after death.
pages.brief: A kiva stands outside and inside: people enter by ladder, with a fire pit in the center and a shaft for fresh air. Some floors have a small sipapu hole, a doorway between spirit and physical worlds. Ancestral Puebloans honor ceremonies and believe living things have spirit selves and life after death.

pages.text: Leaving the Cliffs Between 1280 and 1295, the Ancestral Puebloans left the cliff dwellings. They moved south to New Mexico and Arizona. No one knows for sure why they moved. Archaeologists think that the fact that the climate kept changing played an important role. It got colder, causing a shorter growing season for crops. Watering crops became harder because there were long periods of time with little or no rain. In addition, the soil may have been so overused that growing enough food became impossible. Perhaps by the time the Ancestral Puebloans left Mesa Verde, they had cut down most of the trees for firewood and for building pueblos. Hunters may have killed so many wild animals that the meat supply was gone. Some people think that enemy nations drove out the cliff dwellers. However, that is unlikely because there are no remains of other cultures at Mesa Verde after the Ancestral Puebloans left. Archaeologists find older remains deeper in the ground and newer remains closer to the surface. If enemies drove out the cliff dwellers, evidence of their culture would be found on top of the Ancestral Puebloan remains.
pages.brief: Between 1280 and 1295, Ancestral Puebloans leave cliff dwellings and move south to New Mexico and Arizona. Climate grows colder, rain is scarce, soil is overused, trees are cut, and wild animals are scarce. No evidence shows enemies drove them out; older remains lie deeper, newer remains closer to the surface.

pages.text: Modern-Day Descendants When the ancient cliff dwellers left Mesa Verde, some moved south, settling along the Rio Grande in New Mexico. These are the ancestors of the modern Pueblo nations. Others moved to Arizona, eventually forming the Zuni and Hopi nations. Estella Loretto cleans a bronze statue. Today, members of these nations continue many of the traditions of the ancient cliff dwellers. Many Pueblo, Zuni, and Hopi people continue to farm and perform ceremonies. They still honor their connection with the land and the spirit world. They create exquisite pottery, jewelry, baskets, carvings, and weavings. Ray Tafoya is known for his pottery.
pages.brief: Modern Pueblo, Zuni, and Hopi people continue traditions of the ancient cliff dwellers. Estella Loretto cleans a bronze statue. Ray Tafoya is known for his pottery. Others farm, perform ceremonies, honor connections with land and spirit world, and create exquisite pottery, jewelry, baskets, carvings, and weavings.

pages.text: Preserving the Past Follow these rules to preserve ruins and artifacts. 1. Look, but don’t take. It is against the law to keep artifacts. 2. Do not touch or draw on walls, petroglyphs, or pictographs. 3. Do not climb on walls. Many walls are easily damaged. An example of a damaged wall Protecting the Cliff Dwellings In the late 1800s, many people visited the cliff dwellings. Some photographed, drew, and described the sites, but others took artifacts from the dwellings to sell. Over time, people became concerned about protecting the cliff dwellings from damage and theft. The concern led to the creation of Mesa Verde National Park in 1906. The National Park Service protects the cliff dwellings while also letting visitors enjoy them. Educational exhibits at Mesa Verde and other sites in the Southwest teach people about the Ancestral Puebloan way of life.
pages.brief: People visit cliff dwellings, and some photograph, draw, or describe the sites while others take artifacts to sell. A damaged wall shows the need for care. Concern leads to Mesa Verde National Park in 1906. The National Park Service protects the dwellings, and educational exhibits teach visitors about Ancestral Puebloan life.

books.title: Earth's Water
books.art_why: Earth's water, oceans, ice, clouds, and people using water are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Earth’s water appears in various shades of blue in this image. Water covers over two-thirds of Earth’s surface. Most of it consists of salt water in the oceans. Earth has much less fresh water, and many plants and animals depend on fresh water for survival.
pages.brief: Earth seen from space, with oceans in shades of blue covering more than two-thirds of the surface; land areas and smaller bodies of fresh water are visible. Salt water fills the oceans, while the much smaller amount of fresh water supports plants and animals.

pages.text: Some of this fresh water is aboveground, while other fresh water is groundwater underneath Earth’s surface. What are some ways you use Earth’s water?
pages.brief: A view of land shows fresh water aboveground in a visible body and groundwater held underneath Earth's surface, with layers of soil and rock below. The scene sets up the question of how readers use Earth's water.

pages.text: Different Forms of Water Liquid water is the most common state of water on Earth. When you pour liquid water into a container, it takes the shape of that container. Liquid water is always moving, even if you can’t see it move. Water moves in rivers and streams due Each of these containers holds four cups of water. to currents —the constant flow of moving water. Lakes and ponds are often called standing bodies of water because the liquid water in them moves so slowly. Surface and underwater currents cause ocean water to move, with waves forming and crashing. Winds, the Moon, and the Sun affect the strength of ocean currents.
pages.brief: Several containers, each holding four cups of liquid water, show liquid taking the shape of its container. Nearby, water flows in a river or stream, sits in a lake or pond, and moves in ocean waves and currents under the influence of wind, the Moon, and the Sun.

pages.text: Ice can be carved into many shapes. Not all water is in a liquid state. When liquid water gets very cold, it freezes and forms ice. Ice is another state of water— solid water. Ice can float on liquid water. People form ice into different shapes. You’ve probably made ice cubes to cool down a drink. Artists even carve ice sculptures.
pages.brief: Ice appears as solid water that can float on liquid water. Clear ice cubes cool a drink in a glass, while an artist carves a large ice sculpture into a shaped figure nearby, showing another way people form ice.

pages.text: Sheets of ice cover Earth’s South Pole. Much of Earth’s frozen water is at the North and South Poles, the coldest areas on Earth. Huge masses of ice called glaciers, which are commonly found at the poles, store much of Earth’s fresh water.
pages.brief: At the South Pole, vast sheets of ice cover the polar landscape. Similar frozen water lies at the North Pole and South Pole, the coldest places on Earth, where huge glaciers store much of Earth's fresh water.

pages.text: What states of water can you see in this picture? Some of Earth’s water is in an invisible state as a gas called water vapor. While it’s always invisible, water vapor is all around us. When it is hot outside, more water vapor fills the air than when it is cold outside. Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air. On hot and humid days, the air feels thick with lots of water vapor concentrated in the air.
pages.brief: A hot outdoor landscape under sunlight suggests humid air, even though water vapor itself cannot be seen. The scene shows the surroundings filled with invisible water vapor, with more vapor present on a hot day than a cold day.

pages.text: As this snowperson absorbs sunlight, the snow eventually heats up and melts into liquid water. Changing Water Earth’s water is constantly changing from one state to another. When frozen water is heated, it melts and becomes liquid water, and when liquid water is cooled, it freezes and becomes ice.
pages.brief: A snowperson stands outdoors in bright sunlight, absorbing the Sun's energy and heating up. Around it, the snow melts into liquid water, showing frozen water changing to liquid water when it is warmed.

pages.text: Liquid water can become a gas, too. Have you ever seen a puddle of water dry up on a hot day? Energy from the Sun changed the liquid to a gas in a process called evaporation. Evaporation happens every day as the Sun beats down on Earth’s bodies of water. When water vapor in the air cools down, it changes from a gas to a liquid in a process called condensation. Energy from the Sun causes water to evaporate.
pages.brief: On a hot day, energy from the Sun beats down on a puddle, and the liquid water evaporates into a gas. Nearby, water vapor in the air cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets, illustrating both evaporation and condensation.

pages.text: Clouds drop water on the desert as rain. Clouds are made up of tiny drops of water formed by condensation. The tiny drops stick together, creating larger, heavier drops. If the drops become large enough, they fall as rain, snow, or another type of precipitation. Some rain and melted snow soak into the ground, becoming groundwater. Precipitation and groundwater fill rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds. Water evaporates from bodies of water around the world, and, later, it condenses and falls in other places on Earth.
pages.brief: Dark clouds drop rain onto a desert landscape. The rain soaks into the ground as groundwater and fills streams, ponds, and a lake, while water evaporates from bodies of water and later condenses into clouds elsewhere.

pages.text: Water Is Important Rain keeps plants alive and allows them to grow. People and other animals require water to survive. We also use it for other purposes, such as fighting fires.
pages.brief: Rain falls onto green plants and helps them grow. People and other animals are shown needing water to survive. Nearby, firefighters use water from a hose to fight a fire, showing one of the many ways people rely on Earth's water.

pages.text: It is important to take care of Earth’s water. Human activities are the main cause of water pollution, although sometimes it occurs naturally. Littering and dumping trash lead to dirty and unusable water. Polluted water makes people, plants, and animals sick. Would you want to drink and play in polluted water?
pages.brief: A body of water is polluted with litter and dumped trash, making the water dirty and unusable. Plants and animals near the water are harmed, and the scene asks whether anyone would want to drink or play in polluted water.

books.title: Golf
books.art_why: The book includes early golf history and old equipment that need illustrated scenes.

pages.text: Golf Hole fringe – an area around the green that has longer grass hole – marked with a flagstick (“green” for short) water hazard – a stream or pond bunker – a shallow hole in the ground that is usually filled rough – an area that has trees, shrubs, and.
pages.brief: A golf hole seen from above: a smooth green with a flagstick in the small hole, surrounded by a fringe of longer grass. A pond or stream lies nearby as a water hazard, and a shallow sand-filled bunker sits beside rough ground with trees and shrubs.

pages.text: Golf Clubs Golf clubs have heads of different shapes, depending on what they are used for. • Irons are used for shorter shots. • Woods and fairway metals are used to hit the ball long distances. • Wedges are used for short, high shots or to get the ball out of sand. • Putters are used to roll the ball once it is on the green. Playing Golf Golfers use clubs to hit a small, hard ball into a hole using as few strokes, or swings, as possible. Sometimes the ball must travel a very long way to reach the hole. Sometimes it only needs to move a short distance. At other times, it must fly high in the air to get over long grass or other things. Golfers need to know how to make all these types of shots.
pages.brief: Several golf clubs with different head shapes rest on the grass: irons, woods and fairway metals, wedges, and a putter. A golfer prepares to hit a small, hard ball, showing that it may travel far, move a short distance, or fly high over long grass toward the hole.

pages.text: The sport is played on a golf course, which is a large area of land that is carefully mowed and trimmed to define the areas of the course. A golf course usually has nine or eighteen sections, or holes. Each section begins at the teeing ground, where golfers usually place their ball on a small peg called a tee. They hit the ball down the fairway—the area that leads to the small hole at the far end of the section. The area around the small hole is called the putting green, or simply the green. It almost always takes several strokes to get the ball there. However, lucky golfers sometimes get a hole in one. In golf, the word hole has two different meanings. One is the small hole into which golfers hit the ball (left). The other is each of the nine or eighteen sections of a golf course (right).
pages.brief: A wide golf course with mowed fairways and trimmed sections. At a teeing ground, a golfer places a ball on a small tee and hits it down the fairway toward the putting green and its small hole. The scene also shows a lucky hole in one.

pages.text: This hole is almost surrounded by water and rough, with a large bunker as well. Other holes might have fewer hazards. Golfers need to deal with hazards, which are parts of the course that they try to avoid. Getting a ball out of a hazard may take extra strokes, which is bad for a golfer’s score. One type of hazard is a sand-filled area called a bunker. Streams and ponds are other types of hazards. The rough— the area around each section, which usually has trees, bushes, and longer grass—can also present problems.
pages.brief: A golf hole almost surrounded by hazards: a large sand-filled bunker beside the green, a stream or pond, and rough ground with trees, bushes, and longer grass. A golfer stands near the edge, facing the difficult shot and trying to avoid these parts of the course.

pages.text: A golf game usually involves playing eighteen different sections, called holes. If a golf course has only nine holes, golfers often play the course twice. Each hole on a golf course has a number, called the par. If a hole has a par of four, golfers try to get the ball into the hole in four strokes or less. The number depends on the distance from the teeing ground to the hole. Most holes are three, four, or five par. Par for the course is the total of all the pars for the entire nine or eighteen holes. Golfers who play together in a small group compare their totals for the whole course. The player with the lowest score wins. Scoring a Par Five Hole A golfer’s score is based on the number of strokes compared to par. The sport has special names for scores. Name of Score Number of Strokes Hole in one One Eagle Two strokes under par 5 – 2 = 3 shots Birdie One stroke under par 5 – 1 = 4 shots Bogey One stroke over par 5 + 1 = 6 shots Double bogey Two strokes over par 5 + 2 = 7 shots.
pages.brief: A small group of golfers plays a par-five hole, moving from the teeing ground toward the green. One golfer takes a stroke while the others watch, and the group compares their totals after finishing. The scene suggests good scores like an eagle or birdie and higher scores like a bogey.

pages.text: Golfers respect how much concentration it takes to play the game well. They stand back and stay quiet when another person is taking a swing. It can take between three and five hours to play a round of golf, or eighteen holes. People who golf just for fun often ride the course in golf carts. Professional golfers walk from one hole to the next. Helpers called caddies carry their clubs. Golfers wear shoes with spikes on the bottom for gripping the grass. Their clothing allows them to move easily when they swing a club. Some golfers wear a glove on one hand to help them grip the clubs better and avoid getting blisters.
pages.brief: Golfers stand back and stay quiet while one player takes a swing. A caddie carries a professional golfer’s clubs as the golfer walks to the next hole; elsewhere, players ride in golf carts. The golfers wear comfortable clothing, spiked shoes for gripping grass, and some wear a glove on one hand.

pages.text: A Sport Is Born Scotland is the birthplace of modern golf. The game may have begun as long ago as the 1400s. It probably spread to England in the early 1600s and to India, Australia, and other British colonies soon after. By the late 1800s, golf was played in many countries around the world. Equipment has changed a lot over the years. The first golf balls and clubs were made of wood. In the early 1600s, people started using leather balls filled with feathers. In 1848, a new ball was invented. It was made of tree sap that was dried, heated, and shaped. Players began using metal golf clubs with the new balls. Modern golf balls with rubber cores first appeared in 1898. Golf balls started to have dimples in the early 1900s. The dimples help the balls fly higher and farther.
pages.brief: In Scotland, early golfers play with wooden clubs and wooden balls on a grassy course. Nearby, scenes show later equipment: a leather ball filled with feathers, a dried tree-sap ball from 1848 with metal clubs, and a modern rubber-core ball with dimples from the early 1900s.

pages.text: A Global Game Because golf began in Scotland, the sport is most popular in countries where English is spoken. People in more than 130 countries around the world play the game. The United States has many more golf courses than any other country. However, compared to how many people live in each country, Scotland has the most golf courses. In addition to outdoor courses, many places have indoor digital simulators where people can improve their skills. Miniature golf is played both indoors and outdoors. Top Ten Golfing Countries 2.
pages.brief: Golfers play on outdoor courses in many countries around the world, with the United States having many courses and Scotland having the most compared with its population. Other scenes show an indoor digital simulator and a miniature golf course, both used for practice and fun.

pages.text: Who Plays Golf? More than sixty million people around the world play golf. In the United States, over twenty million people play each year. Programs exist for young people to learn the game and compete. Top men’s golfers compete in the U.S.-based Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) Tour and the European Tour as well as several others. Top women’s golfers from around the world compete in the U.S.-based Ladies Professional Golf Association (LPGA) Tour. In addition, men and women each have several top professional tournaments, called majors. Winning a major earns a golfer respect, fame, and money. Only a small number of golfers earn a living by competing in golf tournaments. Golf competitions sometimes have wildlife hazards. The 2008 Women’s World Cup in South Africa was interrupted by baboons.
pages.brief: Many golfers of different ages play on courses around the world, including young people learning and competing. Professional men and women compete in major tournaments. At the 2008 Women’s World Cup in South Africa, baboons wander onto the course and interrupt play near the green.

pages.text: Jack Tiger Nicklaus Woods Patty Berg Golf Greats Jack Nicklaus is the top golfer in the history of the sport. He competed in important tournaments from 1961 to 2005 and won more than a hundred competitions. He won eighteen majors. Patty Berg was the top woman to ever play golf. As a professional, she competed from 1940 to 1962 and won sixty tournaments and fifteen majors. Tiger Woods may be the greatest golfer playing today. He has done better on the PGA Tour than any other golfer now playing.
pages.brief: Three golf greats are shown: Jack Nicklaus, Patty Berg, and Tiger Woods. Nicklaus swings in an important tournament, Berg competes as a top woman golfer, and Woods plays on the PGA Tour. Each is shown on a golf course with a club.

pages.text: Types of Golf Courses Golf courses are located in many different places. Some are like large, grassy parks with tall trees. Some are narrow strips of land along coastlines. In desert areas, courses often have cactuses and palm trees. The most unusual place golf has been played is... the Moon! Astronaut Alan Shepard went to the Moon in 1971 and hit a few golf balls while he was there. Few players will ever experience golfing on the Moon, but anyone who is interested can find a way to play golf right here on Earth. All you need is a club and a golf ball. With lots of practice, young players will learn what millions of golfers already know: golf is out of this world! Alan Shepard swings a golf club at a ball on the Moon in 1971.
pages.brief: Different golf courses appear: a large grassy park with tall trees, a narrow strip along a coastline, and a desert course with cactuses and palm trees. On the Moon, astronaut Alan Shepard swings a golf club at a ball, while an Earth course waits below with a club and ball ready.

books.title: Deep in the Ocean
books.art_why: Real ocean animals and science today; no named famous person appears, so not cartoon.

pages.text: The deep ocean anglerfish uses the bright end of a spine like a fishing pole to attract prey.
pages.brief: Deep in the dark ocean, an anglerfish uses the bright end of a long spine like a fishing pole to attract prey. The glowing tip of the spine hangs out in the water ahead of the fish, drawing prey toward it.

pages.text: Sunlight warms the shallow parts of the ocean down to 200 meters (656 ft) below the surface. Plants and animals that need sunlight and warm water live there, such as tiger sharks and many species of common dolphins. Deep in the ocean, other animals, including vampire squid, fangtooth fish, and viperfish, live in water that is cold and dark. The warm, shallow waters of tide pools are home to species of starfish, anemones, mussels, and tiny crabs.
pages.brief: Sunlight warms the shallow ocean down to 200 meters, where tiger sharks and common dolphins swim among plants. Below, in cold dark water, vampire squid, fangtooth fish and viperfish live. In warm tide pools, starfish, anemones, mussels and tiny crabs live.

pages.text: Ocean Zones.
pages.brief: The ocean is shown as a simple view of ocean zones, divided into broad layers from the top of the water down to the bottom, with no animals or plants added to the open water.

pages.text: Diving Deep in The deep ocean, below 1,000 meters (3,281 ft), is 39 m (128 ft) freezing cold. The water 7–13°C (45–55°F) pressure below 39.6 meters (130 ft) can harm you if you don’t have the right protective gear. Sport divers wear air tanks 609 m (2,000 ft) 4.5–7°C (40–45°F) filled with a mixture of gases for safety. They also wear special dive computers that help them know how far down they are and how much air they have. Deep divers 6,096 m (20,000 ft) 0–2°C (32–35°F) wear special hard diving suits to protect them from the water pressure. For really deep dives, groups of two or three scientists ride in a small submarine called a submersible. Some of these submersibles have robot arms that can collect samples of water, soil, and small animals underwater.
pages.brief: At the surface, sport divers in air tanks and dive computers descend into the ocean. Farther down, a deep diver wears a special hard suit. Deepest, a small submersible carries two or three scientists whose robot arms collect water, soil and small animals.

pages.text: Oceanographers Scientists who study the ocean are called oceanographers (oh-shuh-NOG-ruh-furs). They often live for months on a ship, working seven days a week, and also teach at colleges and universities. Some of them study what sea animals eat and where they live. Others study the ocean water itself. All of them have to understand biology, chemistry, geology, and physics. Biology is the study of living things. Chemistry is the study of what things are made of and how they react and change when they come into contact with other things. Geology is the study of rocks and soil and the processes that shape and change the Earth. Physics is the study of the natural laws, such as energy, force, and motion, that govern how things work.
pages.brief: Oceanographers work on a ship at sea for months, seven days a week, studying what sea animals eat and where they live, or studying the ocean water itself. Some also teach at colleges and universities, using biology, chemistry, geology and physics.

pages.text: Using Satellites for Tracking Satellites up in space can help to track sea animals’ travels in Earth’s oceans. Scientists tag some animals with electronic sensors to study them. A satellite can track the signal from the tag attached to the animal’s fin or back. The signal shows when, where, and how the animal travels. These tags have been used to track some fish that have traveled up to 75,000 kilometers (46,602 mi). Scientists can use this information to predict the animal’s future movements.
pages.brief: Scientists attach an electronic sensor tag to a fish’s fin or back, and a satellite high above Earth tracks its signal. The fish travels far through the ocean, and the signal shows when, where and how it moves.

pages.text: Counting the Sea Animals What types of animals live in the ocean? Where do they live? How many are there? Oceanographers studied and counted animals for ten years to discover the answers. They looked at all the world’s oceans from the North Pole to the South Pole. They counted everything they could find from the largest whales to the smallest organisms. The surprising report is called the Census of Marine Life. Released in 2010, it contains data from more than 540 different expeditions that began in more than eighty countries. Lionfish swim among coral sea fans. Their long, feathery spines can sting any predator that comes too close. Native to the South Pacific, lionfish were first spotted in United States’ waters in 2000.
pages.brief: Oceanographers on a ship count animals across the world’s oceans, from the North Pole to the South Pole, from the largest whales to the smallest organisms. Nearby, a lionfish swims among coral sea fans, its long, feathery spines held out.

pages.text: The leafy sea dragon blends in with the plants of its surroundings. Its eyes move independently of each other so it can look in two directions at once. The male sea dragon carries the eggs for the female and gives birth. The Census of Marine Life The study revealed new information and several surprises about extreme habitats. One surprise from the study was where things lived: everywhere —in all water levels and temperatures! Marine species lived in the hottest and coldest places. More than seventeen thousand species lived in deep places without light and some without oxygen. Another surprise was how many new species were discovered. More than twelve hundred new marine species have been described, and more than five thousand species are still waiting to be described. Scientists found one species of Jurassic shrimp that was thought to have gone extinct more than fifty million years ago.
pages.brief: A leafy sea dragon blends in with the plants around it, its two eyes looking independently in different directions, while the male carries eggs. In dark deep water, a Jurassic shrimp appears among other marine species found in extreme habitats.

pages.text: Over 2 kilometers (1.3 mi) deep in the ocean, giant tube worms live in the hot water that bubbles up from a lava pillar. Living in Hot and Cold Water The very cold Deep Ocean Zone has more than one million hot volcanoes in it. The water temperature at a volcano can be 400°C (752°F), which is hot enough to melt lead. Species such as eyeless shrimp, white crabs, giant tube worms, and many bacteria live in this very hot water. These animals use sulfur rather than sunlight to live.
pages.brief: Over two kilometers deep in the ocean, giant tube worms cluster around a lava pillar where hot water bubbles up. Eyeless shrimp and white crabs live in the hot water beside them, along with many bacteria; the water is hot enough to melt lead.

pages.text: Huge groups of Arctic and Antarctic animals were also found living in water that is close to or below freezing. Giant squid, Antarctic cod, and the lion’s mane jellyfish are some species that live under solid ice that is 700 meters (2,296 ft) thick. Many of these species slow down their movements to save energy so they don’t freeze. The Antarctic ice fish has no red blood cells. Its thinner blood contains a type of antifreeze. Its special blood helps it survive in the frigid waters beneath ice that would freeze the blood of most fish.
pages.brief: Beneath solid ice 700 meters thick, huge groups of Arctic and Antarctic animals live in water close to or below freezing. A giant squid, an Antarctic cod and a lion’s mane jellyfish are shown, while the Antarctic ice fish swims nearby with its thinner, antifreeze-containing blood. Many slow their movements to save energy.

pages.text: What Did We Learn? Scientists learned that life is even more adaptable than they originally thought. Animals living in the deep ocean have found ways to survive in harsh would be impossible for most other species to live in. The marine This big-eyed squid lives in the cold, deep waters of the northern Atlantic Ocean. more than 230,000 species in more than 30 million records. More than 6,000 new species had never been seen before! Some animals were see-through, or translucent. Some had warning lights that turn on and off so that they can see in the darkness. Others had long feelers instead of eyes to attract prey and learn what was around them. Some had teeth so long that they overlapped their jaws. Others made their own antifreeze to stay warm.
pages.brief: In the cold, deep northern Atlantic Ocean, a big-eyed squid swims. Around it are deep-ocean animals with see-through bodies, warning lights that switch on and off, long feelers instead of eyes, and teeth so long they overlap their jaws; one makes its own antifreeze.

pages.text: What else lives in the deep ocean? Scientists keep discovering new species and new facts. The more they look, the more they find. They think that only one quarter of all marine life has been counted. Not all the animals that have been discovered have been documented and described. There are many more surprises to come! Explore More To learn more about the Census of Marine Life, go to its website at www.coml.org. Each week, new discoveries are added to the marine census project map at www.comlmaps.org/census-on- google-earth. On the Internet, search terms such as deep sea species, blind lobster, or NASA oceanography.
pages.brief: Scientists in a submersible look into the dark deep ocean and observe unfamiliar marine animals. Some of these animals have not yet been documented or described, and the scientists think only one quarter of all marine life has been counted.

books.title: Electric Eels!
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing, and it suits the historical Humboldt scene and cutaway diagrams.

pages.text: The fishermen led about thirty horses into a shallow pond. The eels rose up and gave the horses hundreds of shocks. After the eels became tired and stopped shocking, the fishermen caught five of them. Humboldt learned much about the eels. Shocking Fish Story Not long ago, a scientist supported Humboldt’s report that eels rise up to protect themselves. Before that, some scientists thought Humboldt might have been stretching the truth, like any fish story. This picture was made from Humboldt’s writing about fishing for eels with horses. It shows how powerful electric eels are.
pages.brief: In a shallow pond, fishermen lead about thirty horses into the water. Long electric eels rise up and shock the horses again and again. After the eels tire and stop shocking, the fishermen catch five eels. The scene shows how powerful electric eels are.

pages.text: It’s a Fish! Electric eels are long gray-brown fish with yellow or orange on their throats. These tube-shaped fish are more like catfish than other eels. The group they belong to is called knifefish. All knifefish can use electricity. Electric eels can grow as long as 2 to 3 meters (7–10 ft.). They can weigh as much as 20 to 22 kilograms (44–48 lb.). They can grow to about as big around as an average adult human’s thigh and four times as long. Male and female electric eels are alike in color and size. Electric Eel Facts Scientific Name Electrophorus electricus Animal Type Fish Diet Fish, crustaceans, and amphibians Length 2 to 3 meters (7–10 ft.) Weight 20 to 22 kilograms (44–48 lb.)
pages.brief: A long, tube-shaped electric eel, gray-brown with a yellow-orange throat, swims in dark water. It is more like a catfish than other eels and belongs with knifefish. Beside it, an adult human thigh suggests the eel's thickness, and its body stretches four times longer.

pages.text: Unlike most other fish, electric eels breathe air through their mouths. They have gills, but they mostly use their gills to help them breathe out. Electric eels open their mouths above the water to breathe air in through special organs in their mouths. The waste air they breathe out goes through their mouths and gills. Electric eels need air every few minutes. They can drown if they get trapped underwater. Electric eels breathe air through their mouths.
pages.brief: An electric eel floats at the water's surface with its mouth open above the water, taking air into special organs inside its mouth. Waste air leaves through its mouth and gills. Its gills are visible behind the head as the eel breathes air every few minutes.

pages.text: Like most other fish, electric eels have fins and a backbone. They have small fins on either side of their heads. They also have a long fin on their bellies from head to tail. Their backbones and fins help them move. Electric eels wave their belly fins in an S- shape to Shocking Fact swim, which they do quite Electric eels can slowly. They move quickly regrow the tail parts only when they attack. of their bodies if they’re cut off.
pages.brief: A side view of an electric eel shows small fins on either side of its head and a long belly fin running from head to tail. Its backbone runs along the body. The eel bends its belly fin in an S-shape as it swims slowly through the water.

pages.text: It’s Electric! An electric eel is the most electric fish on Earth. These eels can navigate, communicate, protect themselves, hunt, and stun or kill prey using their bioelectricity. Bioelectricity is the action of electric currents in a body. Other knifefish and some skates, rays, and catfish use bioelectricity, too. Those fish can navigate, communicate, or protect themselves. However, none can zap with as much power as an electric eel. Shocking Medical History Don’t try this at home! Ancient Greeks and Romans held live electric rays to people’s foreheads to cure headaches. A ray’s shock can cause numbness in humans, so it might have worked! Other Electric Fish.
pages.brief: An electric eel swims with electric currents around its body, while other knifefish, a skate, a ray, and a catfish appear nearby. In a second scene, an ancient Greek or Roman holds a live electric ray against a person's forehead to cure a headache.

pages.text: Three organs produce an electric eel’s shocks. The organs start just behind the eel’s head and make up two-thirds of its body. An eel’s body is like a battery. The positive end is at the head, and the negative end is at the tail. 1 Shocking Fact 2 If an electric eel curls its head toward its tail, the move increases the eel’s shocking power. Three Electric Organs The electric eel has three electric organs. It has a main organ (1) and two smaller organs (2 and 3).
pages.brief: A cutaway view of an electric eel shows three long electric organs inside its body, starting behind the head and filling two-thirds of its length. The head is the positive end and the tail the negative end, like a battery. The eel curls its head toward its tail to increase its shocking power.

pages.text: An electric eel can shock prey with up to 650 volts of electricity. The shock can kill small animals and stun large ones. Anything in the water within 9 meters (28 ft.) of the eel can feel it. Electric eels have five times more volts than a typical U.S. wall socket—which can be dangerous to people. Electric eels can’t feel their own shocks, but scientists aren’t sure why. It might be because of their size or how the shock moves. It also might be because of some part of the eel that scientists don’t understand. Scientists do know that eels have special cells called electrocytes. These cells line up in long rows. They each produce a tiny shock at nearly the same time. Together, they create the electric eel’s stunning attack ZAP!
pages.brief: An electric eel releases a strong shock through the water, and nearby small animals feel it within nine meters. Inside the eel, long rows of special cells called electrocytes fire tiny shocks at nearly the same time, creating the eel's powerful stunning attack.

pages.text: Stunning Attack Before an attack zap happens, electric eels must find their prey. Dark, cloudy water and poor sight don’t help. Electric eels are also most active at night. They use small shocks instead of their eyes to see prey. They hunt much like some bats and owls, which bounce sound off objects. Electric eels send out small shocks of electricity—about fifty every second. These small shocks hit plants, animals, and objects. They help the eels sense what’s around them. When an electric eel senses prey is nearby, it sends out a group of two or three larger shocks. The shocks make the prey twitch. The animal can’t stop moving, so the eel senses where it is. Then the electric eel sends out its attack shock, which stuns or kills the prey. The electric eel quickly sucks the prey through its mouth into its stomach. Electric eels mostly eat small fish, crustaceans, and amphibians. Young eels also eat worms and insect larvae.
pages.brief: In dark, cloudy water at night, an electric eel sends small electric shocks that hit plants, animals, and objects to sense what is around it. When prey twitches from larger shocks, the eel sends an attack shock, then sucks the stunned or killed prey through its mouth into its stomach.

pages.text: Don’t Swim There! Electric eels are top predators in the slow- moving rivers where they often live. Scientists have found them in the Amazon and Orinoco Rivers in South America. They also live in nearby freshwater swamps, creeks, ponds, and lakes. Because they breathe air, electric eels can live in water that might kill other fish. They can also live out of water for hours if their skin stays wet. Electric Eel Habitat ATLANTIC Orinoco OCEAN River Amazon River SOUTH AMERICA PACIFIC OCEAN.
pages.brief: An electric eel swims as a top predator in a slow-moving South American river. The Amazon and Orinoco Rivers wind through a landscape of freshwater swamps, creeks, ponds, and lakes. The eel can also live out of water for hours as long as its skin stays wet.

pages.text: Electric eels mostly mate in small ponds. Male eels build nests by making bubbles with their saliva. Female eels lay eggs in the bubbles. Males guard the nests and the baby eels until they are about 10 centimeters (4 in.) long. Then the babies have to live on their own. Because of their weaker shocks, young electric eels are more likely than adults to be prey for other animals, such as crocodiles. Black caimans are related to crocodiles. They are one of the few predators that try to eat electric eels.
pages.brief: In a small pond, a male electric eel builds a nest of bubbles made with his saliva. A female lays eggs in the bubbles, and the male guards the nest and the baby eels until they are about ten centimeters long. A black caiman watches nearby.

pages.text: Future Energy Source Scientists now know more about electric eels than Humboldt did. Even so, there is always more to learn. Scientists at Yale University want to use electrocytes as a model to create cells that act like batteries. Some medical devices—such as pacemakers, which keep hearts beating—contain batteries that could harm a person if they break. Scientists want to create batteries that won’t be harmful and won’t run out of power. Humboldt wrote more than two hundred years ago, “We are, doubtless, very far from having discovered all the secrets of the electrical action of fishes.” What will electric eels help scientists understand next?
pages.brief: Scientists at Yale University study an electric eel's electrocytes, hoping to model new cells that act like batteries. Nearby, a pacemaker shows a medical device that uses batteries. A portrait of Humboldt and his old writing suggest that many secrets of electric fishes remain to be discovered.

books.title: Mysterious Caves
books.art_why: The book is about real caves and explorers that can be photographed today, not a named famous person.

pages.text: A shaft of sunlight helps an explorer see the wonders inside the Hang Son Doong cave in Vietnam. Suddenly, they saw light. A shaft of sunlight was cutting through the darkness ahead of them. As they moved closer, they could tell that part of the cave roof had collapsed long ago, leaving a hole that let in this patch of sunlight. The sunlight revealed the room’s amazing size. They soon realized that they stood in the biggest cave room known to exist. One single area of the room was over 90 meters (300 ft) wide, 180 meters (600 ft) high, and over 4 kilometers (2.5 mi) long. An entire city block of 40-story buildings could fit inside.
pages.brief: An explorer stands inside Hang Son Doong cave in Vietnam, looking toward a shaft of sunlight cutting through darkness. The light falls through a hole where part of the cave roof collapsed long ago, revealing the huge cave room around them.

pages.text: The entrance to the massive Hang Son Doong cave was hidden by dense jungle. This cave, called Hang Son Doong, or Mountain River Cave, is enormous. Where the roof collapsed, letting in sunlight and rain, dense hidden jungles grow. There is also a 60-meter (200-ft) cliff they named the “Great Wall of Vietnam.” The cliff stopped the cavers at first. They returned with equipment to scale the cliff, and continued their journey into the interior. This cave is the biggest yet found, but it may not be the biggest in the world. Adventurous explorers find new caves every year. In this book, you will learn about caves. You will read about how they form, the unusual formations and living things within them, and other caves that are just as wondrous as Hang Son Doong.
pages.brief: The entrance to Hang Son Doong cave is hidden by dense jungle. Where the roof collapsed, sunlight and rain let dense hidden jungles grow. Cavers with equipment scale a tall cliff they called the Great Wall of Vietnam, continuing into the cave’s interior.

pages.text: What Are Caves? A cave is any natural hollow space in the earth. Usually when people talk about a cave, they mean a space big enough for a person to go inside, and deep enough so sunlight never reaches part of it. Caves can occur in rock, in ice, and underwater. Caves are found all over the world. Cave explorers want to see what’s inside. We may think of all caves as being dark and barren. But caves can be gorgeous, filled with amazing formations and unusual animals. Caves lure adventurous people who love the excitement and challenge of seeing a place no one has ever seen before. We know that humans lived in caves as long as 30,000 years ago.
pages.brief: A natural hollow space in rock opens as a cave, large enough for a person to go inside and deep enough that sunlight never reaches part of it. The dark cave entrance is surrounded by rock, showing a place cave explorers want to see.

pages.text: Montana’s Lewis and Clark Caverns contain some of the largest limestone formations in the United States. Types of Caves Caves can form in several ways. Nature uses basic tools such as rock, water, and heat to carve these chambers in the earth. Karst Caves The ground is made of different types of rock. Some types, such as limestone, can dissolve in water. Water from the surface seeps through the soil or trickles through cracks in the ground. If the water hits limestone underground, it slowly dissolves the rock, creating a hollow space. Over millions of years, the water eats away at the rock and creates a karst cave.
pages.brief: Inside Montana’s Lewis and Clark Caverns, large limestone formations fill the cave. Water seeps through soil and cracks in the ground, reaches limestone underground, and slowly dissolves the rock to create a hollow karst cave over millions of years.

pages.text: Molten lava spills into the sea from a lava tube at Kilauea, Hawaii. Primary Caves and Lava Tubes In karst caves, seeping water dissolves existing rock and eventually creates a hole. But in primary caves, the rock contained a hollow space from its beginning. The rock was born with a cave-sized hole in it. Another type of rock cave forms when liquid magma or lava in volcanoes cools and turns solid. In some volcanoes, liquid lava flows over the ground in a stream. The surface of the lava stream quickly cools and turns solid. But the lava underneath stays hot and liquid, and keeps flowing. The flowing hot lava creates long tunnels through the solid lava rock. These long tunnel caves are called lava tubes.
pages.brief: Molten lava spills into the sea from a lava tube at Kilauea, Hawaii. A stream of lava has a cooled solid surface while hot liquid lava keeps flowing underneath, creating a long tunnel cave through the solid lava rock.

pages.text: Sailors explore a vast sea cave on the island of Corfu, Greece. Erosional Caves and Sea Caves Moving water, such as rivers or ocean waves, can carry grains of sand. Ever so slowly, these tough little grains grind away rock in a process called erosion. Erosion creates caves called erosional caves. Erosional caves are different from karst caves in that water physically grinds away the rock. In karst caves, water chemically dissolves the rock. A common kind of erosional cave is a sea cave. Sea caves form when ocean waves continually crash against cliffs, eventually digging out a hollow space.
pages.brief: Sailors explore a vast sea cave on the island of Corfu, Greece. Nearby, ocean waves crash against a cliff, carrying sand grains that slowly grind away rock. This erosion digs out the hollow space of the sea cave over time.

pages.text: Inside a massive ice cave formed beneath the Mendenhall Glacier, in the state of Alaska Caves don’t always form in rock. Glaciers are enormous moving masses of solid ice. At the top of a glacier, the Sun can melt some of the ice, which becomes a stream of warm water. The warm water flows down through cracks in the glacier toward the soil layer beneath. As it runs, the warmer water melts the ice around it, forming a glacier cave. You can also find caves underwater. Most underwater caves formed in the same way as caves on land, except the rock was under a lake or ocean. Some underwater caves were once dry caves that flooded when the sea level rose in an area.
pages.brief: Inside a massive ice cave beneath the Mendenhall Glacier in Alaska, smooth ice walls surround the space. A stream of warm meltwater has flowed down through cracks in the glacier, melting the ice around it to form the glacier cave.

pages.text: Hikers have natural light at the entrance to Milodon Cave, near Puerto Natales, Chile. Inside Caves Caves are made up of three main areas: the entrance, the twilight zone, and the dark zone. The entrance to a cave may be large or small. It can be a doorway into a mountain, a hole straight into the ground, or a crack in a boulder. The twilight zone is any part of the cave where some sunlight still seeps in. If you can see without a flashlight, you’re in the twilight zone. This zone is often cool and damp, and you can find animals and some plants living there. As you might guess from the name, there is no light at all in the dark zone. No plants grow there, but some fungi, molds, and animals have adapted to the total darkness.
pages.brief: Hikers stand at the entrance to Milodon Cave near Puerto Natales, Chile, where natural light reaches them. Beyond the entrance, the cave passes into a twilight zone with some sunlight and then a dark zone where no light reaches.

pages.text: Karst caves are the most common type of cave, so let’s take a closer look inside one. Water and dissolved limestone create all kinds of fantastic formations in these caves. Many people are familiar with stalactites and stalagmites. These form when water drips from a cave ceiling to the floor. The drops contain dissolved limestone. When the water dries or evaporates, it leaves behind bits of limestone. Bit by bit, the limestone builds up, creating stalactites on the ceiling and stalagmites on the floor. These formations only grow about 2 millimeters (about 0.08 in) a year. But they can reach over 10 meters (33 ft) long. Sometimes a stalactite and a stalagmite join to form a column. Helpful Hint Do you forget which is a stalactite and which is a stalagmite? The word stalactite contains the letter c. Think of it as standing for ceiling. Stalactites hang from the top of the cave. Stalagmite contains the letter g, which can stand for ground. Stalagmites point up from the ground of a cave.
pages.brief: Inside a karst cave, stalactites hang from the ceiling and stalagmites rise from the floor. Water drips from above, leaving dissolved limestone behind bit by bit. Where a stalactite and stalagmite join, they form a column.

pages.text: When water drops run down the sides of a cave, they leave behind trails of limestone. These trails can build up to form a drapery, or curtain of rock. Draperies can grow more than 3 meters (10 ft) long, and may be so thin that they are transparent. A soda straw formation is thin and hollow, like a straw for drinking soda pop. Another rare shape is called a cave pearl. These round formations may start as a grain of sand. The grain gets wet with water that contains dissolved limestone. When the water evaporates, the limestone is left behind. Over time, the limestone deposits build up and form thin layers—just like a pearl. It takes a very long time to build a formation, drop by drop—over many thousands of years.
pages.brief: Water drops run down a cave wall, leaving trails of limestone that build into a thin, transparent drapery of rock. Nearby, a thin hollow soda straw formation hangs, and a round cave pearl rests where limestone layers have built up drop by drop.

pages.text: Cave Inhabitants Creatures small and large make their homes in caves. Many scientists divide cave animals into three groups: animals that spend their entire lives in caves, animals that spend part of their lives in caves but can be found elsewhere, and animals that only visit caves. Some types of animals spend their entire lives in caves, and aren’t found anywhere else. They include certain millipedes, Crayfish centipedes, spiders, insects, crayfish, salamanders, and fish. These animals have adapted to survive in total darkness. Many of them are blind, and some have no eyes at all. Other kinds of animals live both in caves and outside. A good example of this are bats. Bats may spend every night in a cave but must go outside to find food. Other examples are some beetles, millipedes, centipedes, and salamanders.
pages.brief: In the darkness of a cave, blind fish, a crayfish, a salamander, a spider, a millipede, and a centipede live entirely underground. A bat hangs nearby; it may spend every night in the cave but must go outside to find food.

pages.text: Ancient cave-dwellers used this doorway in the Great Hall of Bulls, Lascaux, France. Many animals spend most of their time outside but visit caves for shelter, to rest, or to hunt for food. This group includes bears, foxes, pack rats, snakes, raccoons, moths, groundhogs, vultures, crickets, and of course, humans. Many humans have found the enclosed space of a cave to be a good place to live. In Andalucia, Spain, hundreds of people live in caves, while northern China has millions of human cave dwellers. Other places where people live in caves include Turkey, North Africa, and France. Artwork on cave walls and the remains of campfires show that humans have used caves as shelter for tens of thousands of years.
pages.brief: A natural rock doorway in the Great Hall of Bulls at Lascaux, France, shows where ancient cave-dwellers entered. Outside, a bear, fox, snake, raccoon, and moths may visit caves for shelter, rest, or hunting; humans have also used caves as shelter for tens of thousands of years.

pages.text: Prehistoric cave-dwelling artists painted beautiful horses and bulls on the walls of the famous Lascaux Cave in France. Do You Know? In 1940, four boys accidentally discovered one of the most famous art caves, France’s Lascaux Cave. They squeezed into a small hole, entering a large cavern with beautiful paintings of deer and bulls. Luckily, the boys were not hurt, but entering a cave without an experienced cave explorer or guide is a dangerous idea. Later, one of the boys became the cave’s main guide.
pages.brief: Prehistoric cave-dwelling artists painted beautiful horses and bulls on the walls of Lascaux Cave in France. Four boys squeeze through a small hole into a large cavern, discovering the paintings covering the cave walls around them.

pages.text: Caves are very fragile habitats. Many have almost no contact with the world outside. If something new comes into a cave, it can cause trouble for the animals that live there. Bats hibernate in caves. During hibernation, a bat’s body slows down, allowing it to go months Do You Know? without eating.
