Route 66 is also full of unique art, historic gas stations, and theaters. In addition, travelers can see live shows. For instance, you can see a Native American dance ceremony in New Mexico or a rodeo in Oklahoma. One thing’s for sure—you won’t be bored on Route 66!
pages.brief: Travelers stop along Route 66 to visit museums, motels, shops, historic gas stations, and theaters in every state the highway passes through. In New Mexico, people watch a Native American dance ceremony; in Oklahoma, a rodeo thrills spectators. Unique roadside art and live shows keep visitors entertained along the route.

pages.text: Cadillac Ranch sits in a pasture where cows graze. Cadillac Ranch In 1974, some artists buried ten Cadillacs nose down in a field, rear bumpers sticking straight up toward the sky. Now the cars are every color of the rainbow because visitors have covered them with spray paint. At the nearby VW Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, Texas, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.
pages.brief: In a Texas pasture where cows graze, ten Cadillacs stand nose-down in the dirt with their rear bumpers pointing toward the sky. Visitors have covered the cars with bright spray paint, giving them every color of the rainbow. Nearby at Slug Bug Ranch in Conway, five colorful Volkswagen Beetles stick out of the ground.

pages.text: Growing up, Elmer Long collected bottles and other items people had thrown away. Elmer’s Bottle Tree Ranch Folk artist Elmer Long built Bottle Tree Ranch out of recycled bottles, car parts, and other objects—including buffalo jawbones. When the desert wind blows through the open bottles, the air fills with music. Blue Whale What do you give the woman who has everything? Hugh Davis built his wife an 80- foot (24.4 m) blue whale for their anniversary. For many years, kids loved to slide and dive from the Blue Whale’s body into the swimming hole below. The Blue Whale of Catoosa, Oklahoma, has a boardwalk along its spine.
pages.brief: Folk artist Elmer Long stands among bottle trees made from recycled bottles, car parts, and buffalo jawbones; desert wind blows through the open bottles. Nearby, children slide and dive from an 80-foot blue whale built by Hugh Davis for his wife on their anniversary, with a boardwalk along its spine and a swimming hole below.

pages.text: Paul Bunyon, Chicken Boy, Gemini Giant, Atlanta, IL Los Angeles, CA Wilmington, IL A Land of Giants Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory built thousands of huge fiberglass statues. Businesses along Route 66 used them for advertising. The factory added costumes to turn them into cowboys, Native Americans, astronauts, and even chickens. Many of the biggest statues on Route 66 are food statues. Enormous oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones make for a mouthwatering ride. Look out the window near Collinsville, Illinois, and you may see the largest catsup bottle in the world! Brooks Catsup Bottle Water Tower, Collinsville, IL.
pages.brief: Along Route 66, enormous fiberglass statues advertise businesses: a cowboy, a Native American, an astronaut, and even a giant chicken stand beside the road. Other huge food statues show oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones. Near Collinsville, Illinois, the largest catsup bottle in the world rises like a water tower.

pages.text: Dinny cost $300,000 to build and was made from roadside materials. Dinosaurs by the Dozen On Route 66, you can be greeted by prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. Dinny is likely the largest concrete dinosaur in America. He is 150 feet (45.7 m) long and lives at a dinosaur park in Cabazon, California. Claude Bell built the park to attract visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn. The dinosaur park became famous. It was even featured in the 1985 movie Pee-wee’s Big Adventure. Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, is a popular feature at Cabazon Dinosaurs.
pages.brief: At Cabazon Dinosaurs in California, the huge concrete dinosaur Dinny stretches 150 feet long, while Mr. Rex, a three-story Tyrannosaurus rex, towers over visitors. Claude Bell built the dinosaur park to attract customers to his nearby Wheel Inn restaurant. The park became famous and appeared in the 1985 movie Pee-wee’s Big Adventure.

pages.text: Saving Route 66 With Route 66’s popularity came traffic— lots of it. Heavy traffic caused the highway to deteriorate. From 1956 through the 1980s, new interstates—high-speed highways with many lanes—were built around Route 66. As more travelers took interstates, businesses on Route 66 suffered, and many closed. Peeling paint, faded signs, and boarded-up windows became common sights. In 1999, the United States Congress passed a law to protect Route 66. The government offered money to help businesses and towns pay the cost of preserving important landmarks. Now Route 66 is Route 66 Red Rocker, growing popular again Fanning, MO as many return to seek its amusing artwork and creative spirit. The best way to catch the spirit of Route 66 is to drive it. You’re sure to have an unforgettable American experience of your own!
pages.brief: An old roadside business on Route 66 stands with peeling paint and boarded-up windows while new high-speed interstates carry travelers around it. After Congress passes a law in 1999, workers use government money to preserve important landmarks. Visitors return to drive Route 66 and enjoy its amusing artwork and creative spirit.

books.title: The Plague!
books.art_why: The Black Death is a 1300s historical event, before photographs, and this is not a biography of one named person.

pages.text: Spread of the Black Plague by Year Lubeck London Amsterdam Danzig ATLANTIC OCEAN Paris Kiev Vienna Nuremberg Venice Bordeaux Genoa Marseille BLACK Ragusa SEA Barcelona Rome Valencia Naples Constantinople MEDITERRANEAN SEA 1347 1349 1351 Mostly 1348 1350.
pages.brief: A wide historical map of Europe shows shaded regions and sea routes linking cities from London and Paris to Venice, Genoa, and Constantinople, with the Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts visible. Small marked zones suggest the plague’s spread year by year across the continent.

pages.text: The Fleas of Disease In the 1300s, no one had yet made the connection between germs and illness. The idea that bacteria or viruses could cause a cold, the flu, or other sickness was unknown. Many people at that time saw disease as a supernatural event. Some people blamed the plague on how the planets lined up. One doctor described how it could spread if a healthy person looked into an infected person’s eyes.
pages.brief: A medieval doctor in dark robes stands near a sick person, gesturing toward the patient’s eyes while worried townspeople watch. Above them, a night sky with planets suggests supernatural explanations, and the crowded room shows how people understood illness without knowing about germs.

pages.text: People also hadn’t made the connection between the plague and the fleas that were actually spreading the disease. These fleas most certainly had stowed away on the ships that docked at Messina. It was not until 1894— almost 550 years later—that scientists found the type of bacteria that caused the plague. These bacteria get into the gut of a type of flea that normally feeds on the blood of rats. The bacteria killed off the rats they normally lived with. The fleas were then forced to go looking for other animals to feed on, including people. How Rats and Fleas Helped Spread the Plague The plague bacteria 1 A rodent is infected. multiply in a flea’s gut. 2 A flea bites a rodent. 5 A person is infected. 4 A flea bites a person.
pages.brief: A cutaway diagram shows a flea biting a rodent, bacteria multiplying inside the flea’s gut, and the flea later biting a person. Nearby, rats and fleas move among docked ships, suggesting how the disease traveled from animals to humans.

pages.text: Filthy people and cities did not help. In the 1300s, human waste and garbage were often dumped in the streets of overcrowded cities. Bugs were regular houseguests. Getting bitten by fleas and other pests was a fact of life. Not all investigators are convinced that fleas were the only source of the Black Death. Other diseases could also cause deadly outbreaks. However, the bacterium in the fleas remains the leading suspect, based on the kinds of illness that people reported. What seems clear is that humans began passing this deadly disease to one another. A person’s pus, blood, or spit could infect others. In other words, a simple cough could give the sickness to the next victim. At that point, the plague became all but unstoppable.
pages.brief: A crowded medieval city street is littered with garbage and human waste while people go about daily life among bugs and pests. Fleas and rats appear near the residents, and a coughing person stands close to another, showing how infection could pass between people.

pages.text: Death Stalks Europe By 1348 the Black Death was spreading across Europe. Travelers and traders carried it to new areas. It often took weeks before an infected area knew something was horribly wrong. By then, it was too late to do anything about it. At the time, there was no treatment for such a serious disease. As the illness showed itself, victims experienced fever, vomiting, swelling, and strong pain. They might die quickly or live a few days. Historians think only one in five people who got the symptoms survived.
pages.brief: Travelers and traders move along roads and paths into a European town, carrying goods as the plague spreads. Inside, a feverish victim lies in pain while worried people stand near, and the scene suggests that weeks pass before anyone realizes something is horribly wrong.

pages.text: Bubonic Plague General: fever and lack of energy Symptoms Head: headache The word bubonic comes from buboes. They Lymph nodes: are painful swellings of the lymph nodes in the (buboes), neck, armpits, and groin. oozing of pus, In plague victims, buboes can blow up to the size of a chicken egg. They can even burst through the skin. Other forms of plague could attack the lungs, causing a bloody Stomach: nausea cough, or the blood, causing areas on the face, hands, and feet Joints: aches and pains to turn black. Bubonic plague bacteria start by attacking the lymph nodes in the neck, groin, and underarms. Lymph nodes are important organs of the immune system. They help the body fight disease. With plague, lymph nodes swell and blacken with poisoned blood and pus. They become boils called buboes. Plague can also infect the lungs, causing them to bleed. The disease soon reached France and England, spreading in every direction. By 1351, there was hardly a spot in Europe it had not reached.
pages.brief: A human body diagram shows painful buboes swelling at the neck, armpits, and groin, with areas for fever, headache, nausea, and joint aches. Nearby, a victim coughs blood, and darkened skin on hands and feet suggests other forms of the plague.

pages.text: Panic and a Prayer Once people realized that plague had come to their community, many panicked. Frightened families abandoned sick loved ones. Doctors and priests fled the places and people they served. City folk left for the countryside, thinking it would be safer there. By fleeing, though, they often helped spread the disease. Few people had good ideas about how to stop the disease. Desperate people tried useless cures. Many burned incense or wore flowers to cleanse the air. If nothing else, the smoke and flowers may have covered up the awful smells around them.
pages.brief: Frightened families abandon a sick loved one in a medieval home while doctors and priests hurry away. City folk leave for the countryside, and desperate people burn incense or hold flowers to cleanse the air, filling the scene with smoke and fearful faces.

pages.text: Many people turned to their faith in hope of rescue. Bands of Christians walked from town to town, hitting their own backs with spiked whips. They prayed that they would be forgiven for their sins and spared. In some areas, Christian groups wrongly blamed Jews for causing the plague. Many Jewish communities were attacked and their people driven off or killed. A few cities instead used common sense to try to control the disease. Port cities soon realized that visiting ships were one of its sources. They began to block ships that came from plague-infected areas. A forty-day waiting period was used to confirm that the ship’s crew were plague-free. Only then could they come ashore. Officials in some areas also figured out that stopping the movement of people slowed the spread of disease. Infected families couldn’t leave their houses. Officials set limits on travel and trade to and from their cities. Work crews buried victims as soon as possible for fear that their bodies could infect others. In some areas, though, public order had broken down. This made it difficult to force people to follow such rules.
pages.brief: Bands of Christians walk from town to town striking their own backs with spiked whips, praying for forgiveness. In another area, officials stop ships from plague-infected ports and keep infected families inside their houses, while work crews bury victims and public order breaks down.

pages.text: The Aftermath Imagine half the people of your city gone. The shops are empty of food and other goods. That was the experience of many people who survived the worst period of the Black Death. Historians can only guess at the death count. There were about eighty million Europeans before the Black Death struck. Experts think that 40 to 60 percent of those people died, though the death rate varied greatly by location. Cities were usually the hardest hit. The disease spread easily in crowded, dirty neighborhoods. Nearly 60 percent of Londoners died, along with half the people of Paris. After 1351, the plague slowed for reasons researchers are still trying to understand. Survivors may have built up resistance to the disease. The bacteria may also have changed to a less deadly form. Plague outbreaks happened again and again for the next five hundred years. None, though, ever matched the deadliness of the Black Death. After the plague, Europe was left a very different place. There was a huge shortage of workers. The lack of skilled craftspeople and laborers caused big problems. Workers were able to demand better pay and treatment.
pages.brief: A once-busy medieval city stands half-empty, with shops bare of food and goods. Survivors look over crowded, dirty neighborhoods while workers demand better pay, and a large drop in population is suggested by abandoned streets and empty market stalls.

pages.text: The invention of the heavy plow helped end food shortages following the plague years. It allowed farmers to till fields much faster by using horses rather than oxen to pull the plow. Fields were left unplanted or unharvested without peasants to work them. Farm animals died from a lack of care. Because of this, Europeans suffered food shortages and starvation. Survivors’ views about society and the meaning of life changed, too. Many began to question their belief in the church. Some challenged their rulers. The authority of these powerful individuals had proven useless in protecting the people they controlled. There were many examples of progress afterward. Farmers tried new practices to grow more food with fewer hands. Public health and medicine also saw changes for the better. More communities understood the importance of sanitation and cleanliness. They also put in place better ways to handle disease outbreaks.
pages.brief: Farmers use a heavy plow pulled by horses to till fields faster, while peasants work around them. Other fields lie unplanted or unharvested, farm animals wander without care, and townspeople discuss sanitation, medicine, and new ways to grow more food with fewer hands.

pages.text: Rebirth Modern medicine has made another outbreak of the Black Death all but impossible. Modern medicines can quickly cure most cases of plague. Better public sanitation and health programs also help control the spread of most forms of disease. Alexander Fleming Antibiotics: The Miracle Drug Antibiotics are a recent development in human history. Before the mid-1800s, some healers recognized that certain plant molds and other fungi attacked bacteria. In the 1800s, more research led to a better understanding of the link between microbes and disease. Then in the 1920s, Scottish biologist Alexander Fleming accidentally discovered a plant mold that destroyed a dangerous form of bacteria. Out of his research came the wonder drug penicillin, which is capable of killing many forms of bacterial infection. Fleming was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945 for his breakthrough work.
pages.brief: A modern laboratory scene shows Scottish biologist Alexander Fleming examining a plant mold that destroyed dangerous bacteria, with medicine and sanitation workers nearby. The image connects his accidental discovery of penicillin with modern antibiotics that can quickly cure most plague cases.

pages.text: In the mid-1300s, the mystery and horror of the Black Death terrified Europe. Many people who lived through the Black Death believed it was the end of the world. In terms of death rates, it remains the most destructive event in European history. At the same time, some historians link the disaster to helpful changes that followed. From the late 1300s until the 1600s, Europe underwent big changes. This period, known as the Renaissance, was a time of great improvements in medicine, science, and art. Renaissance means “rebirth” in French. After the Black Death, a period of rebirth was exactly what Europe needed. The Peasants Rise King Richard II faces the peasant army in 1381. England went through a period of economic shock in the aftermath of the Black Plague. Farmers and laborers were in such great demand that they saw their wages rise up to 40 percent from the 1340s to the 1380s. This big social shift so alarmed the upper classes and nobility that royal officials passed a law attempting to fix wages for peasants at the levels they had been before the Black Death. They passed another law to prevent peasants from leaving their home villages in search of better jobs. These crackdowns led to a major uprising known as the Peasants’ Revolt in 1381.
pages.brief: King Richard II faces a large peasant army in 1381, while across Europe the Renaissance brings changes in medicine, science, and art. A medieval European town gives way to new ideas, and the scene suggests a period of rebirth after the Black Death.

books.title: Water Cities
books.art_why: The keyword check suggests drawing for this illustrated global tour.

pages.text: Water Cities Around the World.
pages.brief: A broad view of Earth with the continents Europe, Asia, Africa, South America, North America, and Oceania visible, linked by rivers, canals, and coastlines. Small clusters of buildings sit beside water in different regions, introducing the idea of water cities and people living near water around the world.

pages.text: Europe Amsterdam, Netherlands Amsterdam is another European city that is famous for its canals. It is the capital and largest city in the Netherlands. About one-third of the Netherlands is below sea level, and one-sixth is built on reclaimed land—land that was once underwater. The city of Amsterdam is about 2 meters (6.6 ft.) below sea level. The water was pumped out so people could build there. Pumping stations keep the land dry. Amsterdam was surrounded by a moat in the 1500s. More people moved there in the 1600s as the city grew. Workers drained swamps and built three new canals around the downtown area. Amsterdam Amsterdam has more than 1,200 bridges over its canals.
pages.brief: Amsterdam, Netherlands, with canals, bridges, and buildings beside the water. A pumping station works to keep the low land dry, while workers drain swampy ground and build three new canals around the downtown area. The city sits about two meters below sea level, surrounded by more than 1,200 bridges.

pages.text: Since that time, 161 other canals have been built. Amsterdam’s canals total over 100 kilometers (62 mi.) in length. They divide the city into almost 100 small islands joined by over 1,200 bridges. The canals were the city’s main transportation routes for centuries. Now they are mainly used by smaller boats. However, they are still an important part of Amsterdam’s character. Reine, Norway A tiny fishing village more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.) above the Arctic Circle has earned the nickname “The Most Beautiful Place in the World.” Reine, Norway, is located along the coast of one of the Lofoten Islands. The village offers fishing, kayaking, skiing, whale watching, hiking, and beautiful beaches. It’s also a perfect place for amazing views of the northern lights.
pages.brief: Amsterdam’s canal network divides the city into almost one hundred small islands joined by over 1,200 bridges, with smaller boats moving through the canals. In the far north, Reine, Norway, a tiny fishing village on a Lofoten Island coast, sits above the Arctic Circle, with fishing boats, kayakers, hikers, beaches, and northern lights overhead.

pages.text: ASIA Singapore is one of the world’s busiest port cities. Singapore Asia Singapore Singapore is the world’s only island city-state— an island that is both a city and an independent country. It is made up of about sixty-three islands. Singapore depends on goods from other places since it has few natural resources of its own. Singapore is much larger than it was before the 1960s. Like Amsterdam, it has grown by reclaiming land that was once underwater. However, instead of pumping out the water, Singapore has added land by dumping rocks and sand into the sea. A project begun in 2016 will use Amsterdam’s methods to increase its land area.
pages.brief: Singapore, a busy port city and island city-state made up of about sixty-three islands, with ships and docks along the water. Workers dump rocks and sand into the sea to add new land, expanding the city beyond its old size, while a new project plans to use Amsterdam’s methods to increase the land area.

pages.text: Dubai, United Arab Emirates Dubai is a modern city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). One of its largest building projects is Palm Islands—three human-made islands shaped like palm trees. The islands are being built along the coast by piling up huge amounts of sand and rock. They are adding hundreds of miles of coastline to the city as well as thousands of homes. Construction began in 2001. The first island was finished in late 2016. ASIA Dubai INDIAN OCEAN Palm Jumeirah is one of the largest human-made islands in the world. A curved seawall protects the island from strong waves and storms.
pages.brief: Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on the coast beside the Indian Ocean, where three human-made Palm Islands are shaped like palm trees. Huge amounts of sand and rock are piled up along the coast to add coastline and homes, and a curved seawall protects Palm Jumeirah from strong waves and storms.

pages.text: The village of Ganvié is sometimes called Ganvié the Venice of Africa. AFRICA Africa Ganvié, Benin Ganvié (GAWN-vye) is the largest stilt village in Africa. The village is located in the middle of Lake Nokoué (NOHK-we) in the country of Benin. Ganvié has about twenty thousand people and three thousand buildings. Only the school and a cemetery are located on land. This water village began at least three hundred years ago. During that time, a powerful tribe called the Fon captured and sold members of other tribes into slavery. The Fons’ religion did not let them pursue people who lived on water. Another tribe, the Tofinu, escaped to Lake Nokoué to avoid capture. They built the stilt village and set up a way of life that continues to this day. The name of their village means “we survived.”
pages.brief: Ganvié, Benin, the largest stilt village in Africa, stands in the middle of Lake Nokoué with about twenty thousand people and three thousand buildings above the water. Only the school and a cemetery sit on land, while the Tofinu built the village on stilts after escaping capture by the Fon.

pages.text: Most villagers make their living by fishing. They keep and breed fish using underwater fences. They also keep chickens and goats on patches of grass that grow in the water. People travel in long, narrow canoes. Fadiouth (Shell Island), Senegal The people of Fadiouth (fad-YOOT), Senegal, live on an island made of clamshells. For over three hundred years, they have been eating clams and recycling the shells. The shells are held in place by the roots of trees and reeds. The island’s buildings and streets are also made of shells.
pages.brief: In Ganvié, villagers fish from long, narrow canoes and keep fish behind underwater fences. Chickens and goats stand on patches of grass growing in the water. In Fadiouth, Senegal, people live on an island made of clamshells, with buildings and streets built from shells held in place by tree roots and reeds.

pages.text: Uros SOUTH The Uru people make reed canoes for transportation. AMERICA South America Uros Floating Village, Peru Like the Tofinu, the people of Uros Floating Village moved to water for safety. The Uru people escaped to Lake Titicaca over five hundred years ago when other people took over their land. About two thousand Uru now live on about seventy floating islands made of reeds. The islands, which are 1.2 to 2.4 meters (4–8 ft.) thick, break down from the bottom. New reeds must be added on top all the time. The Uru people also use the reeds to make canoes, homes, and furniture.
pages.brief: Uros Floating Village, Peru, on Lake Titicaca, where about two thousand Uru people live on roughly seventy floating islands made of reeds. The reed islands are thick but break down from the bottom, so new reeds are added on top all the time. Uru people make reed canoes, homes, and furniture.

pages.text: NORTH AMERICA Mexcaltitán Mexcaltitán sits on a long sandbar off the coast of Mexico. North America Mexcaltitán, Mexico The Aztec people ruled large parts of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. A story says that they came from an island near the Pacific coast of Mexico. The story also says that their gods told them to find a new place to live. After looking for two hundred years, they founded a city that is now known as Mexico City.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán, Mexico, sits on a long sandbar off the Pacific coast. A story says the Aztec people came from an island near the coast. They ruled large parts of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, and their gods told them to find a new place to live. After searching two hundred years, they founded Mexico City.

pages.text: Some historians think that Mexcaltitán (mes-kahl-tee-TAHN) is where the Aztec people came from. This small human-made island is in the same place as the Aztec island shown on a 1579 map. Also, the early people used small canoes almost exactly like the ones used there today. Mexcaltitán is home to about eight hundred people. This water town is sometimes called the Mexican Venice. In summer, during the rainy season, boats are the only way to travel through the streets. Children play “water soccer” on the island’s underwater soccer field. Locals boat and swim in the streets during the flood season in Mexcaltitán.
pages.brief: Mexcaltitán, a small human-made island off Mexico, with about eight hundred people and small canoes like those used by early people. Historians connect it to an Aztec island on a 1579 map. In summer floods, boats are the only way through the streets, and children play water soccer on an underwater soccer field while locals boat and swim.

pages.text: Auckland is New Zealand’s largest city. AUSTRALIA Auckland Oceania Auckland, New Zealand This city of 1.5 million people is on the North Island of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. It is located between two large harbors on an isthmus less than 2 kilometers (1.24 mi.) wide at its narrowest point. Auckland’s nickname is the “City of Sails.” About one-sixth of its residents own a boat. The city has thousands of beaches. Water-related activities include swimming, surfing, fishing, diving, kayaking, and beach horseback riding.
pages.brief: Auckland, New Zealand, on the North Island between two large harbors on a narrow isthmus in the South Pacific Ocean. The city of 1.5 million people has thousands of beaches, and about one-sixth of residents own a boat. People swim, surf, fish, dive, kayak, and ride horses on the beach.

pages.text: California Italy Aircraft carrier People and Water Many kinds of water cities exist besides the ones you’ve just read about. For instance, Italy has a tiny fishing town with brightly colored homes built on steep cliffs. Northern California has a floating community made up of houseboats. People in the military may spend months living on aircraft carriers. Water means different things to different people. For residents of water cities, it may mean fun, work, safety, a connection with nature, or a way of life. The world’s water cities are proof that people can make a home for themselves just about anywhere.
pages.brief: A tiny Italian fishing town with brightly colored homes built on steep cliffs, a floating community of houseboats in Northern California, and an aircraft carrier where military people may live for months. These scenes show different kinds of water cities and the many ways people connect with water—for fun, work, safety, nature, or a way of life.

books.title: Slithery Snakes
books.art_why: Snakes are living animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Snakes are among the animal kingdom’s most amazing predators. Their ability to adapt to the natural world has enabled them to survive on every continent except Antarctica. Slithery Snakes provides students with a comprehensive look at these fascinating creatures that play an important role in Earth’s natural environment. Introduction Snakes are unusual animals. They are reptiles, a class of creatures that also includes lizards and turtles. Long and limbless, snakes come in many lengths, patterns, and colors. To date, scientists have identified several thousand species of snakes. They live in oceans, in trees, and on land, and they have adapted to survive in many unusual ways. Written by Ned Jensen.
pages.brief: Snakes of many lengths, patterns and colours: one swimming in ocean water, one coiled on a tree branch, one crossing dry land. A lizard and a turtle rest nearby on rock, all shown as reptiles, with the snakes long and limbless.

pages.text: Where Snakes Live Snakes are found on every continent except Antarctica. Some places, however, are snake-free zones. For instance, no snakes live in the wild on certain islands, such as Ireland, New Zealand, and Iceland. Depending on the species, snakes in the wild may live up to twenty-five years. Biggest and Smallest One of the largest snakes is the green anaconda. A full-grown green anaconda can be close to 10 meters (33 ft.) long and weigh more than 230 kilograms (507 lb.). By contrast, one of the smallest snakes is the thread snake. It is only about 10 centimeters (4 in.) long.
pages.brief: A huge green anaconda lies heavy in shallow river water, its thick body close to ten metres long, while nearby a tiny thread snake no wider than a shoelace rests on soil — the biggest and smallest snakes shown side by side for size.

pages.text: Snake Traits Like all reptiles, snakes are cold-blooded, meaning their body temperature changes as the temperature around them changes. If a snake needs to warm up, it basks in the sun. If the snake needs to cool down, it rests in the shade. Snakes become much less active in winter. Some snakes that live through cold winters do not hibernate; instead, they find a place underground or beneath a rock pile or log to stay warm. Another way snakes remain warm in winter is by gathering in a group and looping around each other to share body heat.
pages.brief: A snake stretched flat on a sunlit rock, warming itself, while another rests in cool shade beneath a bush. Nearby a group of snakes loop around one another in a tangled knot, sharing body heat, and one disappears under a rock pile beside a fallen log.

pages.text: A snake’s skeleton is made up of a long backbone, ribs, a skull, and a jawbone. Its hard, bony skull protects its brain. Snakes can have from about 150 to more than 400 vertebrae. Their many vertebrae allow them to move in a multitude of ways. A very limber snake usually has more vertebrae. Like all reptiles, a snake has scales on its body. In addition to providing protection, scales are nearly waterproof, helping keep the snake dry. Scales grow from the snake’s skin. Some scales are colorful. Other snakes have scales for camouflage, which helps them blend in with their surroundings. Since snakes have no arms or legs, they use their muscles and scales to move. The scales on their belly tightly grip the surface beneath them. Their muscles help them move from side to side, or slither, along the ground. Some even use their muscles and scales to climb trees.
pages.brief: A snake's skeleton laid out: long backbone with ribs, skull and jawbone. Beside it a live snake slithers, belly scales gripping the ground, muscles pushing it from side to side; another climbs a tree trunk, and one with camouflaging scales blends against mottled bark.

pages.text: Snake scales look like a single sheet of skin. Snakes don’t actually shed skin. Instead, they shed the outer layers of their scales. Snakes usually shed up to four times per year. This is called molting. During molting, a snake rubs against a hard object such as a rock or log. Rubbing helps its skin stretch and split. Then the snake crawls out and leaves it behind. Snakes shed for several reasons. Young snakes shed more often than mature snakes because they are still growing. Unlike the skin of other animals, a snake’s skin does not stretch as the snake grows. Another reason snakes shed is to get rid of parasites that may have attached to their old skin.
pages.brief: A snake rubs its head against a rough rock, its old outer skin splitting and peeling away, while behind it a shed skin lies crumpled on the ground. Another snake crawls free of its loosened covering beside a log.

pages.text: Scales protect a snake’s eyes, as well as its body. Unlike many animals, snakes do not have eyelids, and their eyes do not move. Instead, each eye is covered with a clear scale that protects the eye from drying out. Because of this, snakes can’t blink. Another difference between snakes and other animals is their ears. Snakes do not have ears on the outside of their skull. Instead, they listen through their jawbone. Sound vibrations pass through the jawbone to the inner ear, which sends a signal to the snake’s brain.
pages.brief: Close view of a snake's head: each eye covered by a clear scale, open and unblinking, with no eyelids. Its head rests against the ground, the jawbone shown as the place where sound vibrations travel as the snake listens.

pages.text: Another important feature of a snake is its tongue. A snake uses its forked tongue to smell. When its tongue is out, scent particles stick to it. The snake pulls its tongue back and touches the roof of its mouth where a special organ identifies the scent particles. Certain snakes, such as pythons and boas, are able to sense the heat of warm-blooded animals nearby. Pits near a snake’s eyes can sense even the slightest change in the temperature around them. Other snakes, known as pit vipers, use two sensitive pits to send a heat image to their brain. The snake can “see” its prey through the heat given off by the prey’s body. This adaptation helps them judge distances while hunting in the dark.
pages.brief: A snake's forked tongue flickers out, scent particles clinging to it. In darkness a pit viper's head shows the small pits near its eyes as it faces a warm-bodied mouse, sensing the animal's heat while hunting at night.

pages.text: Hunting and Eating Snakes are carnivores, or meat eaters. They eat other animals in several ways. Some snakes inject venom, which is a type of toxin, when they bite prey. Other snakes, called constrictors, squeeze prey to death. Some snakes sneak up on their prey, grab it with their powerful jaws, and swallow it alive. Most snakes’ upper and lower jaws are loosely connected. This allows a snake to spread its jaws and open its mouth wide enough to swallow large objects. Snakes’ teeth are mainly designed for catching and holding prey. Their fangs and regular teeth are curved backward, which pushes the food toward their throat. They are even able to push their breathing tube out of their mouth so they can breathe as they swallow their prey whole. Once prey has been swallowed, a snake uses its powerful muscles to move it into the stomach and intestines. Strong acids produced by the walls of the stomach dissolve the prey into a liquid-like mass for easy digestion.
pages.brief: A constrictor coils tightly around prey, while another snake, jaws spread wide, swallows a large animal whole and pushes its breathing tube out. Backward-curving teeth hold the meal; inside, strong stomach acids dissolve the prey into a liquid mass.

pages.text: How Snakes Are Born Most snakes that live in cold areas mate in late spring or early summer. Snakes that live in warmer areas may mate at any time of year. Once they mate, the male snake usually leaves. About two-thirds of all female snakes lay eggs in a safe place and then leave. Snake eggs have soft, leathery shells. Baby snakes grow inside the eggs, and most develop sharp teeth to cut through the egg to hatch. Once a baby snake hatches, it must survive on its own. It is not easy to survive because birds, some mammals, and other snakes eat baby snakes. Some types of female snakes, such as rattlesnakes, hold their eggs inside their body until they hatch. Others, such as common garter snakes, also give birth to live young.
pages.brief: A female snake lays soft, leathery eggs in a hidden safe place and leaves them. Inside one egg a baby snake develops, a sharp tooth ready to cut free. A hatchling emerges alone as a bird and a mammal watch, and a garter snake gives birth to live young.

pages.text: Venomous Snakes Some, but not all, snakes produce venom. Venom is injected through fangs, which are located on a snake’s jaws. Venom is produced in sacs behind a snake’s eyes. Some fangs are hollow so the venom can flow through them from these sacs.
pages.brief: Head of a venomous snake with mouth open to show fangs on the jaw, hollow fangs through which venom flows from sacs sitting behind the eyes, the sacs and the path down the fang shown clearly.

pages.text: Snakes use venom for both defense and attack. They usually inject more venom when they bite in defense. Snakes’ venom paralyzes their prey. Some inject the prey with venom and let it go. Then they use their sense of smell and heat sensors to track the prey until it dies. Other snakes use their teeth or body to hold on to the prey until it dies. Then they eat it. Fewer than half of venomous snakes have venom that is strong enough to kill humans. Venom versus Poison Venom and poison are not the same thing. Poison is absorbed, eaten, or breathed in, while venom is injected into the victim through a bite or sting. Other animals, such as scorpions and certain insects, inject venom by stinging.
pages.brief: A venomous snake strikes in defence at a larger animal, then a second snake bites prey and releases it, following the scent and heat until the prey stops. Beside them a scorpion and an insect sting, injecting venom.

pages.text: Conclusion Snakes are among the animal kingdom’s fiercest predators. Snakes have survived in most environments because their senses have adapted to the natural world in specific ways. Whether they are long or short, large or tiny, venomous strikers or constrictors, snakes are fascinating animals that play an important role in Earth’s natural environment.
pages.brief: A long snake and a tiny one, a striking venomous snake and a constrictor wrapped around a branch, all shown together among woodland and water — fierce predators whose senses are adapted to the natural world around them.

books.title: Acadia National Park
books.art_why: Acadia is a real national park today, with modern visitors, wildlife, and landmarks that can be photographed.

pages.text: Acadia National Park Maine I C N T L A N A T A C E O Maine.
pages.brief: A broad natural view of Acadia National Park in Maine, where land meets the sea under open sky. Shore and calm water fill the scene, with no people present. The quiet coastal park setting introduces the place.

pages.text: Land That Meets the Sea Today, Acadia is one of the most popular national parks in the United States. More than two million people visit each year. The park includes beautiful coastline, islands, forests, lakes, mountains, and rocks. It packs a lot of variety into a small space. Acadia’s water, rocks, and vibrant fall colors make for a lovely combination.
pages.brief: Many families and tourists visit Acadia National Park, spread across coastline, islands, forests, lakes, mountains, and rocks. Fall colors brighten the trees, and water and rocks make a vibrant combination in the small, varied park.

pages.text: The largest part of Acadia National Park is on Mount Desert Island. More than twenty mountains rise from the sea here. At 1,530 feet (466 m), Cadillac Mountain is the tallest. Because of its early sunrise and amazing view, it’s also the most crowded. Acadia has more than 40 miles (64 km) of coastline. Because Acadia’s coast is young, sandy shores are rare. Waves shift around what sand there is, along with rocks and other material. President Barack Obama and his family hike Cadillac Mountain in 2010.
pages.brief: President Barack Obama and his family hike on Cadillac Mountain, surrounded by more than twenty mountains rising from the sea on Mount Desert Island. The tallest mountain has an early sunrise and amazing view, while Acadia’s young coastline below has rare sandy shores and waves shifting sand and rocks.

pages.text: A child studies an Acadia tide pool (main). A starfish, or sea star, rests in a tide pool (inset). During low tides, the ocean leaves behind pools of water. Inside these pools live sea stars, sea cucumbers, hot pink seaweed, and other living things.
pages.brief: A child kneels beside an Acadia tide pool and studies the shallow water. Nearby, a sea star rests in a pool left by low tide, with sea cucumbers and hot pink seaweed visible among other living things. The pool sits along the shore.

pages.text: Tide pools come and go—after all, they are created by tides, which also come and go. Acadia’s tide can rise and fall 12 feet (4 m) during a day. It’s best to visit tide pools when the tide is going out. You’ll have more time to explore them. When the tide is in, some beaches disappear completely! Tide pools return when the tide goes out.
pages.brief: Tide pools along Acadia’s shore appear and disappear as the tide rises and falls twelve feet during a day. One beach is covered by incoming water, while shallow pools remain in the rocks. The tide is going out, leaving more time to explore.

pages.text: The American kestrel is the smallest falcon in North America—and in Acadia. Wildlife Acadia is one of the best bird-watching spots in the country—338 kinds of birds have been sighted there. Each autumn, strong winds push thousands of raptors south as they migrate from Canada to warmer areas for the winter. Cadillac Mountain offers a close look as these hawks and kestrels fly overhead.
pages.brief: An American kestrel, the smallest falcon in North America, perches in Acadia. Overhead, hawks and kestrels fly past Cadillac Mountain during autumn migration, when strong winds push thousands of raptors south from Canada toward warmer areas for winter. Bird-watchers watch the birds from the mountain.

pages.text: This peregrine chick has just been banded by a park wildlife biologist. Leg bands mark birds so biologists can study what they do and where they go. Birds banded at Acadia have been seen in several states and Canada. Return of the Falcon Peregrine falcons are one of the fastest animals on Earth. Long ago, they nested on Acadia’s Mount Desert Island. Their speed didn’t save them from humans, though, whose activities killed many of them. By the 1960s, peregrine falcons had disappeared from Acadia. In 1973, the park began efforts to bring the falcons back. Since 1991, falcon chicks have been born in the park every year.
pages.brief: A park wildlife biologist holds a peregrine chick that has just been banded, with a small leg band visible. The chick is on Mount Desert Island in Acadia. The scene recalls peregrine falcons returning to nest in the park, where chicks have been born every year since 1991.

pages.text: American mink Other parts of Maine have lots of black bears and moose. Acadia has a few of these, but it mostly has smaller mammals, such as foxes, mink, and porcupine. Why small? Because Acadia is not a big park, and that limits the size of animals found there.
pages.brief: An American mink stands near the edge of a natural area in Acadia, with a fox and a porcupine nearby. The park has mostly smaller mammals, while other parts of Maine have many black bears and moose. Acadia is not a big park, which limits the size of animals found there.

pages.text: A Park Made Piece by Piece The most amazing fact about Acadia may be that it became a national park at all. Native people, called the Wabanaki, lived on the land that is now Maine for 12,000 years. Wabanaki means “People of the Dawnland.” Five different tribes united to be the Wabanaki. They made canoes out of birch trees, and fished, hunted, and gathered plants around the area known today as Acadia. In the 1600’s, French settlers arrived and took land from the Wabanaki. When British settlers began moving north in the 1700’s, there was much conflict between the French and British. These conflicts, and diseases brought by European settlers, killed many Wabanaki people and forced others to move away. Although much of Maine was taken by these settlers, the Wabanaki remained in smaller numbers.
pages.brief: Wabanaki people in birch-bark canoes fish, hunt, and gather plants around the land that is now Acadia. Five tribes united as the Wabanaki, who lived in Maine for 12,000 years. French and British settlers later arrived, took land, and brought conflict and disease that harmed the Wabanaki.

pages.text: After Maine became a state in 1820, rich people from big, Eastern cities came to the rocky coastline. The Wabanaki sold baskets, handmade from sweetgrass and birch. The rich people who came to buy land and build fancy summer homes bought them. The Wabanaki Today Five separate tribes joined together to become the Wabanaki. These tribes, or nations, can be found today in Northern Maine and parts of Canada. Those who live near Acadia continue the traditions of their ancestors by building canoes and baskets. They also act as guides for hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, and educate people at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market. Wabanaki people use bark and wood from local birch trees to make their canoes.
pages.brief: Wabanaki people make baskets from sweetgrass and birch and sell them near Acadia’s rocky coastline, where wealthy visitors build fancy summer homes. Today five Wabanaki tribes live in northern Maine and parts of Canada. Those near Acadia build canoes and baskets, guide hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, and teach at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market.

pages.text: By the early 1900s, a few rich landowners had the idea of buying land in order to protect it. A man named George Dorr and others began to donate land to create a park that would preserve the area. By 1913 they had acquired 5,000 acres (20 sq km), which they gave to the government. In 1919 all that land became a national park. The Story of Dorr George Dorr lived alone in a grand house on Mount Desert Island. By the time he died in 1944, he had spent all his money buying land, then turning around and donating it. But Dorr had made his dream come true: Acadia had become a national park. After his death it kept growing, piece by piece, like a patchwork quilt. Even today, landowners continue to donate land around Acadia. Dorr was the park’s and would remain so for twenty-five years.
pages.brief: George Dorr stands near a grand house on Mount Desert Island, looking over land he worked to protect. Other landowners join him in donating land, and by 1919 the gathered acres become a national park. The park grows piece by piece, like a patchwork quilt, as landowners continue to give land.

pages.text: Two young visitors walk on Sand Beach after a hike in Acadia. Conclusion Acadia National Park is a place where sea and mountain meet. People come to see them meet, to breathe the salty air, and, of course, to watch the Sun rise. After greeting the new day, there is plenty more to see and do in Acadia. Visitors can hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle. If you ever get the chance to visit, do!
pages.brief: Two young visitors walk on Sand Beach after a hike in Acadia. Sea and mountain meet nearby, and the setting shows why people come to breathe salty air and watch the Sun rise. Later they might hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle.

books.title: Grasslands
books.art_why: Grasslands, their plants, animals and the people who use them exist today, so real photographs fit.

pages.text: The Grasslands Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Deserts, rainforests, oceans, and tundra are examples of biomes. So are grasslands. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. One is latitude, or how far a location is from the equator. Another is elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. Climate, land, and water are also important building blocks of biomes, as are plants and animals. Grasslands are huge open plains where grasses are the main vegetation. Some have scattered trees, while others are treeless. Grasslands don’t have forests mainly due to fires as well as low and unpredictable rainfall. Grassland Fires Lightning often causes grassland fires. Some grassland plants need fire in order for their seeds to sprout. Plants that burn help to make the soil healthy. Grasses can survive fires because they grow from their roots, which do not get damaged. Trees and shrubs with bark that resists fire also survive.
pages.brief: A vast open plain covered in grass stretches to the horizon, with a few scattered trees on one side and bare treeless grass on the other. In another part of the plain, dry grass burns after a lightning strike while green grasses sprout again from undamaged roots.

pages.text: Earth’s Grassland Regions Grasslands stretch over much of Earth’s land. Although many exist, the two main types of grasslands are tropical and temperate. Grasslands cover about one-fourth of Earth’s surface land and close to half of the land not covered by ice. Every continent besides Antarctica has grasslands, which are mainly found between deserts and forests. Various types of grasslands exist because of differences in temperature, soil, and rainfall, but there are two main types. Tropical grasslands are in hot tropical climates between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. The main plants are grasses and other short nonwoody plants. Some shrubs and trees are also present.
pages.brief: A hot tropical grassland under strong sun, filled with grasses and other short nonwoody plants, with some shrubs and a few trees standing among them. The wide grassy land spreads out between drier ground on one side and denser forest far off on the other.

pages.text: Temperate grasslands are found in cool temperate climates outside the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. By far the most common plants are grasses and other similar plants. Trees and shrubs generally only grow along rivers and other permanent water sources. Grasslands have grass of different heights, depending on rainfall. Drier grasslands have shorter grass. Wetter grasslands have taller grass—up to 4 meters (13 ft.) tall in some places. Some grasslands are home to huge herds of grazing animals.
pages.brief: A cool temperate grassland where grasses grow in patches of different heights, tallest where rain is heaviest, with trees and shrubs only along a river. In the distance, a huge herd of grazing animals moves slowly across the open grass.

pages.text: Animals must be careful when gathering at water holes. They are more vulnerable to predators there. Tropical Grasslands Tropical grasslands are located in large areas of Africa, India, Australia, and South America. By far the largest is in Africa. Almost half of Africa is grasslands. Tropical grasslands in Africa as well as some other areas are called savannas. The climate in tropical grasslands is usually warm or hot year-round. Average rainfall is 51–127 centimeters (20–50 in.) a year. Summer often has frequent thunderstorms. Plants benefit from the water and grow fast, turning everything green, and rivers and water holes fill up. Animals breed in summer, when there is plenty of food and water. During the dry season, usually in winter, rivers and water holes often dry up. Vegetation turns brown, and many fires happen.
pages.brief: A group of animals gathers warily at a water hole on an African savanna, watching for predators. Dark thunderclouds build over the hot grassland as summer rain falls; in another view the same water hole has dried and the vegetation has turned brown.

pages.text: Trees in tropical grasslands have important adaptations that allow them to survive the long dry season. Some store water in their thick trunks. Others have long taproots that reach down to where water is always present. Thick bark allows some trees to survive fires. Tropical grasslands differ widely in how much rainfall they receive, and rainfall affects how many trees grow. The wettest grasslands are nearly 40 percent trees, while the driest grasslands have none. Along with rainfall, soil quality plays a role in the kinds of vegetation that grow. Heavy rainfall tends to wash nutrients from the soil, leaving only a thin layer of humus. This top layer of soil is made up of decomposing organic material, which provides most of the nutrients. With little humus, the soil is generally not very rich in these areas. Baobab trees store water in their thick trunks (left). Kans grass can grow up to 3 meters (10 ft.) in height (right).
pages.brief: A baobab tree stands with a thick trunk swollen with stored water, and tall kans grass rises nearby. Below ground, long taproots reach down toward water, and thick bark covers a trunk that has survived fire on the dry tropical grassland.

pages.text: Many different kinds of animals live in tropical grasslands, and each region is different from the others. In Australia, bats, rodents, and kangaroos are common. Big cats and hoofed mammals abound in Africa. Capybaras, the world’s largest rodent, live in South American grasslands, along with monkeys, marsh deer, and giant anacondas. Indian grasslands are home to leopards, rhinos, and crocodiles. Birds live in all of these grasslands, along with billions of insects. Many animals in tropical grasslands migrate during the dry season to find food. On the African savanna, each species of hoofed animal is adapted to eat slightly different kinds or parts of plants. This allows them to live together without competing for food. Spotlight on the Serengeti Perhaps the best-known tropical grassland is Africa’s Serengeti Plain, in Tanzania. The Serengeti is home to elephants, giraffes, lions, cheetahs, hyenas, ostriches, and many other animals. Poaching— the illegal hunting of animals—is a major threat to Serengeti wildlife, even though much of the area is a national park. Black rhinoceroses and African wild dogs are endangered. Elephants and cheetahs are also in serious trouble.
pages.brief: Tropical grassland animals are shown across the plains: kangaroos and bats in Australia, capybaras and monkeys in South America, leopards and rhinos in India. On the Serengeti Plain, elephants, giraffes, lions, cheetahs, hyenas and ostriches stand among the grasses.

pages.text: Some temperate grasslands, like this one in Turkey, have explosions of wildflowers. Temperate Grasslands Temperate grasslands have few trees. These cooler grasslands go by different names in different parts of the world. They’re called prairies and plains in North America and steppes in Europe and Asia. In Southern Africa they’re known as veldts. In South America they’re called pampas. The climate in temperate grasslands varies with the location. Closer to the tropics, hot summers and mild winters are typical. Areas farther north or south have warm summers and cold, windy winters, often with snow and ice. Rainfall also varies. Closer to deserts, temperate grasslands may only get about 25 centimeters (10 in.) of rain each year. Areas near forests may get 89 centimeters (35 in.) of rain. Rainfall is most common in spring and early summer. In late summer, the soil dries out and grasses turn yellow.
pages.brief: A temperate grassland in Turkey bursts with wildflowers spreading across the low grass, with very few trees in sight. The colorful flowers cover the cool grassland in every direction under an open sky.

pages.text: Grasses in roots. The roots and help keep the soil from washing away. The difference between summer and winter in temperate grasslands is often much greater than in tropical grasslands. Summer temperatures can be above 38°C (100°F), while winter temperatures can fall as low as –40°C (–40°F). Another difference is the smaller amount of rainfall. Lighter rains wash away fewer soil nutrients, so these nutrients build up. This creates a thick humus layer. As a result, the soil tends to be very rich. Plants and animals in temperate grasslands must cope with less rainfall and colder winter temperatures than those in tropical grasslands. Many plants only grow during the warmer months. Because there is less food in winter, animals are less diverse. They are also less diverse because few temperate grasslands around the world remain in their wild state. Most have been turned into farms and ranches. Smaller animals have survived more than larger animals. Hunting has had a significant effect on larger animals as well.
pages.brief: A close view of grass roots spreading through thick dark soil, holding the ground in place. Beyond, the same temperate grassland lies under hot summer sun, then under deep winter snow, and elsewhere the flat land has been turned into farmland and ranchland.

pages.text: In North America, rabbits, foxes, coyotes, snakes, and small rodents are common. Owls, hawks, and ground-nesting birds also live in these grasslands. Rodents, hares, wolves, lynxes, and foxes live on the European and Asian steppes. Foxes, skunks, bush dogs, and many bird species live on the South American pampas. Some larger animals in these regions live in protected areas. However, leopards and zebras survive in the wild in some parts of the South African veldt. Other veldt species include hyenas, badgers, weasels, crocodiles, and pythons. Spotlight on the North American Tallgrass Prairie Most of North America’s tallgrass prairie has been converted to farmland and ranchland. Today, tallgrass prairie is mostly found in eastern Kansas. A small portion of that region is now protected as a United States national preserve. The tallgrass prairie existed in balance for thousands of years, thanks to a perfect combination of rainfall, fire, and grazing. Bison, the largest grazing species, were almost hunted to extinction in the 1800s. Bison were reintroduced to the preserve in 2009. Other animals include coyotes, badgers, lizards, gopher snakes, greater prairie chickens, and monarch butterflies.
pages.brief: Rabbits, foxes, coyotes, snakes, small rodents and ground-nesting birds move through North American grassland, while owls and hawks circle above. Bison graze on tallgrass prairie in eastern Kansas, with coyotes, badgers, lizards, prairie chickens and monarch butterflies nearby.

pages.text: People and Grasslands Native peoples thrived in grasslands for thousands of years. These included Plains Native Americans, Australian Aboriginals, and the Hadza people in the Serengeti region. The arrival of European settlers had a significant impact on these peoples’ traditional lifestyles. Today, much of the land is used for farming and ranching. Grasslands—particularly temperate grasslands, with their rich soils—are ideal for growing crops and grazing livestock. An estimated 20 percent of the world’s grasslands are used to grow wheat and other cereal crops. Over 40 percent are used for grazing livestock. People could not live without grasslands because of the quantity of food they provide. These activities also provide livelihoods for large numbers of residents. In some grasslands, native people still live much as they did long ago. Here, a traditional Mongolian horseman watches over his horses.
pages.brief: A traditional Mongolian horseman sits on horseback watching over his horses on the open grassland. Around him the flat land stretches far away, some of it used for grazing livestock and some of it planted with cereal crops.

pages.text: Some of the beauty of grasslands lies in how big the sky looks. The Humble Grass Plant On first look, one might not think that grasslands are very interesting. The flat, grassy land has very little variety compared to some other biomes. However, grasslands are special and fascinating for other reasons. Take a moment to think about grasses— humble plants that few people would consider special. They cover vast areas of land, moving gently like a living sea when the wind blows across them. They survive fires, droughts, intense summer heat, and below-freezing temperatures. Grasses provide food for an amazing variety of animals, from insects to bison. They also add nutrients to the soil, so much so that this biome has become the world’s main source of grain. The wonder of grasslands lies in the fact that such humble plants are so important to life’s balance on Earth.
pages.brief: Huge sky arches over a wide flat expanse of grass, making the land look small beneath it. Wind sweeps across the grasses so they ripple and move gently like a living sea, stretching away with almost no other variety in sight.

books.title: Natural Wonders of the World
books.art_why: These natural wonders exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: NORTH AMERICA EUROPE ASIA Grand Canyon Mount AFRICA Everest Paricutín SOUTH AMERICA AUSTRALIA Victoria Falls Great Barrier Reef.
pages.brief: A broad view of Earth’s continents shows North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, South America, and Australia, with the Grand Canyon, Mount Everest, Paricutín, Victoria Falls, and the Great Barrier Reef shown as featured natural wonders on Earth.

pages.text: Grand Canyon Between five and six million years ago, the Colorado River wound through a large plateau (pla-TOE), or an area of raised ground. Over time, the river picked up small pieces of the plateau and carried them as it flowed to the sea. This process is called water erosion (e-RO-zhun). Different kinds of rocks factor into water erosion. Some rocks are soft and break easily. Other rocks are hard and resist breakage. As the Colorado River flowed downstream, it carried pieces of the softer rocks and left behind the harder rocks. Over millions of years, this process carved deep canyons in the rocks. UNITED STATES Grand Canyon Arizona The Colorado River slowly carved the rock of the Grand Canyon into the wondrous structure we see today.
pages.brief: The Colorado River winds through a large raised plateau in the Grand Canyon, carrying small pieces of soft rock downstream while harder rocks remain. The river’s long water erosion has carved the deep canyon in the rock.

pages.text: Colorado River Layers of rocks form the Grand Canyon’s walls. They tell the story of what happened in the area over a period of two billion years. These rocks make up the layers in the canyon walls. The top of the canyon, where most visitors enjoy their first view, is the youngest layer of the canyon. The bottom layer, near the river, is the oldest. Scattered rocks located at the bottom of the canyon date back as long ago as two billion years. The Grand Canyon is a great place to study rocks and the Earth’s history because the rock layers are so easy to see and reach. Geologists often visit the site. One of the first geologists to visit was John Newberry. He traveled to the canyon in 1858. Newberry was the first scientist to record the canyon’s layers, although he wasn’t the first to see them.
pages.brief: Layers of rock form the Grand Canyon’s walls, with the youngest layer at the top where visitors enjoy their first view and the oldest layer near the river below. A geologist studies the visible rock layers, first recorded by John Newberry in 1858.

pages.text: Rattling Reptiles More than forty-seven different kinds of reptiles live in the Grand Canyon. While most of these reptiles are harmless, visitors should keep an eye out for snakes. Although they rarely bite humans, the rattlesnakes are venomous. In the winter, rattlesnakes hibernate in dens. Hundreds of rattlesnakes may live in one den. This is one of the only times rattlers live together. In the spring when the weather warms up, the snakes come out of their dens and go their separate ways. In late summer, females give birth to live babies. The babies only stay in the area where they were born for about seven to ten days. Then they shed their first baby skin, add their first rattle, and move on in search of food. As a rattlesnake grows, it sheds its skin at least once a year. It adds a new rattle to its tail with each shed. A mature may grow to be 2 meters (about 6.5 ft) long. It may weigh up to 6.8 kilograms (15 lb). Rattlers can live to be 25 years old.
pages.brief: A rattlesnake rests near rocks in the Grand Canyon, where more than forty-seven kinds of reptiles live. In winter, rattlesnakes gather in dens; in late summer, a female stays near newborn babies before they shed their first skin and add their first rattle.

pages.text: Native Americans lived in and around the Grand Canyon for more than four thousand years before European explorers arrived. By 1150, most of the original tribes had moved away. Only one group remained. Some of them still live and work in the canyon. Every year, millions of people travel to Grand Canyon National Park to hike, raft, and see this majestic wonder of nature. This waterfall is an example of how water continues to carve the western Grand Canyon.
pages.brief: Native Americans have lived in and around the Grand Canyon for more than four thousand years, and some still live and work there. Visitors hike and raft in Grand Canyon National Park, while a waterfall shows how water continues to carve the western canyon.

pages.text: Paricutín Many of nature’s creations are millions of years old. They began forming long before humans lived on Earth. Other creations have formed in modern times. The Paricutín (pah-ree-koo-TEEN) volcano in Mexico is one such formation. Paricutín began UNITED STATES forming in 1943 in a field. A farmer GULF OF MEXICO MEXICO fissure (FISH-ur), or opening in the Paricutín ground, in his PACIFIC cornfield. The OCEAN crack was about 1.8 meters (6 ft.) long. Soon more fissures appeared. Black smoke came from the holes, and ash piled up on the ground, forming a cone. In about twelve hours, the cone had grown to 10 meters (33 ft.) high. After a day, it had grown to 50 meters (164 ft.). The volcano continued to grow. In just a week, it reached a height of 100 meters (328 ft.). Paricutín volcano erupts in 1943.
pages.brief: A farmer stands in a Mexican cornfield in 1943 as a fissure opens in the ground. Black smoke rises from new cracks, and ash piles up into a cone that grows quickly from 10 meters to 50 meters and then 100 meters in a week.

pages.text: A church steeple is all that can still be seen after ash and lava covered the town of Paricutín. The people of Paricutín hoped that their village would be safe. After a few months, however, the cone had grown so large that lava started to reach their town. The villagers had to evacuate, leaving behind their homes and farms. Over a nine-year period, lava and ash eventually covered the entire village of Paricutín and most of the nearby town of San Juan. In the end all that was left of Paricutín was the church steeple rising out of the black rock as a reminder of nature’s power.
pages.brief: Villagers leave their homes and farms as lava and ash from Paricutín reach their town. After nine years, lava and ash cover Paricutín and most of nearby San Juan, leaving only a church steeple rising out of the black rock.

pages.text: Volcanoes such as Paricutín are called cinder cones. They are the simplest type of volcano. Lava is under pressure inside Earth. Cinder cones form when lava shoots out from a central vent in the ground. As the lava explodes into the air, it cools and breaks into small pieces. They harden and fall as rocks and ash, or cinders, around the central vent to form a cone. Most cinder cones have a bowl-shaped crater at the top. Because Paricutín volcano is young, scientists have been able to observe its growth since it first appeared. Today, the volcano stands about 424 meters (1,391 ft.) tall. It covers 26 square kilometers (10 sq mi.).
pages.brief: A cinder cone volcano forms as lava shoots from a central vent, explodes into the air, cools, and falls as rocks and ash around the vent. Paricutín’s young cone has a bowl-shaped crater and now stands about 424 meters tall.

pages.text: AFRICA Zambia Victoria Falls Zimbabwe INDIAN OCEAN Victoria Falls, like the Grand Canyon, was formed by water. Victoria Falls Victoria Falls is the largest mass of falling water on the planet. The water drops 108 meters (354 ft.) into a deep pool. The people of Zambia call the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya (MOH-see wah TOON-yah) (the smoke that thunders). It’s a perfect name. The thunder has to do with the booming sound created of water crashing over the falls into the pool below. The smoke has to do with the water vapor, or mist, that comes up from the bottom of the falls.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls sends a huge mass of water dropping 108 meters into a deep pool between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Mist rises from the bottom as the water crashes with a booming thunder, and people call the falls Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders.

pages.text: Victoria Falls is located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe in Africa. The falls began forming millions of years ago when a shallow crack in the rock appeared across the path of the Zambezi River. The crack was caused when parts of the earth shifted about 150 million years ago. Over the years, the river flowed over the rock. Eventually, the water wore down the soft rock, forming a cliff over which the river now falls. The pool into which the water falls is called a plunge pool. The Scottish explorer David Livingstone visited the Falls in 1855. He was probably the first person from outside of Africa to see the wondrous formations. He named the Falls after Queen Victoria of England. But many people think that Mosi-oa- Tunya is a more accurate name. Victoria Falls is now part of two national parks, one in Zambia and one in Zimbabwe.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls lies on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, where the Zambezi River flows over a cliff into a plunge pool. The falls formed as water wore down soft rock, and explorer David Livingstone visited in 1855 and named them after Queen Victoria.

pages.text: Victoria Falls Fun Facts • Victoria Falls is actually divided into six waterfalls: Devil’s Cataract, Armchair Falls, Horseshoe Falls, Main Falls, Rainbow Falls, and the Eastern Cataract. • A bridge at the Falls is a popular site for bungee jumping. • During a full moon, the park stays open late so people can enjoy the rainbow that is made when moonlight shines through the water vapor. • People go rafting and kayaking on the water below the Falls. They can even surf on the rapids below.
pages.brief: Victoria Falls is divided into six waterfalls, and a bridge at the falls is used for bungee jumping. During a full moon, people stay late to see a rainbow in the mist, while others raft, kayak, or surf on the rapids below.

pages.text: CHINA Mount Everest NEPAL PACIFIC OCEAN Mount Everest Mount Everest, the tallest mountain in the world, is one of the most amazing sites on Earth. Called “Forehead in the Sky” by the Nepali people, this magnificent landform in the Himalaya mountain range reaches a height of 8,850 meters (29,035 ft.). The snowcapped Himalayas might appear old. In fact, they are quite young for mountains. The mountains were formed millions of years ago when two parts of Earth’s crust hit each other. Over time, the pressure of the two parts rubbing against each other caused the ground to crumble and rise above the sea. Since Mount Everest is a young mountain, its peaks are still sharp and steep. They haven’t yet been smoothed down by endless years of wind, ice, and snow.
pages.brief: Mount Everest rises snowcapped in the Himalaya mountain range between China and Nepal, reaching 8,850 meters and called Forehead in the Sky by the Nepali people. Its sharp, steep peaks formed millions of years ago when two parts of Earth’s crust pressed together and the ground crumbled and rose above the sea.

pages.text: Although Mount Everest is beautiful to look at, it’s a bitterly cold place to be. The average temperature is about −36°C (−33°F) and can drop to −60°C (−76°F). Even in July, the warmest month, the temperature only reaches −19°C (−2°F). It never gets above freezing. As a result, the ice and snow at the top of the mountain never melt. Mount Everest’s summit Storms dump more snow on Mount Everest every year.
pages.brief: The summit of Mount Everest is bitterly cold, with temperatures dropping near −60°C and never rising above freezing even in July. Ice and snow at the top never melt, and storms continue to dump more snow on the mountain every year.

pages.text: The fierce cold on Mount Everest makes it hard for animals and plants to survive. One of the only animals that can live on the mountain is the wild yak. This large animal can weigh more than 454 kilograms (1,000 lb.) and grow up to 1.8 meters Wild yak grazing (6 ft.) tall. The yak can survive in part because its blood can take in more oxygen than the blood of other animals. This adaptation is a lifesaver on Mount Everest, where the air contains little oxygen. The people who first settled in the Himalayas believed that the gods made their homes in the peaks. As a result, no one tried to climb Mount Everest until explorers arrived in the early 1900s. The earliest climbers quickly learned about the harsh conditions on the mountain—freezing temperatures, powerful winds, changing weather, and rough terrain.
pages.brief: A wild yak grazes on Mount Everest, where fierce cold makes life hard. The yak survives with blood that takes in more oxygen. Early Himalayan settlers believed gods lived in the peaks, so climbers did not attempt the mountain until explorers arrived in the early 1900s.
