pages.text: AUSTRALIA Great Barrier Reef A diver explores coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef. Great Barrier Reef The Great Barrier Reef is really a collection of many reefs. It is more than 2,300 kilometers (1,429 mi.) long and is located off the northeast coast of Australia. It is full of amazing sea creatures, from sea slugs and urchins to dolphins, whales, and sharks. A reef is a chain, or range, of rocks that lies at or near the surface of the water. The Great Barrier Reef is a coral reef.
pages.brief: A diver explores coral formations on the Great Barrier Reef off the northeast coast of Australia. The reef is a collection of many reefs more than 2,300 kilometers long, full of sea slugs, urchins, dolphins, whales, sharks, and other sea creatures.

pages.text: Coral reefs are found in all tropical oceans of the world. However, none is as large as the Great Barrier Reef. Most established coral reefs are between five and ten thousand years old. At first glance, the Great Barrier Reef might look like a rock, but it’s not. It’s made from the skeletons of millions of animals called polyps (POL-ips). As the polyps die, new ones grow on top of the old skeletons. The many layers of skeletons form the limestone base of a coral reef. Other kinds of plants and animals also help make up the reef. They include algae, sponges, and shellfish. But the tiny polyp is responsible for most of this natural wonder’s structure. The life and death of coral polyps are responsible for the formation of coral reefs such as the Great Barrier Reef.
pages.brief: Coral polyps build the Great Barrier Reef as new polyps grow on the skeletons of dead ones. Many layers of skeletons form the reef’s limestone base, along with algae, sponges, and shellfish, while the tiny polyp is responsible for most of the reef’s structure.

pages.text: Reefs are made from animals, and they supply food and shelter for other animals. Thousands of species live on the reef. They include 1,625 kinds of fish, more than 30 kinds of marine mammals, 500 kinds of seaweed, and 6 kinds of marine turtles. The reef is also an important breeding area for animals, including birds, sea turtles, and the endangered humpback whale. As one of the most interesting and beautiful places on Earth, the reef is popular with scientists, scuba divers, and tourists. Today, environmentalists are working with these groups to protect the reef so future generations can learn from it and enjoy its beauty. Look, But Don’t Touch! Reefs are alive and full of delicate creatures. Responsible snorkelers and scuba divers should always follow these • When snorkeling, float over the reef. Never stand on it. • Take pictures, not coral souvenirs. • Stock saltwater aquariums with fish that are raised in captivity, not those taken from a coral reef. • Always pack out your plastics and other trash. • Learn more about coral reefs and how you can help protect them.
pages.brief: A snorkeler floats over a reef alive with fish, sea turtles, seaweed, and other marine life. The reef supplies food and shelter and is an important breeding area for birds, sea turtles, and humpback whales, while divers and tourists are asked to protect its delicate creatures.

pages.text: Wonders Everywhere From Arizona to the coast of Australia, natural wonders are everywhere. Whether they were formed millions of years ago or within the span of a lifetime, they are all special. These amazing landforms are some of the largest, highest, and most breathtaking places on Earth. Travelers, scientists, and adventure seekers will continue to visit these special places for generations to come. The Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and Great Barrier Reef are only five of the many wonders that surround us. Other well-known natural wonders include: • The Northern Lights, a light show that brightens up the skies in the Northern Hemisphere • The Barringer Meteorite Crater, a massive hole in the Arizona desert that is almost a mile wide and 174 meters (570 ft.) deep • Ayers Rock, the world’s largest solid rock, rising 862.5 meters (2,830 ft.) above sea level Do you live near an amazing and beautiful natural wonder—an incredible mountain, a majestic river, a mysterious cave? These are all examples of wondrous sites you can visit, learn from, and enjoy every day.
pages.brief: From Arizona to Australia, travelers, scientists, and adventure seekers visit natural wonders such as the Grand Canyon, Paricutín, Mount Everest, Victoria Falls, and the Great Barrier Reef. Other wonders include the Northern Lights, the Barringer Meteorite Crater, and Ayers Rock, the world’s largest solid rock.

books.title: The Magic of Migration
books.art_why: The book shows real animals and real migration journeys that can be photographed.

pages.text: What Is Migration? Migration is the word scientists use to describe these long animal journeys. Many different types of animals migrate. These include birds, bats, whales, sea turtles, large grazers such as caribou and wildebeests, salmon, and some kinds of insects. Pilot whales migrate.
pages.brief: A pod of pilot whales swims through the open ocean, their dark bodies breaking the surface as they travel together. The whales move in a loose group, with calm water and open sky around them, showing one kind of animal that makes a long migration journey.

pages.text: Some animals migrate at the same time every year and follow the same path. Others follow more irregular patterns. Their movement depends on local conditions, such as the weather. There are also some animals that only migrate one way. Locusts migrate when their numbers get so big that they need to find a new feeding ground. They stay in a new field until they need another source of food. Locusts swarm a new feeding ground.
pages.brief: A swarm of locusts flies low over a green field, many insects moving together toward a new feeding ground. Their numbers are thick and crowded, covering the air above the crops as the group settles into a fresh field to find food.

pages.text: Hungry bears eat migrating salmon. Migration is one of the most dangerous journeys an animal can make. Migrating animals face many dangers along the way. These include hungry predators, strong winds, ocean currents, hunters, and fishers. But migrating to find better living conditions is important for survival.
pages.brief: A hungry bear stands at the edge of a river and catches a leaping salmon in its jaws. More salmon swim upstream through the water, while the bear waits for another chance to feed on the migrating fish in the wild river setting.

pages.text: The Search for Food and Water The most common reason why animals migrate is to find food and water. One of the most spectacular examples can be found in Africa. Every year more than a million wildebeests, which are large, grazing animals, migrate because of drought. When hot weather dries up grass and water in one place, wildebeests travel in huge herds to find food and water. As these large mammals travel, hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles join them on their journey. Wildebeest.
pages.brief: A huge herd of wildebeests travels across dry African savanna, their hooves raising dust as they search for grass and water. Zebras and gazelles move alongside them, all journeying together through the hot, dry landscape during a drought.

pages.text: Every year Arctic Terns fly 22,000 miles on these migration routes. They travel from the Arctic, where they nest, all the way to Antarctica, where they spend the winter. Many birds also make amazing journeys to find food. Warblers, flycatchers, storks, pelicans, terns, and all kinds of other birds migrate every year.
pages.brief: Arctic terns fly in a long line over the ocean, their white wings spread as they travel between the Arctic and Antarctica. Other birds, including warblers, flycatchers, storks, pelicans and terns, fly nearby on their yearly journeys to find food.

pages.text: Finding a Place to Nest Another reason animals migrate is to find a place to lay their eggs or to raise their young. Many fish, such as salmon and trout, migrate to spawn, or lay their eggs, in freshwater streams. And some, such as freshwater eels, do the opposite. They leave their freshwater homes and migrate to the open sea to spawn. Female salmon To move from freshwater to salt water, eels have an adaptation in their kidneys. Without it, they wouldn’t survive the switch.
pages.brief: A female salmon swims in a clear freshwater stream, her body close to the gravel as she prepares to lay eggs. Nearby, a freshwater eel moves through the water, ready to leave its freshwater home and travel to the open sea to spawn.

pages.text: How Do They Do It? How do animals find their way when they migrate? Scientists are still learning about this. Some animals, such as salmon, use their sense of smell to find the stream where they were born. Others, such as indigo buntings and other night-flying birds, use the stars to guide their way. Day-flying birds use the sun. They also watch for special landmarks, such as coastlines and mountains, to stay on course. Indigo Bunting.
pages.brief: An indigo bunting flies through the night sky beneath a spread of stars. Below, a coastline and mountains stretch across the dark landscape, giving the small bird landmarks as it follows the stars and stays on course during migration.

pages.text: Scientists are still exploring other ways that animals navigate. They think some animals are able to sense Earth’s magnetic pull to guide them. Earth’s magnetic field acts like a giant magnet inside the Earth. Magnetic Brains Think of Earth as a giant magnet. Scientists think that many species of birds navigate by sensing Earth’s magnetic north and south poles. They have found tiny bits of a magnetic substance, magnetite, in some birds’ brains. They think these tiny bits are pulled by Earth’s poles, helping guide birds as they migrate.
pages.brief: A bird flies above open country, its small body seen clearly against the sky. Scientists think birds can sense Earth’s magnetic pull, and tiny bits of magnetite in some birds’ brains may help guide them as they travel along migration routes.

pages.text: Insects, Whales, and Turtles One of the most interesting yearly migrations is that of monarch butterflies. These bright orange and black butterflies travel from the northern and eastern parts of North America. They go to Mexico and southern parts of the United States. They spend the winter on certain trees in the mountains. In the spring, the adults return north. They breed along the way. The adults die after the females lay eggs. The eggs grow into young butterflies that complete the journey back home. Monarch butterflies.
pages.brief: Monarch butterflies with bright orange and black wings rest on trees in the mountains of Mexico and the southern United States. Others fly north through the spring, breeding along the way, while young butterflies continue the journey back home.

pages.text: Many marine creatures migrate. These include huge humpback whales, lobsters, sharks, sea turtles, and tuna. Some, such as many of the sea turtles, follow ocean currents to get from one part of the ocean to another. But scientists still don’t know how these animals find exactly the right beach to lay their eggs. They must find the same one they hatched on years before. Main: Baby loggerhead turtles head out to sea after hatching on the same beach where their parents were born. Inset: Adult loggerhead.
pages.brief: Baby loggerhead turtles scramble across sand toward the sea after hatching on the same beach where their parents were born. Nearby, an adult loggerhead swims in the ocean, while other marine creatures such as humpback whales, lobsters, sharks, sea turtles and tuna move through the water.

pages.text: Migration paths Every year, millions of animals move far away to find food, water, better weather, or a place to nest or raise their young. Some travel alone. Others travel in huge flocks or herds. But no matter how they travel, they all take the magical journey of migration.
pages.brief: Many animals travel together across a wide landscape: birds fly in huge flocks, herds of grazers move over land, and sea creatures swim through the ocean. Some travel alone, while others stay in groups, all making long journeys to find food, water, better weather or a place to nest.
